text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) a member of the U.S. Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) Committee, alongside Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.), Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), Tim Kaine (D-Va.), Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) sent a letter to U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. demanding he explain why the Trump administration awarded a no-bid contract to a Trump-aligned law firm with no apparent immigration law experience, allowing them to represent unaccompanied children who are in the care and custody of the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR).

“Given the political connections between the firm’s senior leadership and the Trump administration, we have concerns about why you sidestepped the competitive bidding process to select this firm to provide legal services for children who are in ORR care and custody, and demand transparency into whether all federal procurement processes were followed,” the senators wrote. “Children deserve competent representation by attorneys who practice at the intersection of child welfare and federal immigration law, but Americans also deserve to know why their federal dollars are being doled out to Trump’s friends and allies.”

The Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), through ORR, has an obligation to ensure that unaccompanied children are provided competent legal aid as they navigate the immigration process. Despite this, Secretary Kennedy has cut legal service funding for 26,000 unaccompanied children, shifting funding to the Trump-aligned Burke Law Group, despite the firm’s lack of experience protecting the rights of immigrant children.

“The firm appears to have little relevant experience with the legal and practical challenges that children face, raising serious concerns about the firm’s ability to provide not just representation but adequate, zealous representation,” the senators added. “Within hours of the notice in the Federal Register, the firm appears to have updated their website to include content about immigrant youth that didn’t exist on the website the previous day. At best, this is concerning, and at worst, it is a part of a coordinated scheme to paper over the firm’s lack of experience.”

Burke Law Group’s inexperience in the area of the law they have been contracted to perform could result in serious harm for the nearly 2,000 children in ORR’s care. The firm itself employs 26 people in total, adding an additional concern about the firm’s capacity to provide adequate legal representation to innocent children, let alone its competency to do so. Instead, the only clear outcome of this contracting award is that another Trump-aligned business will receive millions from the Trump administration.

In the letter, the senators demanded that Secretary Kennedy provide transparency as to why the Burke Law Group received this contract and details about the firm’s plans to provide legal assistance to unaccompanied children.

title: Trump administration sues CT over in-state tuition for undocumented students
authors: Tran Chau, Nolan Page, Nancy Lavin, Christopher Shea, Alexander Castro
description:
The U.S. Department of Justice on Monday filed a lawsuit against Connecticut over state laws that provide in-state tuition and financial assistance to immigrant students lacking permanent legal status.
“Connecticut offers in-state tuition and financial aid to all eligible Connecticut students because all kids deserve the opportunity to learn, to advance, and to achieve their dreams.
Connecticut first provided in-state tuition benefits to undocumented students under the 2011 state law, which required them to have attended high school in Connecticut for four years and earned a diploma.
In 2018, Connecticut passed another law allowing students without permanent legal status to apply for and receive institutional aid at public colleges and universities.
The lawsuit also challenges other state laws involving financial aid at Connecticut State Community College, Roberta B. Willis need-based grants, and the state’s student loan reimbursement program.
text:
This article first appeared on CT Mirror and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.

The U.S. Department of Justice on Monday filed a lawsuit against Connecticut over state laws that provide in-state tuition and financial assistance to immigrant students lacking permanent legal status.

In its complaint, the DOJ argued that Connecticut’s laws unfairly give benefits such as lower tuition and scholarships to students without legal status while denying the same benefits to U.S. citizens who live outside the state. The DOJ also argued that the laws violate federal statutes and encourage illegal immigration to the U.S.

“This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country.”

In response to the lawsuit, Connecticut Attorney General William Tong, who voted for the in-state tuition law in 2011 as a state legislator, said he would defend the state’s policies.

“Note to Trump — stay out of Connecticut,” Tong said in a statement. “Connecticut offers in-state tuition and financial aid to all eligible Connecticut students because all kids deserve the opportunity to learn, to advance, and to achieve their dreams. Donald Trump doesn’t run UConn or any of our state colleges, and we’re not about to let him start.”

Gov. Lamont also defended the state’s policies, saying in a statement, “kids who grow up in Connecticut and graduate from Connecticut public schools should be able to afford to go to college here, including those who have applied for legal status.”

“We are making Connecticut the land of opportunity and education, and we will not accept his attempts to turn back the clock on progress,” Lamont said.

Connecticut first provided in-state tuition benefits to undocumented students under the 2011 state law, which required them to have attended high school in Connecticut for four years and earned a diploma. The state later reduced the high school attendance requirement to two years in 2015.

In 2018, Connecticut passed another law allowing students without permanent legal status to apply for and receive institutional aid at public colleges and universities.

The lawsuit also challenges other state laws involving financial aid at Connecticut State Community College, Roberta B. Willis need-based grants, and the state’s student loan reimbursement program.

The Trump administration has filed similar lawsuits challenging higher-education benefits in 16 other states.

title: Trump's Arresting State | Austin Sarat | Verdict | Legal Analysis and Commentary from Justia
description:
In his administration, arrest threats are now a regular part of the policy process.
That changed last July when the Justice Department began to consider arrest to advance the president’s election security agenda.
Her letter cataloged various federal criminal statutes under which election officials might be arrested and prosecuted.
As a prelude, the DHS Secretary repeated Trump’s allegations about noncitizen voting, praised states that have already complied with the administration’s directives, and denounced activist judges.
Welcome to Trump’s arresting state.
text:
Remember “Lock her up,” Donald Trump’s refrain in his 2016 campaign against Hillary Clinton. Remember the president’s January 2, 2021, phone call to Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, in which he suggested that Raffensperger was committing a criminal offense by refusing to “find” thousands of votes for Trump.

The threats to arrest Clinton began before Trump had any control over the machinery of justice. The call with Raffensperger came just days before Trump was leaving office.

But since his return to the Oval Office, the president and his administration have made threats of arrest a regular part of their repertoire. And not just of political opponents.

He has used them as a tool to try to coerce public officials into cooperating with his agenda. In his administration, arrest threats are now a regular part of the policy process.

We saw another example of that on Friday, July 17, when Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin followed up the president’s White House address on election security by threatening to jail local election officials who don’t help implement the president’s plan to nationalize control of elections and eliminate people from the voter rolls.

Mullin used a press conference to say: “If the election officials, once we gave them the information they need to secure their elections, and they chose not to, then those individuals can also be held accountable by fines, by penalties and even, depending on how far it goes, prison time.”

The Constitution gives the authority to run and control elections to the states, and the president cannot abide that. As is typical in autocratic regimes, rival centers of power must be brought to heel, whether by persuasion or coercion.

We may be tempted to write off the administration’s threats of arrest as tools of policy implementation, but before we do, we should remember M. Gessen’s rules for surviving autocracy. Rule #1: “Believe the autocrat. He means what he says.”

Just ask former Milwaukee County Circuit Court judge Hannah Dugan, who was arrested in April 2025 on charges that she interfered with an arrest by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. She was later convicted and resigned from the bench.

Her lawyers got it right when, as PBS reports, “they argued that the Donald Trump administration sought to ‘crush’ Dugan in an effort to ensure judicial compliance with the ICE strategy of targeting immigrants as they showed up for court hearings.”

In May 2025, Newark Mayor Ras Baraka and Rep. LaMonica McIver were arrested at a protest at an ICE detention center as they tried to obtain access to inspect conditions at the facility. One month later, New York City Comptroller Brad Lander was arrested by federal agents outside federal immigration court for “allegedly assaulting law enforcement and impeding a federal officer while escorting a defendant out of immigration court.”

“Being threatened by the prospect of heavy fines or incarceration, and being forced to needlessly defend oneself in court,” United to Protect Democracy explains, “can be a form of harassment in itself. Legal proceedings are emotionally taxing, time-consuming, stressful for families, and expensive.”

Or as the New Yorker puts it, “The Administration’s political calculus seems aimed at punishing and intimidating Democrats who challenge the President’s agenda.” However, in the cases of Dugan, Lander, Baraka, and McIver, it could be argued that their arrests were unrelated to the duties of their offices.

They were arrested for protesting administration policies. That would be bad enough.

But Mullin upped the ante, threatening public officials not for protesting but for doing their jobs in ways that advance the president’s agenda. His threat did not just come out of the blue.

Last year, the president targeted officials in so-called Sanctuary Jurisdictions and used an Executive Order to accuse them of engaging in “a lawless insurrection against the supremacy of Federal law and the Federal Government’s obligation to defend the territorial sovereignty of the United States.” He noted that “such nullification efforts often violate Federal criminal laws.”

The president directed “the Attorney General and the Secretary of Homeland Security…[to] pursue all necessary legal remedies and enforcement measures to end these violations and bring such jurisdictions into compliance with the laws of the United States.”

But at that time, the administration was using arrest threats primarily in the context of its immigration crackdown.

That changed last July when the Justice Department began to consider arrest to advance the president’s election security agenda. At the time, the New York Times observed that “such a path could significantly raise the stakes for federal investigations of state or county officials, thrusting the Justice Department and the threat of criminalization into the election system in a way that has never been done before.”

The Times calls that effort “a novel and aggressive way to try to find chargeable crimes in a technically arcane topic, but one that is increasingly a political flashpoint as the president and his supporters have made unsubstantiated claims about election data manipulation.”

In addition, the FBI website’s page about Election Crimes calls attention to the fact that “Election crimes become federal cases when…the crime involves an election official abusing his duties.” The example it offers, “let[ting] unqualified voters cast ballots.”

The preparatory work by the FBI, the Justice Department, and the Department of Homeland Security came to fruition on July 7 when election officials in all fifty states received letters from Harmeet K. Dhillon, the Assistant Attorney General in charge of the Civil Rights Division. The letters warned them that they could be prosecuted for allowing noncitizens to remain on their lists of eligible voters.

Dhillon was hardly subtle. Her letter cataloged various federal criminal statutes under which election officials might be arrested and prosecuted.

It concluded by stating that “any election officer, including the chief election officer of the state, who knowingly retains noncitizens on the state’s SVRL or facilitates noncitizens in receiving and casting ballots could be subject to criminal liability” and “encourag[ing]” state officials to “contact us to discuss what steps your state should take to maintain clean voter lists as required by law.”

The “invitation,” backed by an ominous warning about criminal liability, is just the latest in a series of efforts by the administration to allow the federal government to meddle in election administration and to get states to comply with its directives.

Because the courts have struck down most of those efforts, the administration is trying another route.

During Mullin’s news conference, he outlined that route. As a prelude, the DHS Secretary repeated Trump’s allegations about noncitizen voting, praised states that have already complied with the administration’s directives, and denounced activist judges.

When he was done, he left little to the imagination, promising that his department would bring “maximum pressure” to make sure that officials fall in line. Welcome to Trump’s arresting state.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers may soon be outfitted with gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks intended to gain compliance from combative individuals.

ICE plans to spend between $10 million and $20 million to purchase "conductive distraction and de-escalation devices" for officers and agents by March, according to a notice published Monday by the Department of Homeland Security.

The devices are known as the G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, and are manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC of Lexington, Kentucky. They have been used in recent years by some jails and police departments.

The notice said the solicitation for a no-bid contract could be published as early as Friday.

CBS News has reached out to DHS and Compliant Technologies for comment.

DHS told The Associated Press on Tuesday that it was working on a response to an inquiry and offered no immediate comment. Jeff Niklaus, the founder and CEO of Compliant Technologies, told the AP: "Unfortunately, we are unable to speak on this subject."

Civil rights advocates — including from the American Civil Liberties Union — expressed alarm at the plan, saying ICE officers already face criticism for their use of force during President Trump's immigration crackdown.

Compliant Technologies says the devices function as a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate their electrical mode. The gloves must be applied directly to someone's skin to deliver a pain stimulus that typically helps an officer gain compliance within seconds, according to the company.

"It's immediate and sharp, and it will distract you. I call it like a bee sting," John Peters, president of the Institute for the Prevention of In-Custody Deaths, who is studying how the device has been used, told The AP. "If the officer is getting any type of resistance from the person, this is certainly an effective tool."

Peters said he believed ICE's planned purchase would likely be the largest from the company to date. He said he could envision ICE officers using the gloves to help remove uncooperative subjects from cars and houses and in and out of detention facilities.

"For smaller officers or weaker officers or older officers, I think it has a great advantage" because it can produce faster takedowns and shorten confrontations, he said.

The manufacturer warns the device should not be used as punishment, against people merely exhibiting "verbal defiance or belligerence" or on high-risk populations such as children, pregnant women or elderly or disabled people.

Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the ACLU, told The AP the public should have no confidence that ICE officers will use the devices appropriately. She questioned why the devices would be necessary for civil immigration enforcement and noted those getting shocked might have no advance warning.

"ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do," she said. "Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public."

Supporters say the devices are generally used in specific jail and transport situations, rather than broadly to patrol on the streets. They have been used to subdue violent suspects who are refusing to get into squad cars and inmates who are harming themselves and threatening officers, according to Compliant Technologies.

Peters said he expected the devices to be misused by a small number of employees, as with other policing technologies, but he said they are unlikely to cause injuries. He said it would be important for ICE to have robust policies and training in place.

To use the device, officers must complete a course and be recertified every two years, the manufacturer says.

The planned purchases come as ICE expands its crackdown on people accused of being in the U.S. illegally, amid pressure from the White House to arrest 2,000 people per day.

ICE has drawn scrutiny for its tactics during its arrest surge — including attempted vehicle stops in Maine and Texas last month that ended with ICE agents fatally shooting two immigrants.

text:
The articles in this issue of The Judges’ Journal reflect a moment of reckoning for the immigration system in the United States of America.

The starting point is jus soli, the principle that birth within the United States confers American citizenship. Executive Order 14160 is a departure from jus soli that would render a large cohort of American-born children stateless. Their citizenship would be conditioned or jeopardized because of their parents’ immigration status. In “Born in the U.S.A. and Executive Order 14160: A Challenge to Birthright Citizenship,” retired Immigration Law Judge Joan Churchill traces the historical and constitutional foundations of jus soli. Churchill’s analysis of Executive Order 14160 and oral arguments in Barbara v. Trump situates the current birthright citizenship controversy within the common law tradition inherited from England through the 1898 landmark decision in United States v. Wong Kim Ark. Churchill demonstrates the government’s specious argument that “subject to the jurisdiction thereof” in the 14th Amendment refers to political allegiance and is nothing other than a reiteration of positions the Wong majority explicitly rejected a century ago as conflicting with the plain meaning of “jurisdiction,” which is understood in every other context in American jurisprudence to refer to legal authority.

The next three articles pivot from the question of who is a citizen to how those who are not citizens are to be adjudicated in American immigration administrative tribunals.

Jeremiah Johnson served eight years as an immigration judge before his November 2025 termination without explanation. In “When Soft Pressure Hardens: Bureaucratic Control over Independent Judicial Decision-Making Within the Executive Branch,” Johnson traces the transformation of cultural and bureaucratic forces shaping immigration adjudication. He names these forces “soft pressure,” which are turning into something harder and coercive. Johnson chronicles an administrative adjudicatory structure in which immigration law judges ultimately answer, albeit through multiple intervening bureaucratic layers, to the president of the United States. He describes how 51 policy memoranda in a single year, in combination with the termination of more than 100 immigration law judges without stated cause, converted an already structurally compromised administrative adjudicatory system into one in which independence is not merely imperfect but genuinely undermined. Johnson’s account is a firsthand exposition of how “power over a man’s subsistence amounts to a power over his will,” as Alexander Hamilton observed 200 years ago.

In “The Bankruptcy Court Blueprint for an Independent Immigration Judiciary,” Zachary R. Petrarca and Bryan K. Alfred ask the question Johnson’s experience brings to the fore. If a structural defect in the immigration administrative adjudicatory system is serious, what should be done about it? Executive control over ILJs exercising quasi-judicial authority is the constitutional issue confronting the immigration administrative judiciary. It is the same issue the Supreme Court addressed in 1982 in Northern Pipeline Construction Co. v. Marathon Pipe Line Co., when it held Congress unconstitutionally vested judicial power in bankruptcy courts lacking structural independence. In 1984, Congress remedied that problem by reconstituting bankruptcy courts as Article I tribunals, vested appointment authority in the court of appeals, and insulated bankruptcy judges from executive removal by providing term-limit protections. Petrarca and Alfred maintain similar remediation should occur for the immigration administrative adjudicatory system and note the proposal of the Rule of Law Act of 2026.

Karen T. Grisez is an experienced practitioner of immigration litigation. In contrast to Petrarca and Alfred’s structural focus, Grisez takes a ground-level approach in “The Due Process Crisis in U.S. Immigration Courts: Why the Whole Is Now Less Than the Sum of Its Parts.” Grisez catalogs how the absence of the right to appointed counsel, inadequate language access, compressed hearing times, failure to provide required notices, fee increases, and shortened deadlines, among other things, in the aggregate, perpetuate an immigration system in which meaningful administrative adjudication for too many respondents is not a reality.

The structural and enforcement characteristics of immigration administrative adjudication examined in the three articles discussed above are consequential even for proceedings ostensibly not involving immigration. Professor Amelia S. McGowan of the University of Arkansas School of Law, in “The Shadow of Status: Judicial Strategies for Identifying and Mitigating Immigration-Related Domestic Violence,” examines how abusers wield power and control over their victims by weaponizing their victims’ immigration status in custody hearings, protective order proceedings, divorce proceedings, and criminal matters. When an immigrant survivor of abuse reasonably fears appearing in court may result in removal, the court no longer functions as a site for redress or remediation. McGowan offers practical guidance to state and federal jurists to ensure their courtrooms remain “a neutral forum that determines legal outcomes by the merits of the case rather than the exploitation of a party’s status.”

In the ethics column, Marla N. Greenstein’s “Judicial Ethics and Immigration Issues in Today’s Courts” directly engages the issue’s theme. Greenstein examines ethical dilemmas facing judges who encounter immigration enforcement activities in their own courthouses. Drawing on recent disciplinary and criminal proceedings against judges who intervened in immigration enforcement, Greenstein urges courts to adopt advance, clear policies governing law enforcement activities in their facilities that promote judicial integrity and independence while preserving the courthouse as safe forum for litigants.

Who is an American citizen? What are acceptable jurisprudential principles for adjudicating the status of those seeking belonging? How can we preserve and protect the courts’ integrity from weaponization against immigrants seeking redress in certain judicial proceedings? These queries animate the articles in this issue.

This issue additionally includes Judge Herbert B. Dixon Jr.’s regular contribution to the technology column. In “How to Responsibly Implement AI While Waiting on AI Regulations,” Judge Dixon surveys federal and state approaches to the regulation of artificial intelligence. The regulatory landscape is fractured. Judge Dixon, therefore, directs our attention to the Council on Criminal Justice’s Task Force on Artificial Intelligence, which is developing evidence-based standards for guidance.

This issue also contains a profile titled “Black Belt, Servant Leader, Esq.: The Extraordinary Legal Career and Community Service of Attorney Daniel F. Gourash.” The profile sketches Gourash’s decades of complex litigation practice, sustained leadership in the American Bar Association, mastery of tae kwon do, and ministry serving families in Cleveland, Ohio.

text:
The Center for American Progress stood behind a recent report that the Trump administration’s National Guard deployments failed to reduce violent crime, after the president threatened to sue the liberal think tank.

In a statement released Tuesday, the organization accused President Donald Trump of “lashing out” in an attempt to “silence independent research, waste taxpayer money on his failed agenda, and distract from the reality that his policies are hurting the American people.”

“When politicians can’t defend their failed policies with facts, they resort to intimidation,” said Neera Tanden , a former senior Biden White House official who is now the president and CEO of the center. “We’re going to keep delivering the data, exposing the president’s failed leadership, and fighting on behalf of the American people. We will not be intimidated, and we will not back down.”

The Center for American Progress’ July report, authored by the think tank’s associate director of public safety, Chandler Hall , stated that the historic drop in violent crime across the nation began before Trump took office — and well before the president deployed the National Guard to the nation’s capital.

Trump announced one year ago Tuesday that he was declaring a public safety emergency in D.C., despite crime in Washington hitting a 30-year low in 2024. That deployment followed Trump ’s decision to call nearly 5,000 National Guard troops to Los Angeles to tamp down on civil unrest in response to federal immigration raids.

The president’s deployments in other American cities faced stiff legal resistance. But the president has unique powers in D.C., and the deployment is expected to continue through the end of Trump ’s term in 2029.

Hall on Monday appeared on C-SPAN to discuss CAP’s findings and appeared to express opposition to the continued deployment of National Guard troops, which the report predicted could cost American taxpayers more than $1.7 billion if extended through the rest of the year.

“I think it’s unfortunate that the president is continuing to still choose to boast that these deployments, these very costly interventions, are showing any results to try to convince voters that they should sign on for more of these kind of interventions in federal overreach, when, again, there’s no proof that they have any effect,” Hall said on C-SPAN.

Trump on Monday called the report “another Radical Left SCAM” as he threatened to sue the organization.

“This will be met with a lawsuit, which is being drawn now,” Trump wrote in his post. “I am also strongly considering adding some of the contributors to this Fake Organization. Crime is way down since I took Office, and they know it. Liars, at this level, must be held accountable!”

text:
Jessica Watts | August 11, 2026, 7:36 pm

Illinois is continuing its tense relationship with the federal government through an ongoing series of legal battles.

Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul joined “Chicago Tonight” to provide an update on pending litigation against the Trump administration just months before election season. Raoul is seeking reelection for a third term this November.

On suing over imposed tariffs:

Illinois recently filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration over new tariffs imposed last month. The tariffs range from 10% to 12.5% on imports from 60 countries. President Donald Trump said these tariffs aim to enforce bans on goods produced by unchecked forced labor.

This is the third time the state has sued over imposed tariffs since Trump took office last year.

“He does not have the power to impose these tariffs,” Raoul said. “We’ve gone through this twice before. … He’s still violating the law in how he does this and thereby raising prices on American consumers, American businesses, at the worst time to be doing so. At a time when this war that he’s entered into unnecessarily has already risen prices on American consumers and businesses.”

On protecting Illinois voter data:

A federal court recently ruled that the U.S. Department Of Justice cannot demand unredacted voters registration lists from states. Raoul said this decision protects Illinois voters’ sensitive personal information.

“The president seems to have a disregard for the Constitution and the privacy of individuals at that,” Raoul said. “And so, there’s a dual problem. This is one of many actions that we’ve taken to protect the privacy of Americans, but this is also one of many actions we’ve taken to protect the Constitution.”

On proposed funding caps for housing projects to address homelessness:

Illinois is also suing the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development over an attempt to cap funding for permanent housing projects to address homelessness in Illinois. Raoul said HUD’s decision could cause thousands of Illinoisans to lose their homes.

“The administration is exceeding its authority to try to impose these caps at the worst time to be doing so, when people are indeed struggling with homelessness and housing and security,” Raoul said. “And so, the heartlessness of this is one thing, but the illegality is the other thing.”

On Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitian migrants:

Raoul has publicly urged Congress to restore Temporary Protected Status for Haitian migrants in the United States. The son of Haitian immigrants, Raoul said the issue is deeply personal.

“I was disappointed in the Supreme Court’s decision because it disregarded the fact that there’s a mandate that the Secretary of Homeland Security consult with the State Department before making any such decision to terminate TPS,” Raoul said. “Had they done so, they would realize that the State Department does not allow commercial flights to fly to Port-au-Prince, Haiti, because of conditions in Haiti. There’s gang violence, there’s a lack of medical services. This is all spelled out on the State Department’s website as to what the conditions are in Haiti. So if there were ever a situation where TPS should be continued, it obviously exists with regard to Haitians.”

On whether Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch should resign:

Earlier this month, Welch publicly apologized for his handling of sexual harassment alligations against former state Rep. Harry Benton. Welch has since faced calls for resignation from several state lawmakers and other organizations.

“We’re coming up on the beginning of another General Assembly and the members of the House of Representatives will have the ability to assess the situation, and the IG’s report has been made public,” Raoul said. “Our role was to review and to make recommendations on any redactions, but that was our sole role. I think the Democratic process should make the determination of who’s speaker and who’s Senate president.”

text:
A New Jersey mother said she learned her son, who was being held in ICE custody, was dead only after a Newark hospital called to identify his body.

Two Bronx representatives say they're now working together to ensure that never happens to another family. On Thursday, Reps. Ritchie Torres and George Latimer plan to introduce the Families Deserve to Know Act.

The representatives drafted the legislation after New Jersey father Edwin Cornejo died on Aug. 1, approximately six weeks after he was taken into ICE custody. Prior to his detention at Newark's Delaney Hall, Cornejo's relatives said he had been living in the United States for two decades, where he worked multiple jobs to support his family.

His mother, María Cornejo, told Spectrum Noticias there is a "wound in [her] heart that will never heal."

If passed, the Families Deserve to Know Act, first shared exclusively with Spectrum News, would require ICE to record detainees' emergency contacts and notify them of deaths and serious illnesses within 12 hours.

"I think the rightness of it is so obvious it almost requires no explanation. Families have a right to know when their loved ones die, especially in the custody of the government," said Torres.

A document obtained by Spectrum News shows current ICE policy is to notify relevant parties of deaths "to the extent possible."

"It's not a law. It's simply a requirement that exists on paper, but not in practice. And we know from experience that ICE and the Trump administration at large has no regard for the rules," said Torres.

Cornejo, 39, is one of three detainees to die in or after being held at Delaney Hall since it reopened last year. His family says he was a diabetic with high blood pressure and believe he was fatally deprived of appropriate medical care while in detention.

"There is only one doctor for nearly 900 detainees. The staffing shortage is so extreme that it effectively deprives the detainees of their right to health care," stated Torres.

The 1,000-bed privately operated ICE contracted facility has been the site and subject of several demonstrations, including a Tuesday press conference where House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries promised detainees families' that, "'We will get this situation turned around, and we will make sure that there's justice for your loved ones who have been killed or died in custody."

ICE issued a statement on Aug. 3, two days after Cornejo's death. The release stated that the agency notified his family and other appropriate parties of his death.

It also claimed that proper medical care was provided. Spectrum News contacted the agency for clarification, and as of Tuesday evening, ICE had not responded.

title: Deported in the Dark: The Murky State of Media Access to America's Most Dysfunctional Courts
description:
This article will examine the law of public access to immigration courts and what journalists need to know about covering these unique proceedings.
Immigration courts have not typically been a focus of much mainstream media attention, so—relative to more traditional trial and appellate courts—journalists and judges are, predictably, unfamiliar with each other’s practices.
Immigration proceedings are considered civil and not criminal, so the Supreme Court’s open-courts jurisprudence does not directly come into play.
As with immigration court hearings, oral arguments before the BIA are presumed by regulation to be open to the public.
While immigration courts have obtained renewed prominence since Trump retook the presidency, disputes over access are not new.
text:
Public scrutiny of immigration courts has never been more essential. Even before the surge in new cases associated with the second Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, the Associated Press characterized the daily workings of these quasi-judicial bodies as “nonstop chaos.” Veterans of the system describe “an atmosphere of paranoia and fear” among the overworked judges who have survived being purged, tasked with digging their way out of a backlog of more than three million overdue cases.

This article will examine the law of public access to immigration courts and what journalists need to know about covering these unique proceedings. It will describe both the (limited) right to attend and cover hearings, as well as the (limited) right to obtain records pertinent to immigration disputes. As will be shown, the broad right of access to which journalists have become accustomed when covering traditional judicial proceedings applies with diminished force—and, sometimes, not at all—when the proceeding takes place within the shadowy realm of the immigration system.

The Life Cycle of a Removal Case

Media interest in immigration proceedings has spiked during the second Trump administration, as the president has set aggressive deportation goals to expedite removing noncitizens from the country and put record numbers of detainees into immigration detention centers. The prominence of cases such as that of Kilmer Abrego Garcia in Maryland and Mario Guevara in Georgia has intensified the spotlight on immigration courts, at a time when judges are facing overwhelming caseloads and, in some instances, threats to their continued employment.

Immigration courts have not typically been a focus of much mainstream media attention, so—relative to more traditional trial and appellate courts—journalists and judges are, predictably, unfamiliar with each other’s practices. It is valuable for journalists to learn the vocabulary and cadence of these untraditional tribunals to inform their coverage.

People are summoned to appear in immigration court by way of a Notice to Appear issued by the Department of Homeland Security when they are facing removal from the United States as noncitizens who have violated some provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act, such as overstaying a visa. The proceedings begin with a “master calendar” hearing, a relatively short proceeding that is sometimes held by phone or videoconference. At the master calendar hearing, the immigrant (or counsel) will be given an opportunity to respond to the allegations of eligibility for removal, identify any relief from removal being sought, and—if that relief is denied—name a country to which the immigrant would prefer to be sent. The relief available to an immigrant can include asylum—the right to remain in the United States indefinitely, based on a well-founded fear of persecution in one’s home country—or withholding of removal, a half-measure of relief that confers fewer citizenship-like benefits.

Assuming that the immigrant elects to fight removal, the case is sent to an individual merits hearing that is trial-like but with the somewhat relaxed rules associated with administrative hearings. At the hearing, an immigrant seeking asylum must present evidence establishing a history of suffering persecution, or well-founded fear of future persecution, in their home country based on membership in a protected class. Unlike in criminal court, there is neither a constitutionally guaranteed right to counsel nor an appointed public defender for indigent parties, so it is common for immigrants to represent themselves. During December 2025, fewer than 30 percent of immigrants had an attorney present when they were ordered to be removed from the country, according to a report from Syracuse University’s Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, which analyzes government immigration data. A decision on removal may be announced at the hearing or in a subsequent written opinion.

Immigration judges are not Article III presidential appointees but are administrative judges residing within the executive rather than the judicial branch. Their rulings are appealable first to a Department of Justice body, the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA), which is housed in the DOJ’s Executive Office for Immigration Review. Decisions of the board are appealable directly to the federal circuit court. Board proceedings typically take place on paper, meaning there is little opportunity for journalists to cover appeal hearings.

A Constitutional Right of Access?

In a series of landmark cases, the Supreme Court has recognized a constitutionally grounded right of the press and public to attend all critical stages of criminal trials, including jury selection and pretrial motion hearings. In its landmark Richmond Newspapers case, the Court developed what has come to be known as the “experience and logic” test, inquiring (1) whether the type of proceeding historically has been accessible to the public and (2) whether public attendance will contribute beneficially to the conduct of the proceeding. The justices have recognized the salutary effects of open court proceedings, both to ensure fairness to the person facing trial and to assure the public that the law is being applied legitimately. Though the Court has yet to deal squarely with a case involving civil proceedings, most lower courts agree that the constitutional right of access extends to civil trials as well. Although the right of access is not absolute and can be overridden by countervailing concerns—chiefly, the right of a criminal defendant to obtain a fair trial—closure is strongly disfavored and permitted only when supported by detailed findings indicating that lesser curative measures would not suffice.

Immigration proceedings are considered civil and not criminal, so the Supreme Court’s open-courts jurisprudence does not directly come into play. Absent guidance from the justices, the two circuits to directly confront a claim of a First Amendment right to cover immigration court hearings have reached diverging results.

In Detroit Free Press v. Ashcroft, decided in August 2002, the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals considered whether newspaper plaintiffs had a constitutional right to access deportation proceedings. This question of access arose in the wake of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and the subsequent issuance of “the Creppy directive” by Chief Immigration Judge Michael Creppy, mandating the closure of all immigration proceedings associated with “special interest” cases (cases considered to be high-security). Through a multipart analysis invoking principles of constitutional law, immigration law, and administrative law, the court concluded that there is a First Amendment right of access to deportation proceedings. The court disagreed with the government’s position asserting plenary authority over non-substantive immigration laws, including the Creppy directive: “It would be ironic, indeed, to allow the Government’s assertion of plenary power to transform the First Amendment from the great instrument of open democracy to a safe harbor from public scrutiny.” Instead, the court chose to extend judicial review to the question of access to deportation hearings as non-substantive proceedings that implicate constitutional rights.

Having determined it had the discretion to review decisions made under the Creppy directive, the Sixth Circuit then considered which test should apply to determine whether a right of access exists, landing on the test employed by the Supreme Court in Richmond Newspapers because of the uniquely quasi-judicial and adversarial nature of deportation proceedings as opposed to other administrative proceedings. Under the two-part Richmond Newspapers test, evaluating “experience and logic,” the court pointed to a history of presumptive access to deportation proceedings in support of experience and the value of openness as a check on government power and means of accountability to satisfy the logic prong.

Upon determining there is a First Amendment right of access to deportation proceedings, the court then evaluated whether the Creppy directive passed strict scrutiny analysis. While the court found the government had articulated compelling interests supporting the Creppy directive, such as national security concerns, it determined the directive was not narrowly tailored because the government failed to explain why the closure of deportation proceedings could not be made on a case-by-case basis instead. The court ultimately affirmed the lower court’s decision to issue a preliminary injunction to open deportation proceedings to the public and press.

Weeks later in October 2002, the Third Circuit Court of Appeals reached a strikingly different conclusion in a case with near identical facts and questions of law, in which it reviewed the Creppy directive and the question of whether a First Amendment right of access to deportation proceedings exists. The Third Circuit’s analysis and conclusions overlapped with the Sixth Circuit’s in one crucial regard—the application of the Richmond Newspapers test to government proceedings including deportation hearings—but differed in virtually every other way.

The Third Circuit determined that the experience prong of the test was not satisfied, detailing a history of opinions from legislators and agencies that evidenced a history of closure in government proceedings broadly and administrative proceedings in particular. The court was also unpersuaded by the plaintiff’s attempt to analogize access to deportation hearings with access to civil and criminal proceedings, invoking the logic of FMC v. South Carolina Ports Authority, in which the Supreme Court determined that state sovereign immunity protecting nonconsenting states from civil suits extended to protection from administrative proceedings as well. The court emphasized the importance of both prongs of the Richmond Newspapers test in its analysis, stating that satisfying the logic prong alone does not exempt the need for a tradition of public access in support of the experience prong.

Nevertheless, the court found the logic prong was not satisfied either and described numerous justifications as to why open deportation hearings would harm the public good, centered around the concern that open deportation hearings would result in access to sensitive information that could lend an advantage to another foreign terrorist plot or attack. Significantly, by applying a “pluses-and-minuses of openness” analysis, the Third Circuit arguably went beyond the Supreme Court’s jurisprudence, making the “logic” inquiry into a balancing-of-harms test. Having found neither prong of the Richmond Newspapers test fulfilled, the court declined to consider whether the Creppy directive satisfied strict scrutiny analysis, holding there is no First Amendment right to access deportation proceedings—in stark contrast to the Sixth Circuit’s decision. No other circuit has come to a decision on the constitutional question, leaving the matter open for further development.

The Third Circuit’s decision has been resoundingly criticized by legal scholars, who point out that there is little practical difference between criminal trials and immigration hearings, both of which can result in life-altering consequences for those involved. In particular, commentators fault the court’s majority for making the leap from its analysis of the narrow class of “special interest” cases to the broader conclusion that the First Amendment does not contemplate any right of access to any type of immigration hearing. The existence of irreconcilable rulings on a question where geographical variance makes no sense—there is no reason that immigration hearings in Tennessee should be more accessible than those in Pennsylvania—makes the issue ripe for eventual Supreme Court resolution, with the benefit of two decades since North Jersey Media to demonstrate how greatly the immigration court system would benefit from public oversight.

The Starting Point: Hearings Are Presumed Open

In the absence of a universally recognized constitutional right, journalists are left to rely on Justice Department regulations to guarantee their ability to attend immigration hearings. DOJ regulations start with the presumption that all hearings—except for individual “exclusion” hearings—are open to the public and press. The judge, however, retains substantial discretion to close part or all of a hearing to protect “witnesses, parties, or the public interest[.]” Where courtroom space is limited, judges are empowered to ration attendance, “with priority being given to the press over the general public.” Closure is mandatory when the proceeding involves an abused child or consideration of information that is subject to a protective order, and closure is presumed—absent the consent of the immigrant—if the proceeding involves allegations of spousal abuse.

As with immigration court hearings, oral arguments before the BIA are presumed by regulation to be open to the public. However, the board has discretion to grant or deny oral argument, and typically decides cases on paper filings without a public hearing, so the right exists more in theory than practice. In fact, BIA regulations contemplate that a single board member may summarily affirm the immigration judge’s decision with neither a hearing nor a written opinion if the member concludes that the judge committed no harmful error at the hearing stage and that the disentitlement to relief is dictated by binding precedent. Hearings would become rarer still under a proposed new BIA regulation disseminated in February 2026. Under the proposed rule, the default outcome for appeals to the BIA will be immediate summary affirmance, unless a majority of board members vote to hear the case on the merits. Consequently, covering cases at the BIA level is challenging for journalists, and it is no substitute for access to the details available at the hearing level.

The Paper Chase: Getting Access to Court Records

In traditional judicial proceedings, the Supreme Court has long recognized a common-law right to inspect the critical documents that make up the court record. Lower courts have recognized both a First Amendment–based right and common-law right to gain access to court records in civil as well as criminal cases. While some elements of a court record may be judicially sealed, the court’s orders and opinions almost never can be, absent a compelling justification that cannot be satisfied by anything short of sealing.

But until relatively recently, it was not clear that the public had a right to see the vast majority of BIA decisions—arguably the most important of all immigration documents—because they memorialize the final resolution at the agency level. Historically, the public has had only minimal access to decisions issued by the BIA, almost all of which are categorized as unpublished and nonprecedential. In a 2021 ruling, the Second Circuit finally addressed the question directly—not by applying the First Amendment, but by applying the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), which the court held applies to opinions issued by immigration judges just as it applies to records of other executive-branch decisions.

In New York Legal Assistance Group v. Board of Immigration Appeals, the Second Circuit considered courts’ authority to enforce FOIA affirmative disclosure obligations by ordering agencies to disclose records—in this case, over two decades of unpublished decisions made by the Board of Immigration Appeals. Invoking Section 552(a)(2) of FOIA, which imposes on agencies an obligation to “make available for public inspection in an electronic format . . . final opinions . . . [and] orders, made in the adjudication of cases,” New York Legal Assistance Group (NYLAG) asked BIA to make publicly available all unpublished board decisions dating back to November 1996. The BIA denied this request as overbroad, claiming that the decisions sought were not final opinions or orders within the scope of Section 552(a)(2) and that the group may only request the release of documents to themselves rather than to the public. NYLAG appealed this denial to district court, seeking relief through FOIA’s remedial provision, Section 552(a)(4)(B), which permits courts “to enjoin the agency from withholding agency records and to order the production of any agency records improperly withheld from the complainant.” The Southern District of New York dismissed NYLAG’s appeal, concluding that FOIA’s remedial provision gave district courts the authority only to require producing documents directly to the complainant, not the general public.

On appeal, the Second Circuit sided with NYLAG, holding that the remedial provision gave district courts the authority to disclose the withheld records to the public rather than just the complainant. The Second Circuit interpreted the text of Section 552(a)(4)(B) as granting district courts the authority to exercise two distinct powers: (1) to enjoin the agency from withholding records and (2) to order the production of improperly withheld records to the complainant, with only the latter modified by reference to the complainant. The Second Circuit also found that the broader context of FOIA supported the interpretation that making documents available to the public is an acceptable form of relief under the remedial provision, rejecting BIA’s interpretation that the only remedy enforceable by courts was the disclosure of records to the complainant. Turning to the history of the statute, the Second Circuit gave substantial weight to Congress’s 1974 amendment of FOIA, which moved the remedial provision from the section creating an individual right to request access to records to a new, separate section, a decision the Senate Judiciary Committee Report described as intended to permit judicial review of any agency withholding under Section 552.

The Second Circuit determined that the reading of the remedial provision supporting public disclosure of the decisions was in line with the purpose of FOIA as a means of facilitating public access to government information and combating agencies from developing secret law. Ultimately, the Second Circuit vacated the lower court’s decision and remanded the case, holding that any concerns regarding the breadth of NYLAG’s request and the scope of injunctive relief are within the discretion of the district court and that the district court has the authority to enjoin the BIA to release its nonpublished decisions to the public. On remand, the parties entered into an extensive settlement, under which the BIA agreed to post future decisions to an electronic reading room within six months of their issuance, and to begin posting previous decisions dating back to 2017 with a completion deadline of July 2027.

Beyond judges’ rulings, access to the files in immigration cases is somewhat limited. Federal rules provide that—other than the case docket and any orders or opinions issued by the judge—other immigration case documents are presumptively inaccessible through an electronic source such as PACER on privacy grounds. The public may view those files on-site at the courthouse, but not remotely. Judges are, however, empowered to grant relief from the rule and have allowed remote access where a sufficiently persuasive showing is made, and particularly where the immigrant does not object to disclosure. Additionally, redacted records of some appellate decisions of the BIA are available in an online reading room at https://foia.eoir.justice.gov/app/ReadingRoom.aspx.

At the hearing stage, the government has substantial latitude to seek sealing of filings in individual cases. Immigration judges are authorized to accept filings under seal if they find “a substantial likelihood” that disclosure of the information would harm “national security … or law enforcement interests.” Expert declarations setting forth the government’s forecast of substantial harm are reviewed deferentially. Leaking a sealed document can carry harsh penalties; courts can declare the immigrant ineligible for discretionary relief as punishment for unauthorized disclosure, including disclosure by the immigrant’s legal counsel. Once a decision is made to seal court filings, the court is instructed to close any portions of an otherwise-open hearing where the contents of those filings may be discussed. Importantly, the default is that protective orders last forever unless vacated, meaning that “members of the media may be barred from ever reporting on cases that involved sealed documents.”

The Federal Cloud Shading State Records

Significantly, federal regulations can obstruct access to records regarding immigration detainees even when the detainees are being held in state facilities to face state criminal charges. Ordinarily, the records of a state prison or jail are accessible by way of the state-level statutory analog to FOIA, including information identifying those held in jail and the charges they are facing. But the federal government has fought to keep county jails from honoring FOI requests seeking information about cases in which jail inmates are subject to a federal “detainer,” asserting custody to prevent the release of those facing removal. The government has justified keeping detainee records secret on several grounds, including maintaining uniformity among the states, safeguarding detainees’ personal privacy, and preventing the disclosure of information that might interfere with federal investigations.

The tension between state FOI law and federal secrecy interests came to a head with the case of ACLU v. County of Hudson. There, a state requester sued New Jersey counties for records about inmates being held in county detention facilities at the behest of the U.S. Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS), which, at the time, was responsible for enforcing federal immigration law. The trial court found the records subject to disclosure under New Jersey’s Open Public Records Act. But—just five days later—INS issued an emergency interim rule, declaring that detention facilities may not release any records “relating to any detainee,” with an effective date retroactive to encompass the ACLU’s request. The requester challenged the validity of the hastily enacted rule. But a New Jersey appellate court sided with the government, finding that the federal regulation trumped the counties’ disclosure duties under state FOI law because the two obligations—to disclose and not to disclose—were irreconcilably in conflict. The court viewed the regulation with extra-strength deference because it related to immigration, a subject area committed to the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal government. And the court excused INS’s failure to adhere to normal rulemaking formalities, citing the special urgency of safeguarding information about immigration detainees in the wake of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

Subsequently, courts in Connecticut and Wisconsin have followed New Jersey’s lead and given preemptive effect to the federal secrecy regulation. In Connecticut, the state supreme court held that the federal confidentiality regulation is so encompassing that it even applies to records about detainees who are no longer being held—and even precludes former detainees from obtaining their own records. The court noted that Connecticut’s FOI law, as is typical of such statutes everywhere, recognizes an exemption to the normal presumption of public access where federal law precludes disclosure.

Likewise, the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that the INS regulation overrode the state public records law in a dispute over access to immigration detainer forms, known as I-247 forms, that the federal government sends to local law enforcement agencies to place a “hold” to prevent local jailers from releasing people that immigration authorities want transferred to their custody. The court broadly applied the regulation not just to detainees in the legal custody of the federal government, but to anyone with a federal immigration hold, even those incarcerated in county jail on unrelated charges—and, said the court, the secrecy obligation continues to bind the county even after the detainee is released.

In one bright spot for public access, the Michigan Supreme Court broke with the consensus and found that the INS confidentiality rule does not override the state FOIA law. The court observed that Michigan’s FOIA recognizes an exclusion for records “exempted from disclosure by statute,” but that an agency regulation does not qualify as a “statute.” Consequently, the ACLU was entitled to production of records concerning a county sheriff’s three-day detention of its client—a U.S. citizen—who was held under an interagency agreement with ICE. The Michigan decision marks a pathway to argue for access in other states where the carve-out for federally exempt records is limited to those made confidential by “statute.”

Clashes over Access as Immigration Becomes National News

Starting in the fall of 2025, Minnesota became the epicenter of violent and at times deadly confrontations between federal immigration enforcement officers and protesters, as the Trump administration’s DHS surged 3,000 agents into the state. As tensions escalated, staffers at the federal immigration courthouse in Fort Snelling, Minnesota, responded by locking down access to proceedings, including redacting names from the publicly available calendar that journalists relied on to cover cases. Criticizing court security’s decision to bar observers from the courtroom, one human-rights advocate observed: “The whole premise of having open courtrooms is that the public is safeguarded against tyranny.”

During the second Trump administration, immigration courthouses have turned from proverbial battlegrounds into literal ones. It is now a commonplace sight for ICE agents to grab asylum-seekers the moment they step out of the courtroom, whisking them away into confinement, often in remote locations inaccessible to their families. Journalists covering these confrontations have been attacked and threatened by federal agents. The common areas of a courthouse are subject to reasonable and viewpoint-neutral restrictions on expressive activity, so it is constitutionally permissible to, for example, enforce a rule against congregating in hallways in a way that interferes with the flow of foot traffic. But if such rules are selectively enforced only against expressive activity—or, worse, only against those perceived as unsupportive of the government’s views—then the First Amendment is implicated.

While immigration courts have obtained renewed prominence since Trump retook the presidency, disputes over access are not new. A San Francisco journalist recounted repeated difficulties gaining access to the courthouse, or being asked to leave hearings, during the Obama administration in 2017. In 2014, a reporter with the Houston Chronicle was turned away while attempting to attend a master calendar hearing being held at a makeshift courtroom inside an immigration detention center in New Mexico. The government, citing safety concerns, partially relented after pushback and allowed a reporter to watch, but only by remote videoconference. Such detention facilities are rapidly becoming ubiquitous, as the Trump administration pursues its goal of adding 100,000 new detention beds by the end of 2026. One of the many interesting and unsettled legal questions requiring judicial clarification is whether journalists can insist on being admitted to courtrooms on the premises of immigration detention centers, given the considerable body of caselaw declining to recognize a First Amendment right to enter prisons or jails to gather news. Even a decade ago, predating the Trump-era push toward mass incarceration of people who arrive at the border seeking asylum, the Brennan Center for Justice reported that 50 percent of immigration hearings were being held inside detention centers—with the result that rules guaranteeing the public’s right to attend were being “routinely flouted.”

Conclusion

Immigration court is a little-understood process opaque to the vast majority of the American public. The opacity is by design; federal regulations tightly constrain the ability of immigration judges to say anything publicly about their work, a constraint that is the subject of ongoing First Amendment litigation. The decision-making process grew even more impervious to public oversight with the 2022 enactment of a regulation (known as the “Asylum Processing Rule”) that empowers DHS asylum officers—not judges—to make an initial determination on the merits of an asylum claim when applicants present themselves at the border, meaning that applicants can be denied relief without ever setting foot in an immigration courtroom. As the second Trump administration has intensified deportation efforts, the process has become still more secretive, with attorneys representing the government sometimes unwilling even to say their names in court.

When subjected to scrutiny, the immigration court process holds up rather poorly. One former immigration judge has termed the system “dysfunctional” and “generally ‘user-unfriendly.’” In the words of one prominent critic, then-appellate judge Richard A. Posner: “[T]he Immigration Court, though lodged in the Justice Department, is the least competent federal agency, though in fairness it may well owe its dismal status to its severe underfunding by Congress, which has resulted in a shortage of immigration judges that has subjected them to crushing workloads.” Given the demands placed on immigration judges to churn cases—a “performance metric” instituted in the first Trump administration set a goal of disposing of 700 cases a year for judges to be considered satisfactory—there are real questions about the level of care that any application receives. Attorneys who practice in immigration court report high levels of stress and burnout, owing to hostile conditions including public vilification for representing immigrants, as well as shifting legal standards that have made previously winnable cases into losers. A stinging critique from the Brennan Center for Justice concludes:

Despite the important matters it handles, the immigration court system is, by all accounts, a deeply troubled one. A crushing case load and dearth of resources have led to an enormous backlog, and judges are forced to rush through cases that have been pending for years. Most participants have no lawyer and no way to find one. Translation services are spotty.

Because of the well-recognized brokenness of the immigration court system, public oversight can have salutary effects, including helping expose insufficiencies in staffing. Access to immigration courts has allowed journalists to chronicle the escalating aggressiveness of immigration enforcement tactics—a story that would be far less impactful if journalists were forced to rely on second-hand accounts from witnesses who themselves may be undocumented and fearful of reprisals. It is especially valuable for journalists to be in the courtroom during individual hearings because the judge’s assessment of the immigrant’s credibility is such a critical and frequently decisive factor, which cannot be thoroughly reviewed at the appellate level. Arguably, the fact that immigration exists in a space of extra-strength judicial deference to executive-branch policymakers makes public oversight even more essential as a check on runaway governmental authority. Whether judges welcome journalists into the hearing room, or just grudgingly tolerate their presence, media coverage can benefit both the individual participants (as a check on judicial transgressions) and the public as a whole (by demystifying an enigmatic but vital government function).

text:
ICE plans to spend up to $20m (£15m) to purchase thousands of gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks for officers and agents by March, according to a notice published Monday by the Department of Homeland Security.

The devices, called Glove (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter), are manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC of Lexington, Kentucky.

According to the manufacturer, “the discomfort associated with the stimulation is usually effective in bringing individuals into compliance in less than three seconds and leaves no burns, marks or scars”. The company has advertised the device as a “humane, low-optics, de-escalation solution for many situations facing our men and women in uniform”.

The gloves have previously been used in settings such as jails in the US.

Compliant Technologies says the devices function as a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate their electrical mode. The gloves must be applied directly to someone’s skin to deliver a pain stimulus that typically helps an officer gain compliance within seconds, according to the company.

“It’s immediate and sharp, and it will distract you. I call it like a bee sting,” said John Peters, president of the Institute for the Prevention of In-Custody Deaths, who is studying how the device has been used. “If the officer is getting any type of resistance from the person, this is certainly an effective tool.”

Civil rights advocates expressed alarm at the plan, saying ICE officers already face criticism for their use of force with little oversight or accountability while enforcing Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the American Civil Liberties Union, told the Associated Press that she questioned the use of the devices for civil immigration enforcement.

“ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do,” she said. “Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public.”

Peters said he believed ICE’s planned purchase would likely be the largest from the company to date. He said he could envision ICE officers using the gloves to help remove uncooperative subjects from cars and houses and in and out of detention facilities.

The manufacturer warns the device should not be used as punishment, against people merely exhibiting “verbal defiance or belligerence” or on high-risk populations such as children, pregnant women or elderly or disabled people.

Jeff Niklaus, the founder and CEO of Compliant Technologies, wrote in an email: “Unfortunately, we are unable to speak on this subject.”

text:
Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minnesota) is demanding answers from the Trump administration after she discovered that an undercover ICE agent was stationed outside of one of her town hall meetings, raising fears of intimidation by the agency just days before the state’s primary election.

Last Thursday, local law enforcement who were coordinating security for the event in Richfield, Minnesota, noticed that there was a woman parked outside of the building in a suspicious vehicle, as attendees were entering, Omar said on Friday. A police officer ran the plates for the vehicle and found out that the records didn’t match the vehicle, and asked her about why she was there.

The woman initially claimed to be a security officer, but Omar’s team said that she was not involved with their security for the event. It was then that she called her supervisor and admitted that she was an agent of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), a law enforcement agency within Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). She left after speaking with her supervisor, Omar says.

The agent claimed that she was there as part of an undercover drug enforcement operation, though local law enforcement said they received no advance notice of such an operation from HSI. Omar raised doubts about this claim, saying that the event was clearly labelled with a “prominent sign” for the meeting and that a reasonable person would assess that it would not be an ideal place for a drug operation.

In a letter to HSI first reported by HuffPost, Omar also raised concerns about the use of ICE agents as an intimidation tactic, especially against the Trump administration’s political opponents and especially after agents’ violent raid of Minneapolis in Operation Metro Surge earlier this year. She demanded that HSI answer questions on the reasoning for the agent’s presence outside of the event and whether or not HSI is stationing agents with relation to her activities in particular.

The lawmaker also pointed out that she received assurances from Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials when she met with them in March that they were no longer switching license plates on their vehicles, which is against the law. However, this practice appears to be continuing, as evidenced by the incident on Thursday.

“HSI’s actions yesterday evening put an entire community at risk,” Omar wrote.

“It also raises serious and uncomfortable questions about the purpose of HSI’s presence outside of my event,” she went on. “At best, your agent was unable to assess that the parking lot of a community center hosting a Congressional event wasn’t the best place to conduct a drug operation. At worst, it emphasizes many Americans’ growing concern that the Trump administration uses ICE to surveil political opponents and may interfere with our democracy.”

Omar has repeatedly faced racist direct attacks from President Donald Trump, and, amid the ICE raids in January, was assaulted by a Trump supporter with a syringe full of vinegar while she was holding a town hall.

The latest incident occurred just days before Tuesday’s primary election in Minnesota, in which Omar is up for election and is expected to win.

title: Appeals court revives DHS' speedy deportation powers against Biden's paroled migrants
description:
Circuit Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia erased a lower-court ruling that had blocked DHS from using the speedy deportation, officially known as expedited removal, on parolees.
In a 3-0 ruling, the appeals court said the groups challenging DHS lacked legal standing to sue.
Expedited removal was created by Congress in 1996.
In January 2025, after President Trump took over, DHS issued a memorandum directing immigration officers to explore the use of expedited removal on parolees.
A month later, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement circulated an email telling officers they could use expedited removal on parolees.
text:
A federal appeals court on Tuesday breathed new life into the Department of Homeland Security’s plans to use a speedy deportation power on migrants who were paroled into the U.S., potentially giving the Trump administration a new tool to boot hundreds of thousands who were admitted by President Biden.

The U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia erased a lower-court ruling that had blocked DHS from using the speedy deportation, officially known as expedited removal, on parolees.

In a 3-0 ruling, the appeals court said the groups challenging DHS lacked legal standing to sue. The judges said that’s because the groups challenged Trump administration policy but didn’t question the underlying regulation, which appears to let DHS do exactly what it says it’s doing.

“Plaintiffs cannot seek relief that changes nothing for them. The plaintiffs here tried to do just that. So we vacate the stay issued by the district court,” the judges said in an unsigned opinion.

The court withheld its mandate for the decision, presumably to give the full D.C. Circuit Court a chance to review the ruling.

Should it take effect, it could help usher out a large cross section of unauthorized migrants from the Biden era.

Parole is an exception to the usual immigration system, letting someone remain despite having entered without a legal visa.

Before the Biden administration, it was used sparingly, usually in cases in which a migrant had an urgent medical need for treatment in the U.S. or where American authorities wanted a migrant’s presence to help with an investigation.

Under Mr. Biden, it became a loophole to the usual border controls. He allowed in Afghans, Cubans, Haitians, Nicaraguans, Ukrainians and Venezuelans who flew into the U.S., plus a large swath of other migrants who reached the U.S.-Mexico border and preregistered their arrival.

Andrew “Art” Arthur, a former immigration judge who is now at the Center for Immigration Studies, calculated that the Biden team admitted nearly 2.9 million migrants on parole.

He said that’s why the court is confronting the issue of whether it can use speedy deportation on them.

“The reason this has never come up before is because nobody ever did what Biden did with respect to parole before,” Mr. Arthur said.

Expedited removal was created by Congress in 1996. It allows immigrants who have been in the U.S. illegally for less than two years to be ousted based on a finding by immigration officers, rather than requiring a full case in immigration court.

It had previously been limited to border cases, based on policy decisions, though no such restriction is written into the law. The Trump administration has sought to expand its reach.

The appeals court, in Tuesday’s ruling, said as far back as 1997 — six months after the law was enacted — the Clinton administration wrote regulations saying expedited removal applied to people who were paroled.

In January 2025, after President Trump took over, DHS issued a memorandum directing immigration officers to explore the use of expedited removal on parolees.

A month later, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement circulated an email telling officers they could use expedited removal on parolees.

The Coalition for Human Immigrant Rights led a challenge to the memo and the email.

The appeals court, though, said the group never challenged the Clinton-era regulation, so even if the email and memo were to be struck down, the administration could rely on the original regulation and get the same result.

Because of that, there’s no way for the court to redress the coalition’s legal injury. That undercut its legal standing to sue.

James Percival, DHS’s general counsel, celebrated the decision, calling it a “big win.”

He urged those without a full legal status to take DHS’s offer of self-deportation before they are found by immigration officers.

“It’s not too late to take a $2,600 check and a free flight home,” he said.
