text:
Undocumented students are a vital part of the U.S. higher education system and the broader American economy. As students, researchers, and campus leaders, they contribute to academic life; beyond campus, they play an increasingly important role in addressing workforce needs across the country.

Communities nationwide continue to face labor shortages in healthcare and science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) fields. Undocumented students, including those eligible for Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), are pursuing degrees and credentials in these high-demand sectors, positioning themselves to help fill persistent skills gaps while supporting their families, communities, and local economies.

The economic contributions of undocumented students are already substantial. DACA-eligible individuals alone generate billions in household income each year and contribute significantly to federal, state, and local taxes, while also sustaining local businesses through their everyday spending. Many have also worked in essential roles as students, including during the COVID-19 pandemic, underscoring their importance to both economic resilience and community wellbeing. Undocumented students and graduates contribute as entrepreneurs and taxpayers, advancing economic prosperity even when they face constraints on their postgraduate professional pathways.

Recent policy changes at state and federal levels introduce new barriers that limit opportunities for undocumented individuals, both with and without DACA. Heightened federal immigration enforcement, ongoing uncertainty around DACA—including longer wait times for DACA recipients to receive their renewals —and federal challenges to state-level tuition, financial aid, and professional licensure policies are narrowing pathways for undocumented students nationwide. These developments threaten a crucial talent source and undermine the work of higher education work to meet the country’s workforce needs.

Who Are Undocumented Students in Higher Education?

An estimated 525,000 undocumented students are enrolled in U.S. colleges and universities, representing 2.4% of all postsecondary students, according to the American Immigration Council’s analysis of the 2024 American Community Survey (ACS). This marks a modest increase from the 510,000 undocumented students estimated in the 2023 ACS.

At the same time, the share of students eligible for DACA continues to decline. Approximately 129,900 undocumented students (24.7% of the total undocumented student population) are DACA-eligible, down from earlier estimates. This reflects a structural constraint in the program: the fixed 2007 arrival cutoff excludes most current, traditional-aged undocumented college students, regardless of how long they have lived in the United States.

Some DACA-eligible individuals have been unable to apply for the program due to ongoing litigation. In January 2025, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that portions of DACA are unlawful, but it limited the scope of its decision to Texas pending further litigation, preserving the current DACA program nationwide for the time being. The ruling allows current DACA recipients in all states, including Texas, to continue renewing their DACA status and work authorization while the case proceeds through the courts. Following the Fifth Circuit’s March 2025 mandate remanding the case to the district court, the Mexican American Legal Defense and Education Fund (MALDEF) stated that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) should eventually resume processing initial DACA applications, although implementation details in Texas may differ.

However, as of the publication of this report, no new initial DACA applications have been processed, and the district court has not yet issued an implementation order. FWD.us, an immigration and criminal justice policy group, estimates that approximately 400,000 DACA-eligible individuals have been unable to apply for the program due to this pause. It is likely that an even smaller portion of the 129,000 DACA-eligible students enrolled in higher education are active DACA recipients, meaning less than one quarter of all undocumented students in higher education have access to DACA benefits, such as work authorization and protection from deportation.

Undocumented students with DACA have faced escalating threats, despite making good-faith efforts to maintain eligibility, renew their applications, and contribute to the U.S. economy. Reports of hundreds of DACA recipients and other Dreamers—undocumented immigrants who entered the United States as children—facing detention and deportation highlight the instability facing this population and demonstrate the importance of identifying a permanent legislative solution. Recent guidance on deferred action issued by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) also signals a potentially more restrictive approach to how USCIS may exercise discretion when adjudicating DACA requests.

A close look at the age of arrival of the undocumented population emphasizes the importance of including young and adolescent arrivals when considering future policies.

Undocumented students are not a monolithic group. While a majority arrived in the United States as children or adolescents, a substantial share arrived as young adults and are balancing school with work and family responsibilities. Of the undocumented college students, women make up a slight majority (54.5%).

Undocumented and DACA-Eligible Students by Age of Arrival, 2024

The DACA program demonstrates that providing undocumented individuals with access to work authorization and relief from deportation leads to educational attainment and postgraduate success. Legislation that codifies and extends these benefits could support access to professional fields—fields where the United States has a need for workers—for a large number of students and graduates.

Breakdown of the Undocumented Student Population

Region and Country of Origin

Undocumented students reflect the full diversity of the U.S. immigrant population. While Mexico remains the single largest country of origin (30.2%), students come from across the globe, with significant representation from Asia, the Caribbean, South America, and Africa.

Undocumented College Students by Country of Origin, 2024

Race and Ethnicity

The undocumented student population in higher education is racially and ethnically diverse, reflecting broader shifts in immigration patterns to the United States in recent decades. While a slight majority (51.9%) of undocumented college students identify as Hispanic, nearly half identify as non-Hispanic, including 21.7% as Asian, 13.6% as Black, and 8.4% as white, along with a smaller share identifying as multiracial or another race.

This distribution underscores an important point: undocumented students are not defined by a single racial or ethnic identity. Instead, they reflect the full diversity of first-generation immigrant communities, with substantial representation from across regions of the world.

By contrast, the DACA-eligible student population is less diverse, with 75.9% identifying as Hispanic and smaller shares identifying as Asian, Black, or white. The difference reflects the structure of the DACA program itself. The program’s fixed 2007 arrival cutoff includes individuals from earlier migration cohorts, particularly from Latin America, while excluding more recent arrivals from Asia, Africa, and other regions.

As a result, the diversity of the broader undocumented student population is not mirrored in the DACA and DACA-eligible populations. This divergence highlights how policy design can shape not only access to legal protections, but also which communities are most likely to benefit from them.

Degrees and Programs

Undocumented students are enrolled across all sectors of higher education, from community colleges to research universities. Public institutions educate nearly three-quarters (74.3%) of undocumented students, highlighting the central role of state education systems in providing access. One-quarter (25.7%) of undocumented students attend private institutions, including liberal arts, research focused, and faith-based institutions.

Undocumented students pursue a wide range of credentials, from associate degrees to graduate degrees and professional training. While the majority are enrolled in undergraduate programs (84.3%), a growing share are pursuing graduate education (15.7%)—a notable increase from 10.3% in 2019 and 12.8% in 2021. This rise points to an important shift: undocumented students are not only accessing higher education but are increasingly continuing beyond initial degrees into more advanced fields of study.

Among DACA-eligible students, participation in graduate education is even higher (21.1%). Previous research has shown that DACA improved educational attainment among eligible youth by reducing uncertainty and expanding educational and employment opportunities. Taken together, these trends indicate a strengthening pipeline of undocumented students moving into advanced training, including master’s, doctoral, and professional degree programs.

This growth has important implications. As more undocumented students enter graduate education, they are preparing for roles in high-skill sectors that require specialized training, including healthcare, education, research, and technical fields. However, barriers to employment authorization, licensure, and legal status continue to shape whether these investments in education are able to translate into full participation in the workforce.

Impact on Science and Innovation

Undocumented students are an important part of the U.S. talent pipeline, particularly in fields where demand continues to outpace supply. Nearly 16.0% are enrolled in graduate programs, positioning them to enter high-skill professions that are critical to the nation’s economic and social infrastructure.

Among graduate students, many bring strong academic preparation in STEM and health-related fields, both of which are experiencing persistent and worsening workforce shortages. A substantial share of undocumented graduate students have undergraduate degrees in STEM disciplines, and a notable portion of those degrees are in healthcare-related fields. Among DACA-eligible graduate students, these concentrations are even higher.

These patterns are especially significant given the scale of current workforce gaps. Employers across sectors continue to report difficulty filling specialized roles. Undocumented students are actively training to meet these needs, representing a critical but often underrecognized source of future talent in both technical and care-based professions.

At the same time, barriers to licensure, employment authorization, and legal status limit the ability of many of these students to fully contribute their skills after graduation. As a result, the United States risks underutilizing a population that it has already invested in and that would strengthen key sectors of the economy.

Enrollment by State

Undocumented students are concentrated in a relatively small number of states. California, Texas, Florida, New York, and Illinois account for nearly 55% of all undocumented college students.

At the same time, some states have particularly high shares of undocumented students within their college populations, including Florida, Nevada, New Jersey, Texas, and California.

These patterns are shaped not only by student characteristics but also by state policy. Access to in-state tuition, state financial aid, professional and occupational licensure, and driver’s licenses can significantly influence whether undocumented students are able to enroll in college, persist through graduation, and transition into the workforce.

Undocumented and DACA-Eligible Students in Higher Education by State, 2024

Recent policy changes in high immigrant-enrolling states like Florida and Texas may affect future college enrollment and educational opportunities for undocumented students. As of the publication of this report, the Department of Justice has filed lawsuits challenging tuition equity policies in 12 states. This includes Texas, which has also enacted new lawful presence requirements that prevent undocumented graduates from obtaining professional licenses, effectively shutting off career pathways for students who have earned degrees at local institutions. Meanwhile, Florida rescinded its longstanding tuition equity policy, abruptly curtailing access for thousands of current and prospective students. Proposed regulations could bar undocumented students in Florida from enrolling in certain state colleges and universities. Such policy shifts compound the effect of federal and state-level efforts to restrict opportunities for students.

Over time, these shifts may have broader implications for postsecondary enrollment, workforce participation, and state economic development. As states shift from policies that support inclusion and economic mobility and toward systems that restrict access to academic and professional opportunities, they risk reducing workforce participation and undermining their own long-term economic growth. As a result, states that introduce restrictive policies may see reductions in academic performance, increases in food and housing insecurity, and changes in degree attainment and workforce participation.

Policy Environment

The 2024 ACS data reflect a rapidly evolving policy landscape. Three dynamics are especially important:

DACA’s narrowing reach

The program’s fixed eligibility window means that fewer students qualify each year, even as new cohorts graduate from U.S. high schools. Ongoing litigation and delayed renewal processing adds greater uncertainty for current recipients.

Federal attacks on tuition equity policies and state-level retrenchment

Recent rollbacks of in-state tuition access in several states, largely due to lawsuits brought by the U.S. Department of Justice combined with state actions to end access, represent a significant break from two decades of gradual expansion. These changes directly affect affordability and access for thousands of students. The effects of these policy shifts are compounded by other efforts to restrict access to programs and services that support students’ academic success.

Intensified enforcement climate

Increased immigration enforcement can deter enrollment and disrupt students’ ability to pursue and complete degrees. School districts across the country continue to report declines in immigrant student attendance, which research has linked to the federal administration’s immigration enforcement and deportation efforts.

However, states that maintain or expand inclusive policies continue to demonstrate measurable student benefits, including higher educational attainment and stronger workforce outcomes.

Conclusion

Undocumented students are deeply embedded in the fabric of U.S. higher education and the future workforce. They pursue demanding academic paths, contribute to campus life, and prepare for careers in fields critical to the nation’s economic and social wellbeing.

As policymakers debate the future of immigration, higher education, and workforce development, the direction of policies affecting undocumented students will have far-reaching consequences. Decisions about access to higher education and career pathways will shape not only the futures of individual students, but also the ability of the United States to educate, train, and retain needed talent.

title: The Bankruptcy Court Blueprint for an Independent Immigration Judiciary
description:
In 2021, an acting attorney general issued a second iteration before a permanent attorney general was confirmed.
On February 4, 2025, the immigration court system employed 726 permanent immigration judges nationwide.
The same round of removals included 13 members of the Board of Immigration Appeals, the highest appellate body within the immigration court system.
The constitutional problem Northern Pipeline identified in 1978 bankruptcy courts is the same constitutional problem that exists in immigration courts today.
The question is no longer whether an independent immigration court system can be built.
text:
A Court in Name Only: How This System Was Built

Immigration judges exercise delegated authority from the attorney general pursuant to statute, and their decisions are legally issued in the attorney general’s name. Under federal regulation, the attorney general may certify decisions of the Board of Immigration Appeals to herself for review and issue a binding nationwide precedent. Immigration courts themselves operate within the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR), a component of the Department of Justice (DOJ). Although other administrative judges act within the executive branch agencies (i.e., SEC, FAA, DOL), no other court system in the United States permits the nation’s chief prosecutor to function simultaneously as the final appellate authority over the judges appearing beneath her.

That structure did not emerge accidentally. Immigration courts did not begin as courts in the traditional sense. They developed as administrative mechanisms attached to the federal government’s immigration enforcement apparatus, and despite decades of institutional restructuring, they remain there today.

In 1940, Congress and the EOIR consolidated immigration functions under the authority of the attorney general, placing both immigration enforcement and adjudication inside the DOJ. That structure largely survived for more than 60 years. After the September 11 attacks, Congress enacted the Homeland Security Act of 2002, which dismantled the old Immigration and Naturalization Service and transferred immigration enforcement functions into the newly created Department of Homeland Security. Enforcement responsibilities moved into agencies now familiar to immigration practitioners: Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, and United States Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Adjudication, however, did not move with them.

Instead, immigration courts remained inside the DOJ. Immigration judges, therefore, do not exercise judicial power in the constitutional sense. They are DOJ employees operating within the same executive branch, ultimately responsible for immigration enforcement policy and litigation.

That distinction is not semantic. It defines the structure of the system itself.

For practitioners and their clients, the consequences are immediate and concrete. Advising a client in immigration proceedings often means advising them under a body of precedent that may shift not through the ordinary development of law but through unilateral intervention by the same cabinet officer whose department is litigating against them. A respondent’s eligibility for relief, therefore, can depend not simply on the facts of the case or the reasoning of a court but on whether a presidential administration views existing precedent as acceptable.

That is not merely an administrative arrangement. It is a structural choice about what kind of institution the immigration court is intended to be.

The Constitutional Diagnosis: Structure Is the Problem

Not every court needs to be a federal court in the Article III sense. The Constitution does not require that every judge who acts under the color of federal law enjoy life tenure and salary protection—and Congress has never proceeded as though it does. What the Constitution does require is that wherever “[t]he judicial Power of the United States” is exercised, the body exercising it must have sufficient independence from the parties before it to render genuine adjudication rather than administrative output.

Federal adjudication operates across three tiers. Article III courts—the district courts, the circuit courts, and the Supreme Court—carry full judicial power, with judges appointed by the president and confirmed by the Senate to serve during good behavior. At the next tier sit Article I legislative courts: specialized tribunals created by Congress with defined subject matter jurisdiction, structural independence, and term-limited appointments insulated from executive removal. The U.S. Tax Court, the Court of Federal Claims, and bankruptcy courts occupy this tier. At the third tier sit administrative tribunals—executive adjudication bodies that exercise quasi-judicial functions but remain fully within the political branches, subject to policy direction, budget leverage, and at-will employment of those that appoint them.

Immigration courts currently function as the third tier; however, they should be the second.

The distinction matters because the Fifth Amendment does not distinguish between citizens and noncitizens when it guarantees that no person shall be deprived of liberty without due process of law. The Supreme Court has long recognized that due process requires, at a minimum, a neutral decision-maker—one with no institutional stake in the outcome. Where the consequences of adjudication include permanent removal from the country, separation from family, and return to conditions that may threaten life, the consequences of that adjudication are severe. Litigants in immigration proceedings have their liberty at risk, not merely their pecuniary interest. The risk of erroneous deprivation in a system where judges are political employees is not speculative—it is structural. And the government’s interest in efficient administration, however legitimate, cannot override the constitutional floor.

The argument here is not that immigration courts require the full protections of Article III—that elevation is neither politically viable nor structurally necessary. The argument is simpler and more durable: Immigration courts, at a minimum, must be freed from the executive branch and reconstituted as Article I courts with genuine term protections, independent budgets, governance by the Judicial Conference of the United States, and appellate authority that belongs to the court—not the attorney general.

Congress has designed exactly this kind of court before. It has worked both functionally and within appropriate constitutional limits set by the Supreme Court. And the constitutional logic that drove that reform applies here with equal force.

The Self-Referral Weapon: When the Attorney General Becomes the Appellate Court

The most consequential—and least scrutinized—power in American immigration law belongs not to any judge, but to the attorney general, a political appointee. Under 8 U.S.C. § 1103(g)(2), immigration judges exercise authority as delegates of the attorney general. Under 8 C.F.R. § 1003.1(h)(1), the attorney general may certify any decision of the Board of Immigration Appeals to herself for personal review and final determination—without petition from any party, without briefing, and without oral argument. The attorney general’s determination then becomes binding precedent for every immigration court in the country.

No other court in the American legal system—Article I or Article III—grants the prosecuting authority this kind of power over the adjudicating authority. In no other federal court can the cabinet officer whose department opposes a party in proceedings reach into a pending appellate decision and rewrite its outcome as national law. In immigration courts, it is not only possible—it is a routine feature of how the system operates.

The path of the Matter of A-B- illustrates what this power looks like across administrations. In 2018, Attorney General Jeff Sessions certified to himself a case involving a domestic violence survivor seeking asylum and used it to eliminate domestic violence as a cognizable basis for asylum claims—reversing decades of developing caselaw without a single brief filed by the parties most affected by the ruling. In 2021, an acting attorney general issued a second iteration before a permanent attorney general was confirmed. Attorney General Merrick Garland vacated both decisions that same year, restoring the prior legal framework. In September 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi reinstated the Sessions standard through a new self-referral.

Four binding reversals of national asylum precedent. Three administrations. Zero neutral adjudication.

The constitutional problem this creates extends beyond any individual case. Due process requires not only a neutral decision-maker but also fair notice—the principle that persons subject to legal consequences must be able to know, with reasonable certainty, what the law requires of them. A legal standard that reverses based on the identity of a cabinet officer rather than the development of law through adjudication cannot provide that notice. A respondent who qualifies for asylum on Monday may not qualify on Tuesday—not because the facts changed, not because a court followed the rule of law developed by an impartial judiciary, but because the attorney general who directs the agency opposing that respondent chose to rewrite the standard unilaterally. That is not the application of law. It is the administration of executive policy through the guise of judicial machinery.

Scholars have described the attorney general’s self-referral authority as one of the most significant and least-examined powers in the federal legal system. Its obscurity is part of what makes it durable. A mechanism that rewrites the law of the land without briefing, argument, or adversarial review is not a judicial function—it is an executive instrument operating inside a structure that was never truly designed to be a court.

Courts Don’t Fire Judges

The strongest argument against the current structure of immigration courts is no longer theoretical. It is what happened to the immigration bench itself in 2025.

On February 4, 2025, the immigration court system employed 726 permanent immigration judges nationwide. By February 2026, that number had fallen to 520, representing a net loss of 206 judges through firings, resignations, and retirements despite subsequent rounds of hiring. Independent reporting later estimated that nearly 100 immigration judges had been terminated in 2025 alone. By September 2025, more than 125 judges and court personnel had reportedly left the system through firings and resignations connected to the administration’s restructuring of immigration courts.

The manner of those removals mattered as much as the numbers themselves. In February 2025, the DOJ reportedly terminated 20 immigration judges by email in a single day, including several who had not yet been sworn in. The same round of removals included 13 members of the Board of Immigration Appeals, the highest appellate body within the immigration court system. One military judge temporarily assigned to immigration court duties was reportedly removed after his asylum grant rate drew scrutiny from administration officials.

No comparable system exists elsewhere in the federal judiciary. Article III judges cannot be removed by the executive branch because their rulings are politically inconvenient. Neither can judges serving on legitimate Article I courts. Article I judges are typically removed through the standard congressional impeachment process or simply by the expiration of their fixed terms. Bankruptcy judges are not dismissed because discharge rates frustrate political priorities. Tax Court judges are not removed because their decisions conflict with the policy preferences of the Treasury Department. This very suggestion would provoke immediate constitutional alarm because courts derive their legitimacy from decisional independence rather than political alignment.

Immigration courts operate differently because they were never structurally designed to function as an independent judiciary. Immigration judges remain employees of the Department of Justice, supervised by the same executive branch ultimately responsible for immigration enforcement policy. The events of 2025 did not expose a breakdown in the system. They exposed the system functioning exactly as its structure permits.

For lawyers appearing before these courts, the implications are impossible to ignore. Judicial independence does not disappear only when direct orders are given. It erodes whenever adjudicators understand that continued employment may depend, at least in part, on whether their decisions align with administrative expectations. A judge who must remain aware of that reality cannot exercise the degree of independence that meaningful adjudication requires.

The Bankruptcy Blueprint: Congress Has Solved This Before

The argument that moving immigration courts out of the executive branch is legally complex, politically impossible, or structurally unprecedented is contradicted by a chapter of federal court history that deserves far more attention in this debate than it has received.

In 1978, Congress passed the Bankruptcy Reform Act, which created bankruptcy courts as broad-jurisdiction adjudicative bodies and vested them with sweeping powers over the reorganization and discharge of private debts. What Congress did not do was give those courts meaningful structural independence. Bankruptcy judges served at the pleasure of district courts and lacked the protections that the exercise of judicial power requires. Four years later, the Supreme Court said so. In Northern Pipeline Construction Co. v. Marathon Pipe Line Co., the Court held that Congress cannot vest the exercise of judicial power in adjudicators who lack the independence protections that judicial power demands. The bankruptcy court structure, as designed in 1978, was constitutionally deficient for exactly the reason immigration courts are deficient today: The judges were not sufficiently insulated from political and institutional pressures to be genuine courts.

Congress did not respond by creating Article III bankruptcy courts—life tenure and salary protection for every bankruptcy judge in the country was neither practical nor necessary. Instead, Congress passed the Bankruptcy Amendments and Federal Judgeship Act of 1984, which reconstituted bankruptcy courts as Article I courts with structural independence built into their design. Bankruptcy judges are now appointed, not by the president—and not by the attorney general—but by the Circuit Courts of Appeal for their respective circuits, to renewable 14-year terms. They are not employees of the executive branch. Their decisions are not subject to override by the Secretary of the Treasury or the head of any enforcement agency. Their precedent belongs to the court and allows litigants a clear roadmap of how their case will be adjudicated.

The constitutional problem Northern Pipeline identified in 1978 bankruptcy courts is the same constitutional problem that exists in immigration courts today. The fix Congress designed in 1984 is the same fix being proposed for immigration courts now. Legal scholars have drawn this parallel directly, mapping the bankruptcy reform arc onto the immigration court context and concluding that the structural and legislative path is not only available but proven.

The remaining question is not whether it can be done. It has been done. The question is why Congress has allowed immigration courts—which adjudicate consequences more severe than bankruptcy discharge and affect a class of persons with fewer political advocates—to remain structurally behind a standard the federal judiciary resolved four decades ago.

What Article I Independence Looks Like

The structural problems within immigration courts are no longer difficult to identify. The more important question is what a functioning alternative would actually look like in practice.

Fortunately, Congress does not need to invent one from scratch.

Federal law already contains a successful model for high-volume, specialized adjudication that demands expertise, efficiency, and decisional independence simultaneously. Bankruptcy courts operate within precisely that framework. Their judges serve fixed renewable terms, are appointed through the judiciary rather than the political branches, and exercise authority within a court structure insulated from the enforcement priorities of executive agencies. Immigration courts require the same institutional foundation.

The Real Courts, Rule of Law Act of 2026 represents the most developed contemporary proposal for implementing that principle. Under the legislation, immigration judges would serve renewable 15-year terms, balancing decisional independence with meaningful accountability through periodic reappointment review. Appointment authority would move from the DOJ to the federal courts of appeals, mirroring the structure Congress adopted after the constitutional concerns identified in Northern Pipeline. Just as importantly, the proposal would eliminate the attorney general’s unilateral self-certification authority and vest precedential decision-making in an independent appellate division within the court itself. Immigration law would develop through adjudication rather than political intervention.

Structural independence also requires institutional independence. The proposal, therefore, establishes a dedicated administrative structure and independent budgeting process separate from the DOJ. That separation matters because no court can function as a neutral adjudicative body while the same executive branch responsible for prosecution simultaneously controls judicial hiring, precedent, administration, and funding.

Support for this reform is no longer confined to academic commentary or practitioner organizations. The American Bar Association has formally endorsed the creation of an independent immigration court system, recognizing that public confidence in adjudication depends on both the reality and appearance of judicial independence. Additionally, the American Immigration Lawyers Association has similarly argued that meaningful procedural reform is impossible without structural reform first.

That point cannot be overstated. More judges, better technology, and faster scheduling procedures may improve case management, but none resolve the underlying legitimacy problem if the adjudicative structure itself remains politically contingent. A court system cannot meaningfully build public trust while preserving the power to empty the bench or rewrite precedent by executive action the following year.

What Courts Are For

There is an argument about immigration courts that does not require a position on immigration policy. It does not require agreement on border enforcement, asylum eligibility, or the appropriate scope of executive authority in immigration matters. It requires only a view of courts: what they are, what makes them legitimate, and what distinguishes adjudication from administration.

Courts derive their authority from independence. Not aspirational independence. Structural independence. The public does not trust courts because judges promise neutrality. The public trusts courts because the system is designed to protect neutrality from institutional pressure, political preference, and executive control.

That protection is absent here.

Immigration judges remain employees of the same executive branch responsible for immigration enforcement. The attorney general retains authority over precedent, administration, and, ultimately, the structure of the bench itself. No Article III court operates this way. No meaningful Article I court operates this way. Yet immigration courts continue to adjudicate questions involving liberty, family unity, lawful status, and removal from the country under a structure that would be institutionally unacceptable elsewhere in the federal judiciary.

That standard is not sustainable because it is not legitimate.

Congress already solved this problem once. The bankruptcy reforms of 1984 demonstrated that specialized, high-volume adjudication can coexist with genuine judicial independence. The constitutional and structural blueprint already exists. Immigration courts remain outside it, not because reform is impossible, but because the political branches have thus far tolerated a level of executive control over adjudication that the rest of the federal court system rejected decades ago.

The question is no longer whether an independent immigration court system can be built. The question is why it has taken this long to insist that immigration courts satisfy the same minimum standards of judicial independence expected everywhere else in American law. Courts cannot ask for public trust while remaining structurally dependent on the very authority appearing before them.

Independence is not a feature of a court system. It is the condition that makes a court possible.

text:
The Intersection of Immigration Status and Domestic Violence

Within the context of domestic violence, a survivor’s immigration status—or lack thereof—can become a devastating instrument of coercion. This dynamic is not merely a collateral issue in nonimmigration proceedings, but rather it can be a means to silence survivors and subvert the judicial process. Understanding immigration-related abuse is critical for judges presiding over nonimmigration matters where an abuser may leverage a party’s precarious immigration status to influence testimony, discourage reporting or cooperation with authorities, or manipulate outcomes.

A Tool of Power and Control

For noncitizen survivors of abuse in the United States, immigration status is often more than legal designation; it is also a profound vulnerability that abusers may exploit as a primary tool of power and control. These tactics often exist alongside other traditional forms of abuse. As Norma’s story demonstrates, this weaponization of a survivor’s immigration status can manifest as a compounding layer of coercion.

Coercion and threats of enforcement. First, an abuser may leverage a noncitizen’s immigration status as a form of coercion, using it both as a “carrot” to ensure compliance and as a “stick” to threaten the survivor’s security and safety.

Where the abuser is a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident (LPR), the survivor’s legal standing is often tethered to the abuser. For example, an abuser who is married to the survivor may serve as the indispensable “petitioner” for the survivor’s family-based immigration benefits. By threatening to withhold the applications necessary for the survivor to obtain lawful status, the abuser becomes a private “gatekeeper” to the survivor’s legal security. Through this dynamic, the administrative petitioning process becomes a powerful means to ensure compliance and punish defiance.

Similarly, in cases like Norma’s, abusers may leverage the threat of immigration enforcement as a strategic tool of coercion. By threatening to contact immigration authorities or local law enforcement, the abuser not only psychologically harms the survivor but also creates a powerful deterrent against the survivor seeking outside intervention, whether from family, friends, or the courts. This tactic becomes more powerful during periods of heightened immigration enforcement, which can escalate a survivor’s fear of both federal authorities and local justice systems. In many communities, the fear of engaging with local law enforcement is a rational response to the reality of information-sharing and enforcement partnerships between local and federal agencies. Consequently, a survivor may view the local police or the courthouse not as a refuge but as a gateway to deportation and permanent family separation.

In nonimmigration judicial proceedings, these dynamics may manifest as tactical interference with the litigation process. An abuser may unnecessarily disclose a survivor’s immigration status in divorce or child custody proceedings in an attempt to intimidate the survivor or bias the court. Furthermore, this systemic fear may result in a survivor’s hesitation to report violence, cooperate with law enforcement, or appear in court to testify, which may allow the abuser to weaponize the survivor’s silence to influence the outcome of the case.

Document and economic abuse. For noncitizens, personal documents are not only a means of identification; they are also essential to demonstrating authorization to work and live in the United States and to applying for certain immigration benefits. As in Norma’s case, abusers may withhold, steal, or destroy these documents—including passports, birth certificates, marriage certificates, and work permits—to immobilize the survivor legally and economically.

This document sabotage often functions in tandem with direct economic control. Abusers may control the survivor’s finances and, even if the survivor has work authorization, may prohibit them from earning an independent income. As with Norma’s case, abusers also may forge the survivor’s name on financial or property documents under the assumption that the survivor’s legal status (and possible fear of law enforcement) leaves them with little to no recourse.

Norma’s case demonstrates that abusers can use these tactics to prevent the survivor from obtaining outside help or achieving the legal and financial independence necessary to leave the relationship. In the courtroom, this abuse may manifest as the survivor’s inability to present necessary personal documents, hire counsel, or comply with court fees and financial disclosures required in judicial proceedings.

Compounded isolation. Abusers also may use isolation to further marginalize noncitizen survivors, weaponizing their lack of a domestic support network. While isolation is a hallmark of many domestic violence dynamics, it is often aggravated in cases of noncitizens. In these cases, a survivor may lack independent family, friends, or community ties to the United States, and language barriers may further limit their ability to navigate unfamiliar social and legal systems. Abusers may exploit these vulnerabilities by providing misinformation about U.S. laws or by convincing the survivor that seeking help will lead to their arrest and/or removal from the country. In judicial proceedings, this dynamic may result in a lack of corroborating witnesses, a failure to respond to proceedings due to the abuser’s interference with service of process or notice, and a hesitation to disclose abuse to the court.

Structural Barriers to Protection

Apart from their abusers’ direct control, noncitizen survivors also may face systemic hurdles that can make the courthouse intimidating or inaccessible. Abusers may strategically exploit these hurdles as a force multiplier for the tactics of power and control discussed in the previous section. Some of these structural barriers can include

Fear of enforcement at the courthouse: Especially for survivors without legal status, the real or perceived presence of immigration enforcement (including local law enforcement collaborating with federal agencies) can exert a powerful “chilling effect.” Survivors may fear that attending any hearing could lead to arrest, detention, and removal from the United States, which could mean permanent separation from children, other loved ones, and communities. As discussed above, abusers may weaponize this fear by disclosing the survivor’s immigration status in court proceedings.

Language access: Despite the legal right to an interpreter in many contexts, the lack of qualified, trauma-informed interpretation and translation at every stage of a proceeding may create communication gaps. In those cases, especially when compounded by the isolation that abusers impose, the survivor may be forced to rely on the abuser to “translate” court documents or legal advice. This allows the abuser to filter information, misrepresent the court’s orders, and maintain control over the survivor.

The “credibility gap”: Structural barriers also may result in behavior that a judge may initially perceive as a lack of credibility. A survivor’s hesitation to disclose abuse, their decision to recant testimony, or their failure to appear in court may not mean a lack of veracity but could be a rational response to the threats of retaliation described above.

Financial and logistical barriers: If an abuser has committed document and/or financial abuse as described in the prior section, survivors may struggle to pay court fees or fines, secure transportation, or even provide the basic identification necessary to enter government buildings for hearings.

Lack of civil legal access: In civil matters, a pervasive lack of legal access may exacerbate all other barriers. Noncitizen survivors may be ineligible for federally funded legal aid or, if they are eligible, may fear that seeking such aid will trigger enforcement. Without an attorney with specialized knowledge in the intersection of domestic violence and immigration law, a survivor lacks the procedural roadmap and sense of security and empowerment required to navigate a complex legal landscape.

This framework can provide helpful context for courts to distinguish between willful defiance and coerced inability. In a standard proceeding, a party’s failure to produce documents, pay fees, or appear for a hearing could communicate a lack of merit or disregard for judicial authority. However, in cases involving immigration-related abuse, these failures instead may stem from the abuser’s tactical interference—designed to trigger a court’s sanctions against the survivor—combined with systemic barriers. The following sections will discuss actions that both noncitizen survivors can take in achieving immigration security and courts can take in ensuring access and fairness for survivors.

Common Forms of Immigration Relief for Survivors

Because abusers frequently weaponize noncitizen survivors’ immigration status in domestic violence cases, federal law offers several protections intended to decouple a survivor’s legal standing from that of their abuser and to facilitate their independence. This section outlines the primary forms of immigration relief available to noncitizen survivors and the relevance of these protections to state and federal court proceedings.

It is important to note at the outset that these protections target specific criteria and do not apply to all noncitizen survivors. Even for the survivors who do qualify, many are not aware of these legal protections, may not recognize their experiences as abuse (especially if it is not physical), may fear exposing themselves to immigration enforcement by applying, and/or may lack the financial means and autonomy to locate counsel. Therefore, it is essential for judges to be aware of these protections to better understand the legal landscape and systemic pressures that may influence the testimony, behavior, and needs of the parties in their courtrooms.

The Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) self-petition: VAWA provides certain noncitizen spouses, parents, and children of abusive U.S. citizens or LPRs the ability to “self-petition” for lawful status. This process allows survivors who have suffered “battery or extreme cruelty” to seek a green card independently, removing the abuser’s ability to use the immigration petitioning process as a tool of threat or coercion. Because self-petitioners must demonstrate abuse, state and local court documents—including restraining orders, arrest records, and findings of fact in custody orders—often serve as critical proof in these cases.

U visas: The U nonimmigrant visa is available to survivors of certain qualifying crimes—including domestic violence, sexual assault, and felonious assault—who have suffered substantial mental or physical abuse. To qualify, applicants must demonstrate, among other things, that they have been, are being, or are likely to be helpful to government officials in the investigation or prosecution of the criminal activity. Applicants must document this “helpfulness” through a formal law enforcement certification (Form I-918B). As “certifying officials” under federal law, judges presiding over criminal cases may play a role in this process by verifying a survivor’s past or present cooperation within the judicial system.

T visas: The T nonimmigrant visa provides protection for survivors of “severe forms of human trafficking,” which includes both sex and labor trafficking. In a domestic violence context, these visas may provide protection where an abuser uses force, fraud, or coercion to compel a partner into labor (such as domestic servitude) or commercial sex. To qualify, most applicants must demonstrate compliance with any “reasonable request” for assistance from law enforcement and demonstrate that they would suffer “extreme hardship involving unusual and severe harm” if removed from the United States. While the law does not require T visa applicants to submit a law enforcement certification, a certification from a judge or prosecutor may serve as powerful evidence of the survivor’s cooperation.

Special Immigrant Juvenile Status (SIJS): For noncitizen children in situations of domestic violence, SIJS may provide another path to protection. SIJS provides lawful permanent residency to certain noncitizen children under age 21 who have suffered abuse or similar harm. While the federal government ultimately adjudicates the child’s eligibility for SIJS, the process cannot begin without an order from a state court with jurisdiction over juvenile matters making specific findings that (1) the child is dependent on the court or placed in the custody of an individual/agency; (2) reunification with one or both parents is not viable due to abuse, neglect, abandonment, or other similar basis under state law; and (3) it is not in the child’s best interest to return to their country of origin.

Recognizing the availability—and the limitations—of these immigration remedies allows courts to better contextualize a survivor’s behavior and testimony. These pathways also highlight the critical roles that local, state, and federal judges may play in a survivor’s pursuit of legal security. Building on this legal framework, the final section of this article offers practical considerations for the bench to promote procedural fairness and manage the unique challenges present in these cases.

Practical Considerations for the Bench

The combination of an abuser’s tactics and existing systemic barriers often creates an unlevel playing field that can severely distort the fact-finding process. As detailed above, abusers may leverage these factors not only to instill fear but also to weaponize the survivor’s vulnerabilities in an attempt to manipulate the legal process. The challenge for the bench is even more difficult because of invisibility; because of the survivor’s fear, a judge may never know that a party is a noncitizen survivor. However, through a proactive and informed approach, judges can create an environment that abusers are less likely to exploit, benefiting all parties and the justice system as a whole. The following are strategies that can help judges both identify hidden coercion and protect the safety and integrity of their proceedings.

Enhancing Courtroom Access and Procedural Fairness

Addressing structural barriers to access and procedural fairness not only helps survivors but also all parties, as well as the court. In cases involving noncitizen survivors, judges can use the following strategies to address status-based coercion:

Prioritizing meaningful language access: To prevent abusers from withholding or misrepresenting information, courts should prioritize qualified, independent interpreters over family members or children. Where possible, written translation of court notices and orders can prevent the abuser from being the sole source of information for the survivor.

Managing privacy and safety: Courts should limit the unnecessary disclosure of immigration status in open court. Where possible, judges should consider in camera reviews or the sealing of documents containing sensitive immigration information to protect the integrity of the litigation process and the safety of the parties.

Assessing Evidence and Credibility

As discussed above, abusers in cases involving noncitizen survivors may attempt to influence or suppress a survivor’s testimony. Behavior that at first glance may appear elusive, inconsistent, or not credible may actually be a response to immigration status–based threats and intimidation. By understanding the dynamics of status-related abuse, judges can better distinguish between a witness’s lack of veracity and an abuser’s tactical interference. These strategies can help ensure a more accurate and secure fact-finding process:

Distinguishing relevancy from prejudice: Courts should scrutinize attempts to disclose another party’s immigration status. Abusers may attempt to disclose a survivor’s immigration status as a tactic of control or intimidation, even where it is irrelevant to a case’s core legal issues.

Bridging the “credibility gap”: A survivor’s failure or hesitation to report violence, to mention certain details in a police report, or to testify can reflect trauma, intimidation, fear, or language barriers, and not necessarily a lack of veracity. Similarly, when a survivor suddenly recants testimony or expresses a desire to “drop” a protective order or charges against someone, the court should consider whether the choice is voluntary or a response to retaliation.

Identifying “litigation abuse”: Abusers may file meritless motions, seek unnecessary discovery of an immigration status or document, or repeatedly request hearings to force the survivor in public spaces where they may feel vulnerable to enforcement.

Defining Judicial Roles and Responsibility

While local, state, and federal judges do not adjudicate federal immigration benefits, as outlined above, their actions may sometimes serve as a foundation for a survivor’s application for immigration relief. Therefore, courts should maintain clarity regarding these distinct but sometimes overlapping roles:

Clarifying the court’s role: If a party’s immigration status becomes apparent in a judicial proceeding (due to disclosure or a party’s request for a certification, for example), judges should maintain transparency that the court’s primary focus remains on the specific legal matter (such as child custody) rather than the party’s immigration status. This clarity not only reminds parties of the court’s specific focus but also may reduce a party’s fears that the court is acting in an immigration enforcement role.

Executing statutory authority: Judges may hesitate to consider U visa certifications or make the factual findings required for SIJS out of concern that doing so exceeds their jurisdiction or effectively grants a federal immigration benefit. However, federal law specifically designates judges as “certifying officials” for U visas and as necessary issuing authorities for state court orders required in a child’s SIJS application process. These actions are administrative duties authorized by federal law, not adjudications of immigration status. A judge’s verification of a survivor’s “helpfulness” or a determination of a child’s “best interests” are factual findings that federal immigration authorities then use in their own ultimate adjudication of the benefit.

Preventing misrepresentation of judicial findings: As discussed above, noncitizen survivors may use court documents (such as protective orders, child custody orders, etc.) in requests for federal immigration benefits. Especially in these contexts, it is critical for judges to issue clear, fact-based findings rather than vague or generalized conclusions. Precise determinations ensure that federal immigration authorities can correctly interpret the court’s intent regarding the harm the survivor faced, the survivor’s cooperation, or a child’s need for protection.

Facilitating access to specialized resources: Courts can further the interests of justice by making available to all parties lists of free community legal and social service resources specialized in domestic violence and immigration support. Where possible, these resources should be available in multiple languages and clearly note the linguistic capabilities of each organization. Referring parties to trusted organizations ensures that survivors receive accurate legal advice and reduces the risk that survivors will fall victim to “notario” fraud or remain dependent on an abuser for legal information.

Conclusion

Status-based domestic violence can be a surreptitious, but significant, challenge to safety and justice—even outside of immigration proceedings. While judges may not have direct knowledge of these dynamics in a specific case, understanding their signs and effects equips the bench to identify red flags and create safe, equitable environments to advance justice for all parties. Ultimately, a proactive and informed judiciary ensures that the courthouse remains a neutral forum that determines legal outcomes by the merits of the case rather than the exploitation of a party’s status. In doing so, judges reinforce a fundamental promise of the U.S. legal system: that everyone, regardless of their origin, has the right to seek protection under the law.

text:
WASHINGTON – On Monday, United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin met with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) personnel at a cargo screening facility in Anchorage, Alaska, then met with Transportation Security Administration (TSA) workers at the Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport.

“Yesterday I had the privilege of meeting with the men and women of CBP and TSA in Anchorage, Alaska, and got to see firsthand the work that they do every day,” said Secretary Mullin. “Our DHS personnel are on the frontlines of stopping illicit drugs and illegal goods from entering our country and harming our citizens. It is an honor to lead this department and our more than 260,000 employees, and I will always fight for them and provide any support I can to make their jobs easier.”

Secretary Mullin tours a CBP cargo screening facility in Anchorage, Alaska

During the tour of the CBP cargo screening facility in Anchorage, Secretary Mullin observed cargo screening processes and received a briefing on seizure statistics.

Last week, Secretary Mullin toured the southern border in Brownsville, Texas, then met with ICE personnel at an ICE office in Florence, Colorado, followed by a tour of the Olympic training facility in Colorado Springs, Colorado.

description:
After winning the Makerfield by-election in June, Burnham promised to end "HMO Britain" and said he would change Britain's asylum accommodation system.
HMOs, or houses in multiple occupation, have been widely used by government contractors to house asylum seekers, often in lower income, urban areas.
Last week, there were anti-immigration demonstrations in the town of Thetford, Norfolk, with protesters attempting to enter homes where they believed asylum seekers were living.
Government statistics showed there were 97,519 people in receipt of asylum support at the end of March, with 20,885 in hotel accommodation.
Burnham, during his time serving as the mayor of Greater Manchester, threatened to block the region from housing any more asylum seekers in 2018.
text:
"We cannot have a situation where it's only the poorest communities in the country that receive all of the dispersal of refugees and asylum seekers," he told GB News on Tuesday.

His comments came in response to a question about protests which have taken place in the village of Piddington, Oxfordshire over plans to provide accommodation for asylum seekers on a nearby former military base.

But shadow home secretary Chris Philp, responding to Burnham's comments, said: "We shouldn't be housing illegal immigrants anywhere – wealthy or not."

Labour has pledged to stop using asylum hotels, a costly form of accommodation that has become a focal point for anti-migrant protests.

The government has sought to house migrants at military sites across the country instead, announcing in June that it planned to open three more including the site in Bicester, Oxfordshire.

The plans have prompted protests there, with residents of nearby Piddington voting to stage a symbolic referendum on leaving the UK.

Burnham said on Tuesday that he would listen to and address the concerns being raised.

"I don't know the issue yet in detail, but in some ways, as I understand it, it is about creating secure space," he said.

"We understand people's concerns and I will look into the issues raised by the good people of Piddington."

But he added: "I do believe all parts of the country need to work, to play their part."

After winning the Makerfield by-election in June, Burnham promised to end "HMO Britain" and said he would change Britain's asylum accommodation system.

HMOs, or houses in multiple occupation, have been widely used by government contractors to house asylum seekers, often in lower income, urban areas.

Last week, there were anti-immigration demonstrations in the town of Thetford, Norfolk, with protesters attempting to enter homes where they believed asylum seekers were living.

In response to Burnham's interview, Philp reiterated the Conservatives' policy of leaving the European Convention on Human Rights in order to deport migrants to their country of origin or a safe third country.

"Illegal immigrants should all be deported within a week of arrival - to their country of origin or a safe third country like Rwanda."

Government statistics showed there were 97,519 people in receipt of asylum support at the end of March, with 20,885 in hotel accommodation.

The figures added that 72,768 people were in other accommodation, including "dispersal accommodation" - which normally means houses in the community.

The remaining 3,866 people were in receipt of subsistence support only, according to the government.

The regions and nations with the highest number of asylum seekers in receipt of Home Office support included 19,578 in the north-west of England, 13,687 in London, 11,969 in the West Midlands and 8,635 in Yorkshire and the Humber.

The Home Office said the regions with the most supported asylum seekers as a proportion of their overall population were the north-east and north-west of England, with 26 and 25 supported people per 10,000 residents respectively.

It added the local authorities with the highest numbers of supported asylum seekers within them were Glasgow city (3,870), Birmingham (2,142), Liverpool (2,053), Coventry (1,712) and Belfast (1,607).

text:
More than 50 spouses and parents of active-duty U.S. service members have been detained by immigration authorities, triggering a new investigation by Congressional Democrats into whether the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Defense coordinated the enforcement actions.

The investigation follows an Associated Press review that found more than 50 military-connected family members detained. Military.com, citing the AP review, put the total at 52. Among those 52 people, Military.com reported that at least six cases resulted in deportation and at least eight people remained in immigration custody at the time of its article.

More than 60 Democratic lawmakers signed a letter sent Aug. 9, 2026, to DHS, DOD and the Department of Veterans Affairs requesting information about the alleged coordination and its legal and ethical implications. The probe is being led by Sen. Elizabeth Warren’s office, with participation from Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Tammy Duckworth and several House Democrats.

The Trump administration has rolled back immigration protections previously available to certain military families. The changes have had operational consequences for some service members, who have taken leave to care for children after their spouses were detained. In some cases, deployments were delayed.

In their letter, Democratic lawmakers questioned why military recruiters continue to promote immigration protections while protections for military-connected noncitizens have been reduced. They urged the administration to restore policies that shielded eligible military family members from immigration enforcement while allowing them to pursue adjustments to their legal status.

DHS said U.S. military service alone does not automatically confer lawful immigration status or exempt noncitizens from enforcement of immigration laws. The Pentagon declined to comment publicly on the congressional inquiry, saying it would respond directly to the lawmakers. The VA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Defense Department previously addressed its policies toward noncitizen military family members in a December letter to Democratic lawmakers. In that letter, DOD said it had not implemented recent policy changes concerning noncitizen family members and had not conducted an analysis of how deportations affect military readiness or morale.

The congressional investigation comes as the Trump administration has established a separate initiative focused on military families. President Donald Trump established the Military Spouse Commission on Aug. 6, 2026, with Jennifer Rauchet, the wife of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, serving as chair.

The commission is tasked with developing recommendations addressing military-spouse issues, including housing, employment, health care and child care, and is scheduled to meet monthly at the White House. In the Federal Register announcement establishing the commission, Trump said military spouses contribute to military readiness, retention and mission success.

Republican Sens. Roger Wicker of Mississippi and Jerry Moran of Kansas, who chair the Senate Armed Services and Veterans’ Affairs committees, respectively, did not respond to requests for comment.

text:
Biddeford resident Monica Davis was helping a friend move on a Monday morning in July when she saw a girl racing down the road saying, “They’ve just killed someone, ICE just killed someone in the street.”

That was how Davis, who lives a few blocks from Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero’s family, found out that he had been killed by federal immigration agents.

“I will just never forget that moment of discovering that it had happened right here in the center of town, right next to our home,” she said on Tuesday, holding a sign reading “ICE OUT” at a protest outside U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ Biddeford office.

“Using your voice, it’s a rare chance that we have in this world to be able to speak up for the things that we believe,” Davis added. “So I’m going to be just absolutely blasting my resistance to the ICE and Trump regime at every single opportunity that I get.”

Davis was among more than 150 people who lined Main Street on Tuesday, echoing calls for accountability and criticizing Collins for supporting an additional $70 billion in funding for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in congressional Republicans’ latest budget resolution.

The group also took time to remember Guerrero and the dozens of others who have died in detention or were shot by immigration agents nationally since President Donald Trump’s enforcement surge began.

Alessia Gaspar Da Silva, whose husband, Marcos, was taken by ICE in January and still remains in custody, spoke about the harsh conditions her husband has faced in detention, including being fed once every 30 hours, denied medical care, and relocated to different states without her knowledge.

“He’s been gone for seven months. It feels like a lifetime,” she said.

Da Silva told the crowd she has repeatedly reached out to Collins’ office. In response, she said she received a newsletter, listing the senator’s accomplishments.

“Collins has not done anything,” Da Silva said. “She has no accountability. No transparency. No transparency for the people that are … being terrorized.”

Democratic Maine lawmakers, including Sen. Henry Ingwersen from York County, and Reps. Ellie Sato from Gorham and Marc Malon from Biddeford attended, urging the crowd to vote this November.

“Susan’s vote to fund ICE with no strings attached was shameful. And we, as voters across this city, across this district, and across Maine, need to make this very clear to her,” Ingwersen said.

“Turn that anger into getting out to the polls, and we can start then to turn this around.”

Mainers from across the state joined Biddeford locals outside Collins’ office. Pam Ericson, a teacher at Lewiston Public Schools and Bath resident, said she attended the protest because of the fear ICE agents have caused in the community where she works.

“Something like that could have happened in Lewiston. The whole community is afraid,” she said.

“I work with kids who just came to the United States, and they don’t come to school. I have to give them rides, their families won’t go to work,” she added. “It’s very scary.”

Congress to hold field hearing on Biddeford ICE killing

The demonstration, which was organized by the Maine People’s Alliance and Center for Popular Democracy, was held the same day that U.S. Chellie Pingree announced that members of Congress will be holding a field hearing in Biddeford next week on ICE’s use of force in the case.

Pingree, along with U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee, and U.S. Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts will hear from representatives for the Guerrero family, local officials, community advocates, and others who will speak to the state of the investigation and the impact ICE’s operations have had on Maine.

Biddeford Mayor Liam LaFountain said in a statement Tuesday that he hopes that Republican members of Congress would also participate “because this is an issue that deserves serious attention and oversight from across the political spectrum.”

“Johan’s family and the people of Biddeford deserve a full and independent understanding of what occurred,” LaFountain said. “Federal authority must come with federal accountability, and Congress has an important role to play in providing that oversight when the exercise of federal authority results in the death of a member of our community.”

Attorney Ben Gideon, who represents the victim’s family, told Maine Public that the family is actively complying with the Maine Attorney General’s investigation but that no federal investigators have reached out.

The hearing, which is open to the public, will take place at 11:00 a.m. on Monday, August 17, at Biddeford High School’s Little Theater.

text:
SCARBOROUGH — On the shoulder of Manson-Libby Road in Scarborough on Monday, about five people recorded a video of a car pulling out of the Immigrations and Customs Enforcement facility across the road. Two left to follow the vehicle.

The group of individuals has been doing this since an ICE agent killed Biddeford resident Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in July.

“We’re just trying to monitor the facility and make sure that the people who go in for their appointments get out, and figure out where they’re taking the detainees,” said South Portland resident Nicholas Pottle.

According to an ICE spokesperson, the facility at 40 Manson-Libby Road is not a detention center but a processing facility. The spokesperson said people are brought in, processed, then transported to a detention facility.

The spokesperson did not identify themselves.

The Scarborough facility is the only one of its kind in Maine. And following the killing of Guerrero, Scarborough residents pressured the Town Council to attempt to review or remove the facility.

The Town Council complied. On July 29, the council unanimously passed a proclamation that called on Maine’s congressional delegation to work with federal officials to “review the existing facility and evaluate alternatives.” Those alternatives include “the relocation or discontinuation of such operations at that location.”

Since it’s under federal control, the council recognized that for now, the extent of its power lies in asking for a review. Democratic U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, whose district includes Scarborough, asked ICE and the Department of Homeland Security to review the facility and “give meaningful weight to the concerns raised by local residents and elected officials.”

Scarborough town councilors did not respond to a request for comment.

When asked if ICE intends to review the facility, the spokesperson said in a statement that it undergoes its own inspection processes.

“ICE detention facilities operate under federal law, detention standards, and contractual requirements, with multiple layers of oversight, including routine compliance reviews and DHS inspection processes. ICE also facilitates congressional visits consistent with federal law, operational needs, and security protocols. While state and local partners may assist where authorized, federal immigration detention remains under ICE’s authority,” the spokesperson said.

Although the group observing the facility is not part of any particular organization, they work together to maintain a log of ICE vehicles, when they come and go and other information. If the group can identify the families of detainees, they’ll set them up with legal resources.

Pottle said according to their observations, ICE is taking at least two people into the facility and out of state per day.

Directly after the killing of Guerrero, the shoulder across from the ICE facility had a lot more people, Pottle said. Now, the numbers are spread thin as people keep watch for ICE in their own neighborhoods, which has made surveillance of the facility hard.

"We want [ICE] gone,” Pottle said. “We want them out of the state. We want them to all lose their jobs. We want them to be shunned from society.”

text:
Washington, D.C. - Congresswoman Delia C. Ramirez (IL-03), Ranking Member of the House Veterans’ Affairs Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, joined U.S. Senators Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), to lead a bicameral letter pressing the Department of Defense (DoD), the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Veterans Affairs (VA), U.S. Customs and Border Protection, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on their coordinated efforts to arrest, detain, and deport hundreds of veterans and military families.

In April 2025, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) rescinded its long-standing policy that treated military service as a “significant mitigating factor” when deciding whether to pursue immigration enforcement, and replaced it with a new policy stating that military service alone “does not automatically exempt” non-citizens from enforcement actions. At the same time, DoD has continued to recruit new service members with the promise of immigration protections.

Recent reporting by the Associated Press reveals that, since January 2025, more than 50 parents and spouses of active-duty service members have been detained, and at least six have been deported. ICE’s statistics show that the agency has arrested 16 non-citizen armed forces members since the beginning of Fiscal Year 2026. Some service members have reportedly needed to take leave or delay deployment because ICE detained their families.

“These efforts [...] betray America’s promises to the people who put their lives on the line for our nation,” wrote the lawmakers. Alarmingly, DoD has been reportedly targeting individuals at military installations, detaining them on military property, and turning them over to ICE — effectively converting military bases into “traps” for noncitizens. For example, a 22-year-old military wife was recently detained while attempting to obtain a military spouse I.D. Military officials allegedly called DHS and held her in a room until ICE agents arrived to take her to a detention center.

“DoD’s participation in civil immigration enforcement activities raises both ethical and legal concerns, including potential violations of the Posse Comitatus Act, which prohibits using the armed forces of the military for civilian law enforcement,” wrote the lawmakers.

The members also warned that if service members were to be swept up in any of these enforcement actions, it could separately constitute a violation of the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which provides protections to all members of the United States military on active duty, including non-citizens, from civil actions—such as immigration proceedings—that interfere with their military duties.

The lawmakers requested that the agencies explain the enhanced coordination between DoD and DHS, restore long-standing immigration protections for family members of service members, and explain what steps they are taking to protect troops, veterans, and their families from unjust immigration enforcement by August 23, 2026.

In the House, the letter was coled by Representatives Chrissy Houlahan (D-Pa.), Maggie Goodlander (D-N.H.), Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), and Lizzie Fletcher (D-Texas) and signed by Representatives Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.), Nanette Barragán (D-Calif.), André Carson (D-Ind.), Greg Casar (D-Texas), Sean Casten (D-Ill.), Joaquin Castro (D-Texas), Gil Cisneros (D-Calif.), Bonnie Watson Coleman (D-N.J.), Daniel Davis (D-Ill.), Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.), Diana DeGette (D-Colo.), Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.), Maxine Dexter (D-Ore.), Veronica Escobar (D-Texas), Bill Foster (D-Ill.), Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.), Chuy García (D-Ill.), Sylvia Garcia (D-Texas), Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.), Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.), Hank Johnson (D-Ga.), Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), John Larson (D-Conn.), Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.), Seth Magaziner (D-R.I.), Seth Moulton (D-Mass.), Kevin Mullin (D-Calif.), Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), Mike Quigley (D-Ill.), Jan Schakowsky (D-Ill.), Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.), Marilyn Strickland (D-Wash.), Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Mark Takano (D-Calif.), Dina Titus (D-Nev.), Marc Veasey (D-Texas), Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), joined in signing the letter.
