text:
The US Department of State has canceled more than 175,000 visas since Donald Trump returned to office, quadrupling the pace of revocations under Joe Biden’s final year in the White House, according to a new tally released by the department this week.

The announcement said the revocations targeted foreign nationals who allegedly broke the terms of their visas, committed crimes, called for violence against Americans, defrauded US citizens, abused the immigration system or endangered national security. Many followed run-ins with law enforcement, the department said, with assault, drunk driving, theft and drug offenses the leading causes, alongside reckless driving, sexual assault, child abuse and fraud.

The state department published some anecdotal cases to bolster its revocation campaign . They included a man charged with felony rape and sexual battery of a victim with a mental disability, and another accused of kidnapping, trafficking and sexually exploiting a minor. Also cited were a man arrested on charges including drunk driving and domestic violence, and another accused of driving with heroin in his system while more than three times over the legal blood alcohol limit.

Biden’s state department revoked about 40,000 visas in 2024. Trump’s administration cancelled more than 100,000 in 2025 alone, and the monthly pace has kept climbing this year, from roughly 8,000 revocations a month in 2025 to more than 10,000 a month in 2026. The department has not said how the 175,000 figure breaks down by category, leaving unclear how many revocations stem from serious crimes as opposed to lesser infractions such as overstaying a visa.

Several revocations touched on political speech. The best-known case is that of Rümeysa Öztürk, a Turkish doctoral student at Tufts University whose visa was pulled after she co-wrote an opinion piece criticizing the university’s stance on the war in Gaza. She was detained by immigration authorities, though a judge later dismissed the case against her, and has since moved back to Turkey.

But the department said it had canceled the visas of multiple foreign nationals who commented on the killing of the conservative activist Charlie Kirk last September, including one who said Kirk had “died too late”.

Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, has also determined that a number of foreign nationals are deportable on foreign policy grounds, the department said, naming a Cuban national linked to an influence campaign tied to Havana, Iranian nationals connected to Tehran’s government and a Kuwaiti national accused of voicing hostility toward the US president.

Officials said a US embassy in north Africa had cancelled more than 100 visas held by parents accused of travelling to the US mainly so their children would be born American citizens. Trump has separately sought to restrict the practice through an executive order that is being challenged in court after a supreme court setback.

One case cited by the department involved a Laotian national, Tou Lue Vang, who was deported last month. Vang had been pardoned weeks earlier by the Minnesota governor, Tim Walz, over a 2005 conviction for sexually abusing a child.

Visa cancellations are separate from deportations, which fall to the Department of Homeland Security. That agency has said more than 605,000 people have been removed from the country since Trump took office, part of what the administration calls the largest deportation operation in US history.

Some immigration law experts have argued that the revocations are part of a broader effort to shrink legal immigration, all while providing as little information as possible.

“The Department of State’s statement lumps foreign policy cases together with DUI arrests and people’s political speech, making the headline number almost meaningless,” American Immigration Council’s senior policy counsel, Adriel D Orozco, said, “and raises serious questions about how much discretion the administration is exercising without meaningful accountability.”

The department described the revocations as the product of a continuous vetting system introduced last year, which screens roughly 55 million foreign nationals holding valid US visas for signs they no longer meet the conditions of their status.

“A US visa is a privilege, not a right,” the department said in the press release.

Federal prosecutors argue that the Connecticut law discriminates against U.S. citizens.

The Trump administration has filed similar lawsuits against 16 other states over the past few months.

In statements, Governor Ned Lamont (D) and Attorney General William Tong (D) said they planned to fight the lawsuit and remain committed to access to education for everyone.

“Connecticut is proud to have one of the best education systems in the nation, and we believe that our economy works best for everyone when more people have access to education opportunities,” Lamont said. “The Trump administration’s priorities remain completely out of touch with working families and the middle class.”

“Note to Trump—stay out of Connecticut,” Tong added. “How we run our schools and teach our kids is none of your business and you have no authority to force the sovereign State of Connecticut to deny our kids a future.”

text:
Dozens of people signed what they describe as a ‘people’s public health order’ on the west steps of the Capitol Monday. The action is in response to an active case of tuberculosis confirmed in June at an ICE, or U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, detention center in Aurora.

“We actually took the last health order that was issued by the state department of health [CDPHE], and we essentially just edited it out to say kind of what it should be saying at this point,” said Andrea Loya, executive director of Casa de Paz.

The event kicked off with a bit of theater as one speaker dressed in a similar costume to what Gov. Jared Polis wore to celebrate Colorado’s birthday earlier this month, a campy full red, white and blue cowboy suit. Another represented the health department, CDPHE, in a white doctor’s coat.

A surprise guest, Jill Hunsaker Ryan, the agency’s executive director, showed up as well, in solidarity, standing off to the side of the speakers in a red dress.

“I absolutely want to show support for the community. I understand their concerns,” said Ryan, who spoke publicly about the situation for the first time. “And really the issue is with GEO. And they could end this any day by letting public health gain access to their facility and providing the information that they need.”

When asked by CPR what’s stopping the state from acting, either by filing its own public health order or suing, she said that it has been acting, starting with “the communications route.” The state has not issued a Public Health Order.

“The community wants to see a public health order. Public health orders are great tools. It's one option. Everything is on the table,” she said. She added that she had hoped communications with GEO Group, which runs the facility, and ICE would be more expeditious.

In a statement, the agency she leads said GEO can end this impasse by providing the outstanding records and allowing public health officials to verify that everyone potentially exposed was identified, tested, and connected to appropriate care.

“That's the route we wanted to start with just because a public health order doesn't guarantee compliance. So we're hoping that that would work. But, like I said, all options are on the table, and we're evaluating this day by day,” Ryan said, noting the state used to have a collegial relationship with GEO.

The Adams County Health Department issued a public health order in June requiring compliance with a public health investigation. The state followed that up with a letter requesting records, contact tracing information and access to the facility in mid-July, as well as a deadline for cooperation, which is now three weeks old.

When asked about Ryan's presence at the event, Loya said: “The true form of solidarity is to actually issue a public health order.”

Speaker after speaker blasted ICE and GEO, punctuated with cries from attendees of “Shame!”

“They do not care about life or humanity. If they care, if they were doing a good job contact tracing, if they were doing a good job making sure this disease didn't spread, we don't know what's happening, said Miriam Ordoñez Rodriguez of the American Friends Service Committee. “It is a dark hole, and we need our agencies to go inside.”

They also had sharp words for state leaders.

“I want people to be aware of what's happening inside the GEO detention center. It's inhumane, it's cruel, and now with tuberculosis where we actually have state laws that could let public health go in there and do their job,” said Maureen Daly, an MD and retired public health physician. “GEO is calling the shots and not allowing them in.”

Since news of the TB case was announced in June, ICE and GEO have refused to let local and state public health officials investigate or comply with requests for cooperation and information. ICE has said there are no active cases at the GEO Aurora ICE Processing Center, that the person with the original case was removed, but it has provided no proof of any investigation or access to local public health.

The event was organized by the American Friends Service Committee, Casa de Paz, and The Shut Down GEO Aurora campaign.

They said they invited the governor, but he did not attend.

CPR reached out to GEO Group and ICE. GEO referred questions to ICE.

“This matter is under current litigation, and as of right now there is nothing else to add,” said an unnamed spokesperson from ICE Denver Public Affairs, noting nothing has changed since its last statement.

The Governor’s response

The governor’s office sent a press release to CPR that said: “The state is actively monitoring the situation and takes very seriously any claims that patients are not receiving the care needed when experiencing symptoms of illness.”

“The state is considering next steps including the option of a public health order should it be necessary,” said spokeswoman Ally Sullivan, via email.

She noted that since June, the state has requested access to the facility, sent “repeated demands” for information and transparency to the operator, “urged multiple federal agencies to demand GEO give us the information we need,” and has coordinated with public health agencies and partners to ensure access to testing following release.

“GEO asserts there is not an active case or an outbreak at the facility, and we hope that is true, but we lack critical information to ensure that is the case,” Sullivan said, adding that the state will continue to evaluate the public health risk and is asking GEO to work with Adams County Health or CDPHE to promptly resolve this matter.

text:
A federal appeals court cleared the way for the Trump administration to revive directives that put hundreds of thousands of migrants at risk to be deported under a fast-tracked process.

A three-judge panel for the US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit on Tuesday lifted a lower court order striking down the directives, which instruct officers to consider expedited removal for certain migrants who came to the US under a Biden-era humanitarian program.

The judges found that the immigration organizations that sued don’t have grounds, or standing, to challenge the directives. The groups didn’t show that a ruling in their favor would shield their members from deportation, because a decades-old regulation already gives officers the authority to place some migrants in a faster deportation process, the panel said.

“Plaintiffs cannot seek relief that changes nothing for them,” the panel wrote in a per curiam opinion.

Chief Judge Sri Srinivasan, an Obama appointee, and Judges Neomi Rao and Justin Walker, both Trump appointees, sat on the panel.

Tuesday’s ruling deals a blow to immigrant advocacy groups that challenged the policies, which affect migrants from Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua, and Venezuela who were living in the US under the prior administration’s so-called parole program. The Trump administration moved to end these protections shortly after taking office, and the Supreme Court gave the government the green light to do so last year.

The ruling throws out an August 2025 decision by Judge Jia Cobb of the US District Court for the District of Columbia, who halted the deportation directives. Cobb, a Biden appointee, said in her opinion that these migrants “played by the rules” and the government then “changed the game.”

The appellate panel appeared skeptical during March oral argument that Cobb’s ruling could be effective, given the presence of a 1997 regulation that defines migrants who entered on parole, a temporary means of entering the US, as “arriving aliens” subjected to expedited removal.

Esther Sung of Justice Action Center, an attorney for the immigrant groups, argued at the hearing that the more recent directives factually created a different situation, since so few migrants who entered under parole previously faced expedited removal.

However, the appeals court found Tuesday the organizations had what it described as a “fatal redressability problem.” Even if the number of migrants put in a fast-tracked deportation process increased as a result of the challenged policies, that doesn’t mean striking the directives down “will reverse that trend,” the panel said.

The decision represents the latest victory for the Trump administration’s deportation agenda. In June, the DC Circuit upheld the administration’s efforts to expand eligibility for expedited removal in a separate challenge. The Supreme Court also blessed earlier this year the administration’s move to end Temporary Protected Status, another form of deportation relief for immigrants from certain countries in crisis, for Haitians.

The case is Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights v. Markwayne Mullin, D.C. Cir., No. 25-05289, 8/11/26.

text:
WASHINGTON, Aug 11 (Reuters) – Four leading U.S. human rights groups on Tuesday sued the Trump administration over its campaign aimed at dismantling the International Criminal Court, calling the effort unconstitutional.

President Donald Trump last ​year issued an executive order authorizing sanctions on prosecutors, judges and ‌others working with the court for pursuing cases against officials from the U.S. and its ally Israel, neither of which are members of the ICC.

Human Rights Watch, the Open Society Institute, the American Friends Service Committee and the Center for Constitutional Rights said in ‌their ​lawsuit filed in New York that those sanctions prevent ⁠them from working with ⁠the court to seek justice for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity around the world.

“The plaintiffs are seeking an end to this sanctions regime, which transgresses the president’s authority and violates international and U.S. law, ​including the rights to freedom of expression and religion,” lead counsel Andrew Loewenstein of Foley Hoag LLP, which is representing the human rights groups, said in ⁠a statement.

The lawsuit comes after a similar ⁠lawsuit filed last month by advocacy groups who work on ​human rights for Palestinians. In response to that lawsuit, the State Department said ​the groups were seeking to “enable ICC overreach” and said the court ‌posed a threat to U.S. sovereignty.

Three ICC judges have separately sued the Trump administration over the sanctions.

Trump’s opposition toward the ICC goes back to his first term. A similar executive order Trump issued in 2020 was blocked by a judge, who ⁠said it likely violated the First Amendment, before being rescinded by President Joe Biden’s administration in 2021.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio last month said the administration would step up ⁠efforts to undermine the ‌court in The Hague, including with a diplomatic campaign aimed ⁠at persuading other countries to quit it. Rubio argued ​that ‌the court posed a threat to U.S. personnel carrying ​out Trump’s hardline ⁠immigration policies or strikes on boats accused of carrying drugs, as well as other U.S. service members.

Trump during a July 31 cabinet meeting said in response to an update from Rubio that the campaign was aimed at defending Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and others, rather than Trump himself.

(Reporting by Simon Lewis; ​Editing by Stephen Coates)

text:
The United States has deported hundreds of Mexican children who crossed the border without their families on flights to southern Mexico, where many have gotten stuck without the resources to go home safely.

Multiple organizations that monitor and support children who are migrating without parents or guardians raised alarms over the issue in a hearing with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights on Aug. 3. The organizations said they have confirmed more than 350 cases, but it’s not clear how many children in all have ended up by themselves in Mexico’s southern cities.

Though the U.S. began deporting Mexican adults and families to Tapachula and Villahermosa soon after President Donald Trump returned to office, flying unaccompanied children south appears to be a more recent change.

The policy, which organizations said they discovered in December of last year, has resulted in disappeared children — along with concerns that some may be dead.

“It doesn’t make sense to send a minor 2,000 miles from their family member, ever,” said Savi Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First. “That’s just never appropriate.”

Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the U.S. agency responsible for deportations, did not respond to a request for comment from Capital & Main.

Many children deported by plane to southern Mexico live in northern border towns, where, recruited by criminal organizations to assist in leading other migrants to the U.S., they have crossed and returned many times in what is known as circuit migration, according to Derechos Humanos Integrales en Acción, an organization that works to reintegrate these children in the border city of Ciudad Juárez.

These children have a particular set of needs and vulnerabilities because they come from areas where a lack of economic resources pushes them into working for criminal organizations, according to the testimony from civil society organizations at the international human rights hearing.

Before Trump returned to office, U.S. border officials deported Mexican children who cross without parents or guardians rapidly at the land border, where they go into the care of Desarrollo Integral Familiar, commonly known as DIF, which serves as the country’s child welfare services agency, said Blanca Navarrete, director of Derechos Humanos Integrales en Acción.

Local offices known as Procuradurías de Protección de Niñas, Niños y Adolescentes, or offices for the protection of girls, boys and adolescents, which are part of DIF, are responsible for helping the children return to their families and reintegrate in their communities.

In the border state of Chihuahua, Derechos Humanos Integrales en Acción has had an agreement for roughly nine years with the local protection office to support children reintegrating from circuit migration, Navarrete said. The organization assists the children with exams to get certificates for primary and secondary school so that they can continue with their education and offers scholarships to help. Its staff also give psychoemotional support and referrals for children needing help with addiction and substance abuse.

More than 200 children are currently participating in the organization’s program, Navarrete said.

But in Tapachula and Villahermosa, both cities with scarce resources for supporting even their own residents, the local protection offices aren’t used to serving this particular profile of needs, according to Rosalba Rivera, who works on issues relating to children with IMUMI, a Mexico City-based nonprofit that supports migrant women and children.

“There’s no justification, from our point of view, for sending them all the way there,” Rivera said in Spanish. “On the contrary, it seems to be a type of punishment, because they’re not attending to the causes of the problem, the reason why these adolescents were or are dedicated to what they’re dedicated to.”

In the southern Mexico cities of Tapachula and Villahermosa — and more recently in Mérida on the Yucatán Peninsula — the children end up in shelters called centros de asistencia social, or social assistance centers, which are more accustomed to caring for children migrating north from other countries, Rivera said. Because some of the deported children worked for different criminal organizations, the centers have to separate those who might consider themselves rivals, according to Rivera’s colleague Sandra Mejia, an attorney with IMUMI.

Many families do not have the money to pay for their children to return home, so some have languished for months in the southern cities.

Mejia said some of the children don’t have families to go home to, and others’ families are themselves involved in criminal organizations, complicating the process of determining what would be safest for those children.

Arvey from Human Rights First said that some families are able to get their children as far north as Monterrey on flights, but then the children have to figure out the rest of the journey to Tamaulipas, the border state where many are from. She said cartels have even paid for some children’s flights in order to re-recruit them.

“Now this is just making the security situation worse,” Arvey said. “It’s also making it more likely they’ll be re-recruited instead of reunited with family and accessing services like with DHIA.”

Both Derechos Humanos Integrales en Acción and IMUMI have watched with growing concern the increasing number of reported disappearances of deported children from the children’s centers in the south.

“They’ve found some, and some we don’t know exactly what happened to them,” Rivera said. “But what’s certain is that there’s no restoration of their rights, nor in all of the cases has there been a safe family reunification.”

Navarrete said her organization has received information that suggests the possible deaths of three children who had traveled north to return to their communities, but she hasn’t been able to confirm the details or circumstances.

“We’re worried because the authorities haven’t said anything or announced any investigation,” Navarrete said.

Mexico’s child welfare agency, DIF, did not respond to a request for comment from Capital & Main.

At the Aug. 3 hearing, representatives from several organizations sitting on one side of the room listed questions they wanted answered by the Mexican government, including what is in the agreement with the U.S. that has allowed deportations of unaccompanied children by plane to the south and how many children overall the policy has affected.

“It’s a concern about another opaque agreement,” Arvey said. “We know the U.S. and Mexico have these opaque, unwritten agreements supposedly about sending third country nationals to Mexico. This is another agreement between the two governments with no transparency and putting vulnerable people at harm.”

Commissioners with the international human rights tribunal also asked questions, including how Mexico is addressing the root causes of the children’s need to join the criminal organizations to begin with, as well as whose responsibility it is to protect the children once they’ve arrived in southern Mexico.

Mexican officials sitting on the other side of the room said that Mexico offers consular services to children in U.S. custody and that the country has set up the program México Te Abraza, or Mexico Embraces You, to receive and support deportees.

“The Instituto Nacional de Migración offers information, orientation, protection, security, attention and dignified treatment to repatriated Mexican nationals when they return to our country,” said César Villanueva, who directs the Human Rights and Democracy Office in Mexico’s foreign affairs department. “Beyond the law of migration and its rules, the institute has a solid legal framework with mechanisms for the protection of girls, boys and adolescents.”

But, the Mexican officials did not address the civil society organizations’ questions about the unaccompanied children sent away on deportation flights.

“Our fear has come to pass,” Navarrete said during the hearing. “We’ve heard the information provided by the Mexican state about how protocols for repatriated children and adolescents should operate in a general manner, but we haven’t heard the responses to why norms aren’t being implemented or why the absence of specific protocols for adolescents at high risk or with vulnerabilities.”

She told Capital & Main that even though the deportation flights started with a U.S. decision, she’s focusing on holding Mexico accountable for what happens to its citizen children after they arrive in the south. That, she said, is entirely Mexico’s responsibility.

“What worried us was the lack of answers by the state of Mexico at the hearing,” Navarrete said. “The majority of the questions are still in the air.”

text:
Over four sessions, the American Civil Liberties Union of San Diego and Imperial Counties will teach attendees about immigration enforcement, student rights, interactions with law enforcement and the detention and deportation system.

Written by Kate Morrissey, Edited by Lauren J. Mapp

The American Civil Liberties Union of San Diego and Imperial Counties is hosting a series of free, virtual education sessions beginning on Thursday to teach people about immigrant rights.

The first session will include a panel discussion about what immigration enforcement is looking like across the country and how communities are responding, and the second will focus on immigrant student rights in and around K-12 schools. The third will teach attendees what rights they have when interacting with immigration officers and agents, and the final session will cover the detention and deportation system.

“We're living in a time where there's a lot of fear and confusion and misinformation about people's rights, and this administration, the tactics that they're using are changing daily,” said Eddie Meyer, senior policy advocate on advancing immigrant rights for the organization. “I'm excited to be able to provide information to anybody who wants to learn how they can protect their rights, how they can protect other people's rights and safely observe something that is going on that they feel is unjust and how to report it.”

The series is part of a larger effort this year by the organization called EmpowerEd, which has offered sessions on housing, public safety and education.

Meyer said interpreters will translate all of the immigrant rights sessions into Spanish, and that attendees can request potential support for other languages in advance.

Community members have been asking the local ACLU for more Know Your Rights workshops specific to immigration enforcement, Meyer said.

The first session will include a discussion of what communities hardest hit by aggressive immigration enforcement have found successful for protecting each other, he said.

“I think the most important thing we need to do right now is ensure that people understand what their rights are, that people are reporting what they witness and feel safe about it,” Meyer said. “You should be able to observe what's going on, record it and report it if you think there was some illegal activity or civil rights were violated.”

“Like all Americans, Washingtonians deserve local control and accountability,” Bowser said. “My North Star remains clear: protect Home Rule, protect DC’s autonomy, and protect DC residents.”

Bowser said the federal intervention brought national attention to the District’s lack of statehood and autonomy at a time when D.C. officials were already working to reduce crime following a post-pandemic spike.

“One year ago, an unprecedented federal intervention brought national attention to D.C.’s lack of statehood and autonomy,” Bowser said.

According to the mayor, overall crime is down 20% year over year, 26% compared with 2024 and 40% compared with 2023. She also said homicides have declined sharply.

Bowser credited the District’s response during the federal surge, including the creation of an Emergency Operations Center, with helping protect D.C.’s Home Rule authority while maintaining a focus on public safety.

“We preserved our autonomy, we saved lives by keeping our focus on public safety, and throughout the surge, we ensured DC residents were able to peacefully exercise their First Amendment rights,” Bowser said.

The mayor argued that the District’s response demonstrated there was no need for extended federal emergency action.

Her statement comes as District and federal officials mark one year since the federal surge began in Washington.

text:
BALTIMORE —

Baltimore police bodycam footage shows the aftermath of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting Jesus Acevedo-Sanchez and his wife, who lack legal immigration status, outside Commodore John Rodgers School in June while their children were in the vehicle.

The video begins with Baltimore police responding to a call from a distraught school employee who witnessed the incident.

"We've been informed they're not supposed to do that; they cannot come onto our property. They chased the vehicle, took a man, dragged him out of his vehicle in front of children, in front of his daughter, his son," she said, becoming emotional while describing the scene.

An officer on the scene informed the employee that Baltimore police could not intervene because the matter involved ICE. He explained how the school could follow up on its concerns.

"Look, I understand, I mean, the kids, someone's own kids shouldn't witness that, but let alone the whole school," the officer said. The employee responded, "Yeah, it was very traumatizing."

The officer also expressed concerns about ICE's operations.

"Everything with ICE, like I said, our policies and the guidelines and laws we abide by, it seems like they operate totally different, you see what I'm saying?" he said.

A police supervisor arrived shortly after and reiterated the employee's concerns.

"They're not supposed to be on school property, hospitals, or courtrooms, but unfortunately, the political era we're in now, they do what they want," the supervisor said. The original officer added, "That's what I was telling her, you know, we don't get involved because they operate in a manner we don't operate in, you know what I mean?"

The supervisor later commented, "Boy, oh boy, that's why it's important that we vote."

ICE officials stated that Acevedo-Sanchez resisted arrest, fled to the school, and dragged an agent in the process. Late last month, a federal court judge ruled that ICE officers conducted an "invalid" and "warrantless" arrest, violating Acevedo-Sanchez's Fifth Amendment right to due process.

The judge ordered the release of both parents, and the family's attorney has requested privacy.

text:
According to DHS, the initiative is intended to improve processing efficiency, reduce operational costs, strengthen fraud detection capabilities, and enhance national security screening by increasing the availability and accessibility of immigration data.

What the New Rule Does

The rule does not immediately make all USCIS forms electronic-only. Instead, it gives USCIS authority to require online filing for any immigration form that:

Has been available for e-filing for at least 180 days; and

Has been specifically designated by USCIS for mandatory electronic filing.

Before a form becomes mandatory for e-filing, USCIS must provide at least 60 days’ advance notice on its website.

Applicants will generally submit filings through a USCIS online account by either:

Completing the form online; or

Uploading a PDF version of the completed form and supporting evidence.

Why USCIS Is Making the Change

DHS states that the agency continues to process millions of paper filings each year.

In FY 2025:

USCIS processed more than 14 million benefit requests.

Lockbox facilities handled approximately 453 million pages of paper submissions.

USCIS spent approximately $396 million operating lockbox intake systems and more than $10 million in postage costs alone.

DHS believes mandatory e-filing will reduce manual handling, data entry, shipping, storage, and scanning costs while accelerating adjudication workflows.

Forms Already Available for E-Filing

USCIS currently offers electronic filing for numerous forms, including:

Form I-130 (Petition for Alien Relative)

Form I-765 (Application for Employment Authorization)

Form I-821 (Temporary Protected Status)

Form I-589 (Asylum Application)

Form I-907 (Premium Processing)

Form N-400 (Naturalization)

Form I-129 H-1B filings

Various citizenship and travel document applications.

USCIS reported that approximately 44% of filings in FY 2025 were already submitted electronically.

New Waiver Process for Individuals Unable to File Online

Recognizing that not all applicants may be able to file electronically, DHS is creating a formal waiver process.

Individuals who believe electronic filing would create an undue hardship may request an exemption by filing a new form:

Form I-936, Request for Waiver of E-Filing Requirement

Key details include:

Filing fee: $25

Waivers granted at USCIS discretion

Applicants must demonstrate why they cannot reasonably use the online filing system

USCIS may consider factors such as geographic location, socioeconomic conditions, and access to technology.

USCIS noted that lack of familiarity with online filing alone will generally not qualify for a waiver.

Fraud Detection and National Security Benefits

A major focus of the rule is improving immigration system integrity.

DHS states that electronic filing enables:

Faster fraud detection;

Better identity verification;

Improved data analytics;

Enhanced information sharing among government agencies;

Greater consistency in adjudications; and

Expanded national security vetting capabilities.

The agency noted that digital filings are easier to search, analyze, and cross-reference than paper records, making it easier to detect suspicious filing patterns and potential fraud.

title: How an immigration enforcement stalemate with Home Depot reached the Capitol - Sacramento Bee
description:
Newman said Home Depot had declined to provide a list of locations where raids occurred and refused to acknowledge immigration enforcement actions were taking place at its stores.
At the center of the debate was how much responsibility private retailers should bear when federal immigration enforcement takes place on their property.
In an attempt to deliver on President Donald Trump’s promise of record-level deportations last summer, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement shifted tactics.
“The number of people that have been impacted as a result, the number of people that have been harmed as a result of these immigration raids, that have been killed as a result of these immigration raids, it’s all important,” Pérez said.
“We’re not asking for the moon and the stars from Home Depot,” Newman said.
text:
After immigration raids swept across Southern California Home Depot parking lots last summer, advocates hoped they could work with the retailer to address the fear that had taken hold among day laborers who gathered outside the stores looking for work.

But a September 2025 meeting between Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, National Day Laborer Organizing Network representatives and Home Depot executives instead convinced NDLON that voluntary cooperation had reached a dead end, general counsel Chris Newman said.

Newman said Home Depot had declined to provide a list of locations where raids occurred and refused to acknowledge immigration enforcement actions were taking place at its stores.

“If you’re not even willing to acknowledge where these raids are happening, how can we talk about a shared strategy to mitigate a human rights crisis that is clearly happening at their stores?” Newman said. “People have been killed. And so the rest of the meeting, obviously, was quite awkward.”

That stalemate would eventually move from Los Angeles City Hall to the state Capitol, where the legislative process proved more conducive to negotiation. At the center of the debate was how much responsibility private retailers should bear when federal immigration enforcement takes place on their property.

Nearly a year later, lawmakers are considering a compromise that has substantially narrowed that divide.

In an attempt to deliver on President Donald Trump’s promise of record-level deportations last summer, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement shifted tactics. Stephen Miller, a senior White House official, instructed the agency to target places where migrants often congregate, including Home Depot.

Instead of operations aimed at specific individuals, federal agents increasingly conducted sweeps outside of Home Depot storefronts — where day laborers have long gathered to be hired for work. Several of the raids grew violent, and one ended in the death of 52-year-old Roberto Carlos Montoya Valdez, who was struck by a vehicle in August 2025 while fleeing immigration enforcement in Los Angeles.

Home Depot remained largely silent about the enforcement activity occurring on its properties. It said only that it did not receive advance notice of raids and could not interfere with law enforcement. Newman believes the company’s silence on the raids was a political calculation.

“My guess is that they continue to be more afraid of being denounced on the Sean Hannity show, or by Tucker Carlson or Steve Bannon, than they are of the denunciation of protesters outside their stores,” Newman said. “In part, because they borderline have a monopoly on small residential retail services.”

Newman said with the company seemingly unwilling to collaborate, NDLON approached state Sen. Sasha Pérez, D-Alhambra, to explore whether legislation could accomplish what voluntary discussions had not.

Pérez worked with the organization to introduce SB 1103, a bill that has since undergone months of negotiation in the Capitol. If passed, it would require large retail stores to preserve and provide documentation of immigration enforcement activity occurring on their premises when requested by the California attorney general or county governments.

After Valdez was killed fleeing a Home Depot in her district, Pérez said his family had reached out to the retailer for video surveillance footage. It did not provide the footage at the time. Without it, she said, Valdez’s family was left with unanswered questions about his death and the broader community did not feel justice had been served.

“The number of people that have been impacted as a result, the number of people that have been harmed as a result of these immigration raids, that have been killed as a result of these immigration raids, it’s all important,” Pérez said. “There is value to us monitoring what has happened here.”

The initial version of the bill, which Pérez named the REPAIR Act of 2026, placed much of the reporting burden on retailers themselves. Large home-improvement chains would have been required to send documentation of immigration enforcement activity to the California attorney general within 24 hours and publish daily reports detailing raids at their stores.

In committee, however, legislators debated whether private companies should be responsible for monitoring federal law enforcement. Lawmakers eliminated the daily reporting requirement and shift responsibility for tracking and publicizing enforcement activity to local and state agencies.

“I think the amendments were fair. I feel really good about where the bill is,” Pérez said. “It would be the first in the nation to pass and gives us a way to better track these events.”

Loading…

Rachel Michelin, CEO of the California Retailers Association, which represents retailers including Home Depot, praised Pérez for listening to the industry’s concerns and working with retailers to amend the bill.

The association remains opposed, however. Michelin said its remaining concerns include a provision allowing designated county agencies to request records from retailers, which she worries could be misused.

Home Depot referred requests for comment on the bill to the California Retailers Association, but did not answer follow-up questions about whether it shares the association’s position.

Nearly a year after their meeting, Newman said neither Home Depot nor Mayor Bass has responded to NDLON’s requests for further discussion. The organization wishes the legislation went further, he said, but for now, it is focused on getting something to the governor’s desk.

“We’re not asking for the moon and the stars from Home Depot,” Newman said. “To the contrary, we’re asking them to do more than they are currently doing, which is nothing. Nothing at all.”

text:
Sign up to receive the Early Edition in your inbox here.

A curated weekday guide to major news and developments over the last 24 hours. Here’s today’s news:

IRAN WAR

President Trump told reporters yesterday that the United States is “the only one” that controls the Strait of Hormuz, calling the U.S. naval blockade on Iran a “steel wall.” Trump also responded to Iran’s conditions for a peace deal with his own demands that Iran pay compensation for people killed in wars, attacks, and protests, telling reporters, “if there’s damages to be paid, I think Iran should pay those damages.” In particular, Trump said Iran should compensate families of the 17 U.S. sailors killed in an October 2000 attack in Yemen on USS Cole, which has been attributed to al Qaeda, not Iran. Duarte Dias reports for CBS News; Steve Holland and Jacon Bogage report for Reuters.

IRAN WAR – OTHER DEVELOPMENTS

Last month, Trump flew out of Ankara in secret on an alternate military aircraft while the White House said he was aboard Air Force One, the Washington Post learned, following a credible threat to Trump’s life involving Iran. The mission was carried out unbeknownst to journalists and some White House staff members who believed they were on the same plane as the president, according to material reviewed by the Post and a U.S. official. Dan Lamothe, John Hudson, Andrew Ba Tran, and Joyce Sohyun Lee report.

RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR

Russian attacks this morning killed at least six people and wounded 20 in the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, officials said. A further three civilians were killed by Russian drones and artillery in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. The strikes also hit Kyiv, triggering fires in the capital. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian forces used ballistic missiles supplied by North Korea on Zaporizhzhia. Reuters reports; Illia Novikov reports for AP News.

Ukraine is considering shipping grain by rail through Moldova as a more secure export option than by sea and has asked authorities in Chisinau for a low freight tariff, sources in both countries told Reuters yesterday. The need for a rail route has arisen in connection with Russian attacks on the Odesa port hub. Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said yesterday that his country should not lose ⁠the ​opportunity to earn millions of euros in transit revenue from Ukrainian grain ​cargo. Pavel Polityuk and Alexander Tanas report.

Russia’s Supreme Court yesterday blocked Russia’s only antiwar party, Yabloko, from running in next month’s parliamentary elections, citing alleged copyright violations and claims that it threatened Russia’s territorial integrity. Nataliya Vasilyeva reports for the New York Times.

Former Ukrainian detainees and Ukrainian officials yesterday accused Russia of systematically torturing prisoners of war and civilian detainees. Russia rejected the allegations made at an informal U.N. Security Council meeting, with its Deputy U.N. Representative Maria Zabolotskaya calling it “a disinformation campaign” and alleging that Russian prisoners in Ukraine were subjected to “torture and degradation and moral and physical abuse.” David Brunnstrom and Andrea Shalal report for Reuters.

ISRAEL-HAMAS WAR

A Board of Peace official said yesterday that its 15-point Gaza plan is still operative and discussions with Israel are continuing, even after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu restated his rejection of the plan. Steve Holland reports for Reuters.

OTHER GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTS

A Syrian court today sentenced ousted Syrian President Bashar al-Assad and his younger brother Maher to death in absentia for crimes against humanity and war crimes during Syria’s 14-year conflict. Ghaith Alsayed and Samar Kassabali report for AP News.

Turkey yesterday adopted a law aimed at advancing its peace process with the Kurdistan Workers’ Party. The law, which passed by a vote of 468-to-88 in Parliament, could allow for the repatriation of thousands of militants from the group, known as the P.K.K. It may also lead to the suspension of prison sentences for people convicted of belonging to or supporting the group. Ben Hubbard and Safar Timur report for the New York Times.

Taiwan yesterday carried out a 30-minute planned disruption of mobile data as part of an effort to test how the island might cope if a Chinese attack disrupted communications. The activity was part of Taiwan’s annual civil defense exercise, when the government tries to give citizens a sense of how they should respond if China tried to seize the island. Chris Buckley and Amy Chang Chien report for the New York Times.

A 7.4 magnitude earthquake hit Colombia yesterday, killing at least 111 people, according to Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella. Search and rescue efforts remain underway this morning. Astrid Suarez, Manuel Rueda, and Megan Janetsky report for AP News.

TECH DEVELOPMENTS

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg yesterday published a 6,500-word essay, entitled “The Future is for Everyone,” setting out his thoughts on AI distribution, regulation, safety, and cooperation. Zuckerberg said Meta would release more open-weight AI models and establish a $1 billion fund for communities where Meta hosts data centers. Meghan Bobrowsky reports for the Wall Street Journal.

A federal appeals court yesterday allowed thousands of lawsuits against Meta, Google, TikTok, and Snapchat over claims they designed their products to be addictive to young users to proceed. The court rejected an appeal by Meta and TikTok, ruling that the companies had appealed too early against a lower court ruling rejecting their Section 230 immunity defense. Diana Novak Jones reports for Reuters.

U.S. FOREIGN AFFAIRS

The International Atomic Energy Agency will soon remove nuclear material stored at a clandestine site in Syria linked to the Assad regime’s former nuclear program after the Trump administration reached understandings with Syria and Israel, according to U.S. and Israeli officials. Barak Ravid reports for Axios.

U.S. IMMIGRATION DEVELOPMENTS

The State Department said yesterday that it has revoked more than 175,000 visas from foreign nationals under Trump’s second administration. Most visas were revoked following “law enforcement encounters,” with assault, driving under the influence, theft, and drug crimes as the leading causes, the department added. Reuters reports.

The New York Times reports that the Trump administration has sharply intensified efforts to identify and deport noncitizens who appear on voter rolls, including some who say they registered accidentally or never voted. Madeleine Ngo, Nick Corasaniti, and Hamed Aleaziz report.

U.S. DOMESTIC DEVELOPMENTS

Former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall said yesterday that he will file a lawsuit to force the Trump administration to restore his security clearance, which was revoked on Friday after claims that Kendall had disclosed sensitive information about the Qatar-gifted jet now serving as Air Force One. Nicholas Riccardi and Konstantin Toropin report for AP News.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ACTIONS

Trump signed an executive order promoting a childhood vaccination schedule that spaces shots out and separates the MMR vaccine into individual doses, despite medical groups warning this could increase the risk of preventable infections. Speaking about the order, Trump repeatedly suggested that the number or timing of vaccines could play a role in rising rates of autism spectrum disorder. Ali Swenson and Collin Binkley report for AP News.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION LITIGATION

A federal judge yesterday dismissed five of Minnesota’s six claims against the Trump administration’s interpretation of Title IX, the federal law that bars sex discrimination. The judge allowed the remaining claim to proceed because Minnesota could lose roughly $2.9 billion in federal funding. Bianca Quilantan reports for POLITICO.

text:
Revenue grew more than 27% for private prison operator CoreCivic as the Tennessee company profited from contracts with Immigration and Customs Enforcement that support the Trump administration's mass detention and deportation agenda, according to a shareholders' report released last week.

Revenue from ICE, alone, increased more than 50% compared to the same three-month period last year as the company housed more immigrants and negotiated higher daily fees for detaining them at facilities across the country. CoreCivic also contracts with states to operate prisons across the nation, including four in Tennessee.

CoreCivic's profits are also linked to several lucrative real estate deals with the Department of Homeland Security to expand the federal government's detention capacity. Since July the company has sold four lockups in California, Minnesota and Kansas to the federal government to house immigrant detainees. In total, it earned $2.2 billion from the sales. CoreCivic will continue to operate the same four detention facilities under new managment contracts with ICE.

In last week's earnings call, CEO Patrick Swindle expressed optimism about future deals with ICE. The company's immigrant detainee population is on pace to rise – it has grown by nearly 18% since April. Swindle said the company is in negotiations to potentially sell more of its detention centers to the federal government.

"The solutions we provide to our federal customers, including primarily ICE and the U.S Marshals Service continue to be a significant component of our business," Swindle said. The company contracts with the U.S. Marshals Service to house federal prisoners.

CoreCivic is a longtime ICE contractor, but the size and scope of its contracts with federal immigration enforcement quickly ballooned after Congress last year approved of a $75 billion budget boost for ICE and a $64 billion increase for Customs and Border Patrol over the next four years.

The federal contracts are now responsible for more than half of the company's overall revenue.

The amped-up immigration detention and deportation policies of the Trump administration, which have controversially included detaining individuals with no criminal records in detention facilities far from home without access to bond hearings, has drawn condemnation from human rights groups.

"Private prison corporations have long profited off the harm and death of Black and brown bodies across the country," said Lisa Sherman Luna, executive director of the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition.

"Now, Trump's mass detention and deportation machine is driving record profits into the pockets of billionaires while families are separated and Tennesseans struggle to put food on the table. Most Americans agree that the attacks on immigrants go too far," she said.

Swindle, speaking on a public earnings call last week, did not address those criticisms directly, but characterized the company's detention operations as humane and efficient.

"We remain confident that the corrections and detention beds that we provide are the most humane, most efficient logistically, most compliant, most secure, readily available and provide the best value to the government," Swindle told investors.

CoreCivic is not alone among Tennessee companies reaping windfalls from a federal immigration spending spree.

Tennessee companies have entered contracts to supply materials for a wall at the nation's southern border, parkas for ICE agents, mylar blankets and underwear for immigrant detainees and tactical breaching equipment for ICE officers.

With three months remaining until a new fiscal year begins Oct. 1, the total value of contracts between Tennessee companies and the federal immigration enforcement agencies is approaching $1.7 billion, a figure that does not include CoreCivic's property transactions. In 2024, the total value of those contracts stood at $255 million, according to usaspending.gov, a public repository of federal government contract information.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said Saturday it expects every officer and agent in the field to be equipped with a body camera by the end of August, a rapid expansion that could provide an unprecedented visual record of the federal government’s immigration enforcement operations.

But whether the public will get to see that footage remains largely up to ICE.

The agency defended its body-worn camera policy amid questions about provisions allowing ICE leadership to withhold or indefinitely delay footage after serious injuries or deaths in custody. Acting Director David J. Venturella said the restrictions are intended to protect investigations and privacy and are consistent with federal law and policies at other federal law enforcement agencies.

Venturella’s statement came in response to an Associated Press report on ICE policy, including a provision calling for the expedited release of footage after a serious injury or death in custody when doing so is determined to be in the “best interests of the agency.”

Venturella said the AP “mischaracterized” the policy by conflating that provision with ICE’s broader authority to release body-camera footage. He said the policy clarifies that footage should not be released when doing so could compromise investigations or privacy.

The AP report did not say the provision governs every release of body-camera footage. It focused on ICE’s policy for releasing footage after some of the most consequential encounters with the public: those involving serious injury or death.

The AP sought comment from ICE before its initial story on Friday. The agency provided partial responses, without addressing the provision that footage would be released when in its “best interests.”

ICE has been under heightened scrutiny since the fatal shooting in July of a 25-year-old motorist in Maine by an ICE officer with a history of violent behavior. Days earlier, another ICE officer shot and killed a Houston homebuilder driving to work. Neither shooting was recorded with body cameras.

Venturella said ICE was “committed to transparency and accountability” and was “on track to equip every officer and agent in the field with body-worn cameras by the end of August.”

The AP quoted Christopher Schneider, a sociology professor at Brandon University in Canada, who said that selective releases are routine in some law enforcement agencies but usually not so clearly contemplated in policy. “In some ways, ICE is saying the quiet part out loud,” he said.

The story noted that ICE’s sister agency, Customs and Border Protection, has not released footage of the fatal shooting of Alex Pretti in Minneapolis in January. CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott told lawmakers that it was part of an investigation and would be made public “when it’s appropriate.”

title: Federal contract documents show ICE 24-hour call center planned for Adams, Tennessee
description:
The Department of Homeland Security has awarded a $63 million contract to an Alaska corporation to operate a national immigration enforcement call center in rural Tennessee, a federal contract database shows.
The call center will also help locate unaccompanied migrant children and develop new technologies for ICE, contract documents show.
Local leaders, including Adams City Manager Anna Redfern, told the Lookout Monday they were unaware the town was even being considered.
A spokesperson for ICE did not respond to a request for details about the newly awarded contract.
“Tennessee is ground zero for this administration’s insidious attempt to embed immigration enforcement in all facets of our everyday life,” she said.
text:
The Department of Homeland Security has awarded a $63 million contract to an Alaska corporation to operate a national immigration enforcement call center in rural Tennessee, a federal contract database shows.

The city of Adams, a Robertson County town of about 600 people near the Kentucky border, is identified in the database as the future site of the planned call center, intended to function round-the-clock to support local police and sheriffs’ departments across the country that have entered into cooperative agreements with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The call center will also help locate unaccompanied migrant children and develop new technologies for ICE, contract documents show.

The one-year contract, effective Aug. 6, was awarded to Koniag Government Services. The company is a subsidiary of Koniag, a for-profit Alaska Native corporation created for the benefit of 3,400 Alutiiq shareholders, according to its website.

Local leaders, including Adams City Manager Anna Redfern, told the Lookout Monday they were unaware the town was even being considered. Officials could not immediately identify a potential physical location within the town’s 2.5-square-mile borders and expressed skepticism about the capacity of the city’s existing infrastructure to support a call center.

“I don’t know that little, ole sleepy Adams has got the things that you need to put in a call center,” Chris Traughber, assessor of property for Robertson County, said of the town that is perhaps best known for the 19th century legend of the “Bell witch” haunting that attracts supernatural enthusiasts and other visitors today.

Traughber said he was unaware of any recent property transactions that could account for an incoming call center. Portions of Adams lie within Montgomery County. The county’s property assessor referred the Lookout to online records, which did not yield any recent transactions by the Koniag company.

Republican State Sen. Kerry Roberts, whose district encompasses Adams, said he had “heard rumors” about the plans but that his office “has had no contact with anyone with the federal government” about the project.

“They could handle it,” from an Internet connectivity standpoint because high-speed fiber is available, he said of Adams, but cautioned that a building likely would have to be constructed. Roberts said it is also unclear where the company would draw its workforce.

A Koniag spokesperson referred questions about the contract to ICE, including a facility’s precise location, estimated workforce and its physical size.

“Unfortunately, we are not at liberty to discuss this very recently awarded contract at this time,” said Joanie Barr, senior vice president for business operations for Koniag Government Services.

A spokesperson for ICE did not respond to a request for details about the newly awarded contract.

Contract documents show the primary function of the call center will be to handle an estimated 6,000-7,000 daily inquiries from law enforcement agencies across the nation that have entered into cooperative agreements with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Call center employees will “analyze data, perform database cross-checks and confirm enforcement actions in the field,” contract documents say. Employees will work round-the-clock eight-hour shifts

The documents, however, show the company will be tasked with a much wider range of duties, including tracking and reporting the locations of unaccompanied immigrant children and identifying “emerging technologies” to increase the effectiveness of local law enforcement’s work with ICE.

The center will also be tapped to “reduce the non-detained docket” of millions of non-citizens living in the U.S. — non-citizens who are going through immigration court proceedings — by providing law enforcement officers and sheriffs with “targeting focus and material.”

The establishment of a national immigrant and enforcement call center represents a significant expansion of the Trump administration’s coordination with local law enforcement departments and sheriff’s offices around the nation as the number of participating agencies increases.

Administration officials have called the agreements a “force multiplier” to extend the reach of enforcement actions into communities by local police and sheriffs deputized to perform immigration agent duties.

While the so-called 287(g) cooperative agreements have been in existence since the 1970s, they have dramatically expanded under the second Trump term from fewer than 200 to more than 2,179, as of August, according to publicly-posted ICE data.

Lisa Sherman Luna, executive director of the Coalition for Immigrant & Refugee Rights, characterized the plans as “trying to set up shop in middle Tennessee to facilitate this terror on a massive scale.”

Sherman Luna cited an expanded federal presence conducting immigration enforcement as part of the Memphis Safe Task Force and a package of recent Tennessee GOP immigration legislation, crafted in meetings between Republican House Speaker Cameron Sexton and White House advisor Stephen Miller.

“Tennessee is ground zero for this administration’s insidious attempt to embed immigration enforcement in all facets of our everyday life,” she said.

Jean Wilson Brutus, a 41-year-old from Haiti, died Dec. 12, 2025, after he was brought to University Hospital from the detention center.

It is a detention center of cruelty and chaos,” Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-10th) said in a recent interview with NJ Spotlight News.
text:
WASHINGTON — The death of Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, a 41-year-old migrant from El Salvador, drew public grief and elected officials’ calls to shut down Delaney Hall, the Newark detention center where he was detained.

The demise in late July of a still-unknown man, who had been released from Delaney, attracted no such notice. And soon, as a result of a Trump administration policy change, it’s the sort of loss that may go entirely undisclosed by federal authorities.

Like Lopez-Cornejo, the unknown man had been held at Delaney Hall. Unlike Lopez-Cornejo, though, he was not in federal immigration custody at his death. The Trump administration in June rescinded a policy compelling the Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the federal agency spearheading the president’s deportation agenda, to report the deaths of recently released individuals.

“ICE confirmed to Representative Rob Menendez during an August 3 oversight visit that a man had died after a medical emergency during intake at Delaney Hall in the week of July 20, a death the agency never announced and that his office had first heard about on July 24,” Austin Kocher, an immigration researcher at American University’s Center for Latin American and Latino Studies, wrote online Sunday.

‘Substandard and abusive’

Established in 2021, the Biden administration-era rule required that ICE report to Congress and investigate the deaths of former detainees that occurred within 30 days of release. The policy was designed to thwart the agency from releasing seriously ill individuals in an attempt to avoid legal responsibility for them. ICE called the reversal “common sense.”

New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport said the turnaround “alarmed” her when it was announced.

“This decision comes amid increasingly frequent reports of substandard and abusive conditions at ICE detention facilities,” Davenport and other Democratic attorneys general said in a letter to Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, which includes ICE. “This change comes as deaths in ICE custody have risen to historic levels, with 51 detainee deaths occurring since January 20, 2025, as compared to 19 in the two years prior,” said their letter, sent in late June.

The administration of President Donald Trump, who campaigned in 2024 on mass deportation and has publicly said that immigrants are “poisoning the blood” of America, has closed or attempted to close at least three internal ombudsmen at DHS. One of those agencies, the Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman, was established during Trump’s first term to run unannounced inspections of ICE sites.

“The hamstringing of offices like OIDO must be considered in conjunction with limitations on congressional visits to ICE detention facilities and other measures that block transparency at a critical time,” Raul Pinto, deputy legal director for transparency at the American Immigration Council, an advocacy group, told NJ Spotlight News.

At least three deaths

Lopez-Cornejo fell ill at Delaney Hall. He was pronounced dead Aug. 1 at University Hospital.

“When Lopez-Cornejo experienced a medical emergency while in ICE custody, GEO facility staff and medical staff responded immediately and called 911 for emergency medical services,” ICE said in a statement Aug. 3. “The official cause of death remains pending further medical examination.”

Boca Raton-based Geo Group, a publicly traded company valued at $4 billion, is the private operator of the detention center for ICE. At least three detained individuals linked to Delaney Hall have died during the Trump administration. Jean Wilson Brutus, a 41-year-old from Haiti, died Dec. 12, 2025, after he was brought to University Hospital from the detention center.

An unnamed ICE spokesperson, in an email to NJ Spotlight News, defended the decision to stop reporting deaths of released detainees.

“Under this updated policy, when an individual is no longer in ICE custody then ICE will no longer be responsible for monitoring or reviewing deaths that may occur,” said this person, who did not identify themself when NJ Spotlight News asked. “This is common sense. ICE is not responsible when an individual passes away weeks after leaving their custody.”

The person said the policy “outlines procedures for timely notification, review and reporting of deaths occurring in ICE custody, including notifying next of kin, consulates, Congress and the public.”

Davenport on Friday said her office was investigating Delaney Hall for potential civil rights violations, adding that her office issued subpoenas.

“ICE and the Geo Group have continued to block our efforts for a full health inspection and there are now reports that visitations have been stopped,” Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, said Friday afternoon. “I have long opposed private detention facilities, and my position is clear that Delaney Hall should be closed.”

Separately, labor officials are investigating Delaney Hall for potential workplace violations.

Staff from the Occupational Safety and Health Administration conducted an unannounced inspection in May, after a complaint “alleging hazards involving maintenance employees who are employed by the GEO Group,” according to an OSHA spokesperson.

Needed medication

Delaney Hall had an average 812 people in custody as of July 9, according to data from TRAC, a watchdog group. In recent months the average was 900 individuals.

The capacity of the Elizabeth Detention Center, 9 miles south of Delaney, is significantly smaller: An average 300 people are housed there, according to TRAC figures.

More than 600,000 people have been booked into ICE detention centers since Trump took office on Jan. 20, 2025, according to Kocher.

Lopez-Cornejo’s mother, Maria Cornejo, told the immigrant advocacy group Movimiento Cosecha that her son was prescribed medication for diabetes, high blood pressure and seizures. He was denied access to his medications, she said.

“Delaney Hall needs to be closed. It is a detention center of cruelty and chaos,” Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-10th) said in a recent interview with NJ Spotlight News. “And we continue to see examples of this with another death there.”

In June, Congress approved $70 billion in additional funding for ICE, with Republican support and Democratic opposition. That money is now in the hands of the agency.

title: ICE considering buying immigrant detention facilities in Pa. - Altoona Mirror
description:
As existing detention contracts in certain locations approach expiration, ICE is working to ensure continued access to detention capacity in those areas.
As part of this effort, ICE is evaluating options, including the potential purchase of turnkey detention facilities where appropriate, or other contracting solutions to support continuity of operations."
Clearfield County's five-year contracts with ICE and GEO Group are set to expire in late September.
Activist Tim Smith, who says he has been fighting against immigration detention facilities for 23 years, first alerted commissioners about the RFI in an email on July 13.
As for a potential contract between ICE and GEO Group, the warden had no information, Glass said.
text:
CLEARFIELD -- In mid-July, ICE published a request for information on "turn-key detention services" for four regions across the country, including central Pennsylvania, where it already has the largest immigration detention facility in the Northeast.

Local activists worry ICE is either trying to contract directly with GEO Group -- which owns and operates Moshannon Valley Processing Center -- or even potentially buy the facility.

When asked about what the RFI means for Moshannon, an ICE spokesperson told Spotlight PA in an Aug. 10 email that "ICE has access to over 80,000 beds across its entire detention network in a mixture of dedicated and non-dedicated facilities. As existing detention contracts in certain locations approach expiration, ICE is working to ensure continued access to detention capacity in those areas. As part of this effort, ICE is evaluating options, including the potential purchase of turnkey detention facilities where appropriate, or other contracting solutions to support continuity of operations."

Currently, Clearfield County acts as a middleman between ICE and GEO Group, an arrangement that provides the county government with a "minor" level of oversight over the facility, which has long been accused of physical and psychological abuse, poor healthcare, and inhumane conditions.

Clearfield County's five-year contracts with ICE and GEO Group are set to expire in late September. The setup offered a workaround to former President Joe Biden's 2021 executive order banning private federal prisons, which President Donald Trump reversed in 2025.

Activist Tim Smith, who says he has been fighting against immigration detention facilities for 23 years, first alerted commissioners about the RFI in an email on July 13.

Smith was a plaintiff in an October 2021 lawsuit filed by the ACLU of Pennsylvania against the Clearfield County commissioners for failing to comply with the state's open meetings law in regard to approving contracts with ICE and GEO Group.

"What's happening now is even more stark than what was happening five years ago," Smith said during public comment at the July 14 commissioners meeting. "I would hope that today on Bastille Day that we take at least an emergency measure to show your disapproval of what is coming."

"The [Moshannon] warden talked to us and swears GEO isn't selling the facility to ICE," Clearfield County Commissioner Dave Glass told the newsroom in a July 22 email. As for a potential contract between ICE and GEO Group, the warden had no information, Glass said. "And we've heard nothing else."

The warden did not return a request for comment, nor did GEO Group.

However, the company's founder and CEO George Zoley told shareholders in a second-quarter earnings call last week that GEO Group is "engaged in an active process for the sale of several of our turnkey facilities, subject to mutual agreement on price and our continued management of those facilities under long-term support services contracts."

He also said that "several other GEO facilities have support services contracts that expire later this year. ICE has initiated a procurement process involving four facilities that we hope will result in new long-term support services contracts being awarded."

Zoley did not specify during the call which facilities he was referring to for potential sales or renewed contracts.

According to the RFI posting, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security "requires one or more Contractor Owned/Contractor-Operated detention facilities" in the Denver, Miami, Seattle, and Philadelphia "areas of responsibility."

The Philadelphia AOR -- which includes Pennsylvania, Delaware, and West Virginia -- facility should have a minimum of 1,800 detention beds and be located within 30 driving miles of State College Regional Airport.

Moshannon Valley has a bed capacity of 1,876 and is a roughly 27-mile drive from the airport.

The airport has become a major hub for ICE flights, with a massive jump from two flights in all of 2025 to 28 in April, 25 in May, and 23 in June, according to data from Human Rights First, a nonprofit that advocates for refugees and immigrants.

The RFI expands potential sites to include turnkey existing facilities, those requiring upgrades, and new constructions, with the caveat that properties must be able to begin housing detainees within 30 days of contract award and only house ICE detainees.

ICE is using the RFI to see what markets have available and how quickly it can ramp up its detention numbers, said Cesar Cuauhtemoc Garcia Hernandez, a law professor at Ohio State who specializes in the intersection of criminal and immigration law.

With the lack of transparency, it's difficult to say whether this RFI is an effort to get ahead of Clearfield's upcoming contract renewals with ICE and GEO Group, Garcia Hernandez told Spotlight PA.

"So often, it's hard to understand just what they're doing, nonetheless, why they're doing it, and the reason for that is that oftentimes they don't tell us," he said.

In September 2021, Clearfield County commissioners voted to enter into a five-year intergovernmental service agreement with ICE "to provide detention services for detainees," according to the agreement.

Commissioners also approved a services contract with GEO Group, an international company based in Florida that owns and operates correctional and detention facilities around the globe. It "requires GEO to perform all duties and accept all responsibilities incumbent upon" the county under its agreement with ICE, according to the contract.

With the contracts ending in September, some community members worry that ICE will cut the county out of the equation rather than renew the arrangement.

For Jasmine Rivera, executive director of the Pennsylvania Immigration Coalition, it doesn't matter who holds the contract, because the facility is still running, separating families, and incarcerating loved ones.

"It's always unjust, always abusive, and it's always unnecessary, regardless of who or how detention centers are being operated," Rivera told Spotlight PA.

Pennsylvania U.S. Reps. Chris Deluzio, Madeleine Dean, and Summer Lee, all Democrats, wrote letters to ICE and GEO Group last week "to demand answers on GEO's failure to comply with federal standards of adequate staffing and medical care to detainees, as well as obstruction of congressional oversight," according to a news release.

Dean conducted a visit to Moshannon Valley Processing Center on June 17. Lee and Deluzio also went to the facility unannounced on May 28, and spoke to pregnant women who said they were receiving poor medical care.

"These failures are not accidental; they are the predictable result of a privatized, for-profit detention business model," Dean, Deluzio, and Lee wrote in their letter to GEO Group.

Local activists have implored commissioners to take on more oversight at the facility. The intergovernmental agreement allows commissioners to enter the facility with 24-hour notice, but the officials have been denied access in the past, raising concerns about how much oversight they actually have.

"I think we all need to just be very honest that this 'so-called' oversight doesn't prevent abuse," Rivera said.

"We are the lowest common denominator," Commissioner Tim Winters said during the July 14 meeting. "We cannot open or close this facility. We have a minor say and a minor oversight."

At the July 28 commissioners meeting, Winters said there have been no updates to ICE's and GEO Group's contract with the county, but that it's "in process." Commissioners noted that this is in line with the time frame of the 2021 contract.

"If they offer a contract, we'll certainly look at it. I've already said I'm going to vote no on it," Glass said during the July 14 meeting.

text:
WASHINGTON - US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents have arrested a pregnant South African woman who was detained at an airport in Las Vegas.

Nqobile Malangeni was detained on 30 July at Harry Reid International Airport as she prepared to board a flight to Connecticut, where she lives with her fiancé.

She had travelled to Las Vegas on 27 July to celebrate her birthday.

Footage shared with US media shows six ICE agents surrounding Malangeni. In the video, the agents tell her she had overstayed her authorised period of stay and that there was a final order of removal against her.

ICE records show Malangeni was being held at the Henderson Detention Center.

Her fiancé, who served in the US armed forces, told local media he was distraught.

The couple had planned to marry, he said, and he feared he would not get to meet their child if Malangeni was deported. He has called on the government to release her.

In a statement, ICE said Malangeni entered the US on 2 December 2023 and was authorised to remain in the country until 19 June 2024.

“[She] overstayed the legal period of her admittance,” the statement said.

ICE added that an immigration judge issued a final order of removal on 9 February 2026.

“She will remain in ICE custody pending removal,” the statement said.

Meanwhile, the US has revoked over 175,000 visas from foreign nationals as part of a sweeping immigration crackdown.

The State Department has targeted foreign nationals accused of breaking the law.

It cites cases including assault, theft and drug crimes and possession of child sexual abuse material.

Over 100 visas have been revoked for those who allegedly gave birth to secure their children US citizenship.

Others were cancelled for celebrating the assassination of Charlie Kirk.

Human rights advocates have criticised the crackdown, warning it could threaten free speech as the government expands vetting of social media accounts.
