title: States, cities try to keep ICE out of schools - Stateline.org
authors: Shalina Chatlani, Tim Henderson, Kevin Hardy
description:
On June 11, ICE agents trailed a car into the parking lot of Commodore John Rodgers Elementary/Middle School in Baltimore.
ICE agents pulled Jesus Acevedo Sanchez from the vehicle, pinned him to the ground and arrested him for being in the country illegally.
But the incident in Baltimore was a stark illustration of the limits of state and local authority when it comes to immigration enforcement.
Katherine Currie, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, said that ICE is not targeting schools, but that immigration enforcement “is a clear federal responsibility” under the U.S. Constitution.
“ICE is not going to schools to arrest children — we are protecting children.
text:
On June 11, ICE agents trailed a car into the parking lot of Commodore John Rodgers Elementary/Middle School in Baltimore. For the family riding in that car, an everyday school drop off quickly devolved into chaos.

ICE agents pulled Jesus Acevedo Sanchez from the vehicle, pinned him to the ground and arrested him for being in the country illegally. They also handcuffed and detained his wife, Adriana Gavilan Sanchez, as the couple’s two daughters watched from the back seat and school staff whisked other students away from the scene.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson later told CNN that Acevedo Sanchez “refused lawful commands, violently resisted arrest, and used his vehicle to evade law enforcement, dragging an ICE offer in the process.”

But two weeks ago, a federal judge ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement to release him, ruling that agents did not have probable cause to make the arrest. In the courtroom, Judge Julie Rubin rebuked the ICE officers for failing to follow due process and described the incident outside the school as a “stomach churner.”

Since President Donald Trump began his second term with a vow to crack down on illegal immigration, more than a dozen states have enacted laws designed to keep ICE away from schools. But the incident in Baltimore was a stark illustration of the limits of state and local authority when it comes to immigration enforcement.

Both Maryland and the city of Baltimore have enacted such measures, but neither one prevented ICE agents from making arrests in full view of arriving students at the Commodore John Rodgers Elementary/Middle School.

“Schools are places where children should feel safe, where parents should be able to drop off their kids without fear, and where educators should be able to focus on teaching — not where federal agents carry out immigration enforcement actions in front of children,” Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore said in a statement he released on the day of the incident.

In a phone interview, Zeke Cohen, the Democratic president of the Baltimore City Council, said “the behavior of ICE has been tragic, traumatic, and in violation of all of the principles that we hold dear in Baltimore.”

“They are reckless, they are lawless, and they do whatever they please,” Cohen said. “It’s a challenging situation for cities like Baltimore that prize diversity and inclusion when you have a government that does the opposite.”

The day after its inauguration, the Trump administration announced that it would reverse guidance in place since 2011 that restricted migrant arrests at “sensitive locations,” including schools, hospitals and places of worship. Since then, there have been at least 17 ICE encounters on school grounds, according to a tracker maintained by K-12 Dive, an education news website.

Katherine Currie, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, said that ICE is not targeting schools, but that immigration enforcement “is a clear federal responsibility” under the U.S. Constitution.

“ICE is not going to schools to arrest children — we are protecting children. Criminals are no longer able to hide in America’s schools to avoid arrest,” Currie wrote in an email.

“If a dangerous illegal alien felon were to flee into a school, or a child sex offender is working as an employee, there may be a situation where an arrest is made to protect public safety.”

Warrant required

The state and city restrictions on ICE activity in schools don’t challenge the supremacy of the federal government under the Constitution. Instead, they mostly limit what state, local and school officials can do to assist ICE, often specifying that federal agents should not be granted access to school property without a judicial warrant.

Matthew Lopas, director of state advocacy at the National Immigration Law Center, a nonprofit that advocates for immigrants, said blocking ICE agents from entering school premises without a warrant “is not in conflict with federal law.”

“It is merely saying that this is not a place where immigration enforcement should be coming on fishing expeditions,” Lopas said.

State, local officials plan for potential immigration enforcement at schools

Verjeana McCotter-Jacobs, president of the National School Boards Association, said there are very few situations in which ICE would be justified in showing up at a school.

“We don’t see a need for law enforcement to be executing any activities on school grounds, unless it’s in response to an emergency situation,” McCotter-Jacobs said. ,“It causes stress and distractions to learning, which impacts every single child and every child in the building as well as staff.”

She added that when it does happen, it’s crucial for school officials to be on the same page with state and local law enforcement.

“Some states are unfortunately aligned with the feds in executing arrests on school grounds, and so that leaves the local school district kind of perplexed as to what they’re supposed to do,” she said.

Indiana, for example, enacted a sweeping law this year that bars school districts and universities from implementing any measure that prohibits or restricts public employees from cooperating with ICE. In November, Republican state Attorney General Todd Rokita sued the Indianapolis Public Schools for violating the law.

Ohio is another Republican-led state where political leaders are largely supportive of the Trump administration’s immigration policy, and it has not enacted a law restricting ICE activities on school grounds. But Chad Springer, superintendent of the Athens City School District in Chauncey, said his district’s immigration enforcement policy does focus on whether agents have a warrant.

As soon the Trump administration reversed the “sensitive location” policy last year, Springer said, he visited each of his campuses to explain how the district wanted them to respond in case of an ICE enforcement action.

“At any given time, there’s always a central office staff that’s going to respond if immigration did show up to a campus, and then we would be the ones to deal directly with immigration officials,” Springer explained. “And our board policy dictates we ask them, unless a judicial warrant is involved, to conduct business outside of the school day, not on school grounds.”

Feds sue cities and states to block sanctuary policies

Springer said that every school board across the country should be crystal clear about how it would handle any law enforcement activity on campus. He said he understands his own district’s policy, but he’d welcome more direction from the state.

“In the absence of clarity, you have unclear measures, and that leads to confusion,” Springer said. “I would appreciate clear, explicit guidelines from lawmakers as to when we allow or don’t allow [officers] to be there…right now, all I can lean on is board policy.”

The coming school year

In Ohio and elsewhere, the Trump administration’s announcement late last month that it will terminate Temporary Protected Status for more than 330,000 Haitians living in the U.S. will heighten the potential for ICE enforcement at schools. In Ohio alone, there are about 30,000 Haitians who formerly had that status, which allows people from certain countries to live and work in the U.S. if returning to their home country would be dangerous.

Jeff Wensing, president of the Ohio Education Association, said educators, particularly in cities such as Springfield with large Haitian populations, are concerned about what the new year might bring.

“So we gave guidance to our members in Springfield: ‘Here are your rights,’” Wensing said. “I don’t care who you are — if you are a stranger, including ICE agents, we have a policy, we’re not letting strangers into the school.”

As far as he’s concerned the law is clear.

“They have a legal right to attend a public school, regardless of their immigration status,” Wensing said. “When you make children pawns in a bigger game, that’s never a good thing.”

text:
FOX 9 has extended an invitation to all the candidates polling above 5% in both the Minnesota Governor and Senate primary races to appear on our All Day program for an interview. Last Friday, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan joined us as she makes a bid for the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate.

Her primary opponent, Rep. Angie Craig, appeared last week.

Lt. Gov. Flanagan on fraud and criticism of the Walz administration:

"Let’s say a couple of things. The first thing that I would say is that as the former executive director of a nonprofit that serves children and families, I am appalled by the fraud that has occurred. Minnesotans are upset about it. They’re angry and I am too. I can tell you that this administration has taken steps. There’s a new office of inspector general that was passed this last legislative session. We’ve added staff to the attorney general’s office to root out Medicaid fraud. And, there was an aggressive action of shutting down a program that was being utilized by criminals. I think more absolutely needs to be done. And I think our next governor also – I like her chances – Senator Amy Klobuchar will really take some strong stances here too. This issue of fraud is unacceptable, and there’s been work here. But what I also want to say is that Republicans are going to run against every Democrat on fraud, from Amy Klobuchar to Keith Ellison to the DFL legislators, because they don’t want to take accountability for Donald Trump and, frankly, everything that he’s done to make life unaffordable for Minnesotans. We’ve watched – frankly, he fired 17 inspectors general right out of the gate, whose entire job was to police fraud at the federal level. He pardoned 70 white-collar criminals, including one individual who stole over a billion dollars in Medicare and Medicaid fraud, and is making money hand over fist from the Oval Office in a crypto meme coin. I don’t think Republicans want to talk about that, and we’re going to take it to them in the fall."

Lt. Gov. Flanagan on fraud response:

"I mean, I would say this: the attorney general’s office has been quite active in rooting out and going after fraud. And listen, 100 people have been charged, and they should be convicted. Aimee Bock, who is the ringleader of Feeding Our Future, has been sentenced to 41 years plus eight months, and I say good. If you are stealing taxpayer dollars for your own grift, you should be charged and prosecuted. That should be the expectation of Minnesotans. And we’ve seen that happen through the attorney general’s office. And, you know, this work is ongoing. And our state leaders are going to have to be clear now and into the future that they’ll need to stay two steps ahead of these criminals, who grow more and more sophisticated. And I think it is incredibly important that we are clear that these folks have been charged, they should be prosecuted, and that fraud of any kind is completely unacceptable. And I just, I think the governor has said that more should have been done sooner, and I agree with him. And now action is being taken, and that work will need to continue into the future."

Lt. Gov. Flanagan on dismantling ICE and immigration reform:

"I want to say to folks that what we have experienced over the last year has been horrific. 3,000 ICE agents here in Minnesota who terrorized our neighbors. I think about our children who will now have an ACE score, an ‘adverse childhood experience’ score, simply because there were federal agents in their neighborhoods. And two Minnesotans were killed: Renee Good and Alex Pretti. ICE has been, you know, allowed to kill 11 people with impunity. That’s outrageous, and none of us should stand for it. I think we can have secure borders. And I also believe that we can have comprehensive immigration reform, which ensures that it is grounded in safety, dignity, and also ensuring that we have a pathway to citizenship for folks who are here, who are law-abiding and part of our community. We need an immigration system, but ICE itself has been horribly broken. And we see that the destruction to our economy, to our children here in Minnesota and across the country, is horrific. And I think this is actually one of the places where there’s a significant difference between me and my primary opponent, Congresswoman Craig, who voted for Donald Trump’s immigration bill, for the Laken Riley Act, three days into the second Trump administration, that stripped immigrants of due process and has allowed for indefinite detention of adults and children. She was the only Minnesota Democrat to do so. And then, when Trump was separating families and ICE was in the city of Los Angeles, literally waiting outside of schools after elementary school graduations, what we saw was them picking up family members. And I just have to say that her vote then to thank ICE, again as the only Minnesota Democrat to do so, is pretty out of step. And so I think we can have comprehensive immigration reform and secure borders. But I also think that we shouldn’t allow for indefinite detention, which I think, you know, without due process, which really I think is an affront to our Constitution."

Lt. Gov. Flanagan on Medicare for All and rural health care:

"I think it’s very realistic because what we are seeing right now is that individuals are paying an incredible amount of money for health insurance and not actually getting a lot of health care. As I’ve traveled across Minnesota, what I’ve heard from people is that they have $16,000 deductibles, $20,000 deductibles and are spending $600 for a five-minute med check. It is untenable for folks, and I think we can have a system that allows for people to have access to high-quality and affordable care. What I’d also say is, on the way there, I think we need to get rid of prior authorization because I don’t think that some dude behind a desk or, worse yet, an AI bot should be able to determine whether or not you get the life-saving health care that your doctor has prescribed. We can do better. Right now, people are paying a tremendous amount of money and not getting much for it. I think Medicare for All’s time has come, and people all across the state, and I would say in particular in Greater Minnesota, where folks have less access, fewer options, and we see rural clinics closing and even I talk to a lot of families who say, ‘I’m worried now that I don’t have access to maternity care and have to drive two hours, three hours to get in.’ We know babies famously come right on time, right? With no complications. Folks deserve better. And I think that this is one of the ways for us to get there. And we also have to restore the cuts to Medicaid that will have disastrous consequences for local economies all across Minnesota. You know, to remind people that those cuts were made in exchange for trillions of dollars in tax cuts for billionaires, while working, you know, families are being left behind. We can do so much."

Where have human rights gone?
Can we still truly believe in human rights?” He added: “Were those people really police officers or bandits?
Working with the Human Rights Legal Project and based on Samos, Choulis helped collect testimony from survivors after the incident.
text:
Home to a little more than 32,000 people, the Greek island of Samos draws hundreds of thousands of tourists each year. Situated in the eastern Aegean Sea, the island boasts of 159 kilometers (99 miles) of coastline, famed locally produced Muscat wines, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Pythagoreion and the Heraion of Samos. Because of its proximity to Turkey, though, it also sits along the busy migration route to Europe. In September 2021, a deadly crime allegedly took place in the azure waters off the island’s coast.

The summer heat was beginning to ease that month, and a group of 36 people reached the coast of Samos with the hopes of seeking asylum. Masked individuals apprehended 28 of these displaced people, robbing and brutalizing them before shuttling them back out to sea and abandoning them in orange life rafts in Turkish waters. Among those forced off the island were children, infants, and pregnant women. The Turkish Coast Guard later documented their rescue. But it was only one of the crimes that befell the desperate people who had reached Samos that day.

Four of the passengers who had evaded capture eventually reached the island’s refugee camp, while three men who had broken away from the group slept in the forest. Later, while walking along one of Samos’s roads, these men were allegedly apprehended by people who identified themselves as police officers.

As hoards of late-season tourists ate meals at the island’s seafood tavernas that day, a Greek coastguard boat pushed off from one of the nearby ports. Aboard were the three men captured on the road. They had been handed over to a group of masked individuals. In violation of the Geneva Convention as well as national and international law, the men were not only denied their right to request asylum — they were ferried out to sea and thrown overboard.

The two men who drowned that day, Didier Martial Kouamou of Cameroon and Sidy Keita of the Ivory Coast, joined the ranks of the more than 35,000 people who have died or gone missing while crossing in the Mediterranean Sea since 2014, according to the International Migration Organization’s data. Since the spike in arrivals in 2015, a period known as the European refugee crisis, countries across the European Union have ramped up border enforcement. Across the last 11 years, Europe’s far right has lobbied for stricter border controls while countries including Greece have stood accused of widespread violence on their frontiers.

Effectively left for dead, one of the three men miraculously survived the ordeal. Ibrahim managed to reach Turkey, and he later returned to Greece on a dinghy, armed with the story of what happened. In February 2022, he recounted his version of events to a consortium of journalists who reported on the incident, drawing on the testimonies of other survivors, officials, and lawyers to reconstruct the grim details that unfolded in the waters of Samos.

By September 2021, the practice of pushbacks — the forced expulsion of refugees and migrants who are denied the opportunity to apply for asylum — was already widely documented in Greece. Pushbacks are prohibited under international law, but lawyers and journalists had increasingly sounded the alarm on their use. In response, the Greek government issued blanket denials. Though the EU occasionally offered muted criticism of the measures Greece used on its land and sea borders, pushbacks continued unabated. After all, Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the EU Commission since 2019, had described Greece as Europe’s “shield” only a year and a half before the Samos incident.

Five years on from the deadly incident off Samos, no one has been held accountable in court for the pushback that took place that day or the deaths of the two men.

Venant Olinga, a 38-year-old from Cameroon who was cast adrift at sea in Turkish waters that day, witnessed the events. Once in Turkey, he was eventually able to reach Europe again and now lives in Paris, where he has refugee status. The sense of impunity, he said, still haunts him. “I’m terrified to know that, for nearly five years, no action [and] no judgement has been taken on this serious case,” he said.

The people in his group, he explained, had “hoped to find refuge in a country that ratified the Geneva Convention,” but they “set foot on European soil only to be brutalized by border guards. How can people like that remain unpunished to this day? Where have human rights gone? Can we still truly believe in human rights?”

He added: “Were those people really police officers or bandits? Because, from what I was taught, a police officer is first and foremost a man of the law; yet they denied us the right to asylum — a right available to everyone.”

There are a “variety of reasons,” according to lawyer Dimitris Choulis, that no one has been held accountable in this case or others like it. Working with the Human Rights Legal Project and based on Samos, Choulis helped collect testimony from survivors after the incident. One reason is the fact that pushbacks, by their very nature, often make it difficult to find survivors. A more chilling reason, he said, is that “the authorities responsible for doing the crimes are the ones investigating them,” adding that “the core of the problem is [that] this is the policy of the government.” With authorities uninterested in punishing themselves, the hard work of collecting forensic evidence falls on the survivors’ lawyers. “There should be specialists doing this, but we are the ones doing it all.”

Choulis pointed to the example of the deadly June 2023 Pylos shipwreck. The Adriana, a fishing trawler traveling toward Europe with some 750 refugees and migrants aboard, sank in the Ionian Sea around 50 nautical miles from Greece’s southwest coast. More than 500 people are believed to have died, making it one of the deadliest Mediterranean shipwrecks in recent history. Only 104 people survived the incident. Survivors accused Greek authorities of attempting to tow the boat in the moments before it went under, an allegation the government has strenuously denied.

“There should be specialists doing this, but we are the ones doing it all.” – Dimitris Choulis, lawyer

Following the incident, authorities accused nine Egyptian men of smuggling-related charges and put them in pretrial detention for 11 months. A court subsequently dropped their charges after ruling it lacked jurisdiction in the case. It wasn’t until May 2025 that a Greek Naval Court charged 17 members of the Hellenic Coast Guard, reportedly on charges ranging from obstructing transport to causing or helping cause a shipwreck

Julia Winkler of De:Criminalise, an organization that supports refugees and migrants accused of smuggling in Europe, said the Pylos incident “lays bare the profound hypocrisy of the EU’s border regime: people on the move are turned into criminals for acts of survival, while deadly violence by the state at the border is met with silence and impunity.”

Winkler added, “A system that can mobilize courts and prisons against the most vulnerable, yet fails to hold those in power accountable, does not simply fail migrants; it destroys its own legitimacy.”

Rights groups and watchdogs, meanwhile, say both the deadly incidents in Samos and Pylos are symptoms of a broader European phenomenon. Across the past decade, countries along the EU’s external borders have been accused of carrying out illegal pushbacks. In 2021, for instance, a group of journalists documented instances of Croatian border guards abusing and forcing migrants back across the border to Bosnia. Croatian authorities initially denied any systematic wrongdoing and said it would investigate the footage. There has been no evidence that any criminal prosecutions of officers over these allegations has ever taken place.

In November that same year, a similar pushback occurred further north. For months, asylum seekers, most of whom had fled Iraqi Kurdistan, had been lured to Belarus by false promises they would be able to easily cross into Poland. Belarusian authorities then transported them to the border, subjected them to physical abuse, and forced them into an “exclusion zone” between the two countries. Poland responded by introducing legislation that legitimized pushbacks on its borders. Many people died in the tall pine forests that blanket the border region, though the exact number is unknown. Some estimates suggest that more than 80 perished, but the true figure is likely higher due to the fact that hundreds of people were reported missing.

Three years later, in December 2024, three teenage boys who had left Egypt froze to death in the forests on Bulgaria’s border with Turkey. They had called for aid, and though a nonprofit group attempted to rescue the boys, Bulgarian authorities allegedly stymied these efforts despite the subzero temperatures. In an internal report, the rights arm of Frontex, the EU’s external border agency, concluded that Bulgaria “failed to implement adequate measures in time that resulted in loss of lives” and likely obstructed rescue efforts.

Although both rights groups and EU institutions have pointed to the rule of law’s erosion on the bloc’s borders, a collective of European nations released a chilling joint statement in May 2025. Issued by eight countries, the statement chided some immigrants for creating “parallel societies and distancing themselves from our fundamental values of equality, democracy, and freedom.” More worryingly still, the statement went on to question the validity of human rights law on the bloc’s borders, arguing that the court’s interpretations of the European Convention on Human Rights had at times “limited our ability to make political decisions in our own democracies.”

These countries, the statement insisted, needed to be able to “to take effective steps to counter hostile states that are trying to use our values and rights against us. For example, by instrumentalizing migrants at our borders.” The statement acknowledged the “sensitive” nature of the topic and added, “Although our aim is to safeguard our democracies, we will likely be accused of the opposite.”

As these countries debate whether human rights apply to displaced people, the EU’s increasingly harsh border measures mean “violations” continue without pause, according to Delphine Rodrick, a senior legal advisor with the Border Justice Program at the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights. In fact, Rodrick believes recent reforms to the bloc’s asylum framework are “likely to perpetuate conditions that facilitate abuse at Europe’s borders.”

Because survivors and witnesses of violent border incidents are often forced to other countries after their documents and cell phones have been destroyed or stolen, Rodrick explained, “violations at the border are doubly difficult to pursue accountability for.” She added, “In practice, this makes it easier for states to avoid their investigative obligations by failing to identify and include victims and witnesses in proceedings, deferring to explanations by state officials, and closing the few investigations that do occur without findings of wrongdoing. When states refuse to take investigations and prosecutions of these violations seriously, they are in effect facilitating their continuation and maintaining impunity.”

At the same time, refugees and migrants as well as humanitarians and activists face ever-present legal risks. “The regular prosecutions of people on the move and those who act in solidarity with them — for example, on charges that they have ‘facilitated’ entry — stand in stark contrast to an overwhelming absence of accountability for human rights violations at the borders.”

In the EU and across Europe, the prosecution of migrants is widespread. In the United Kingdom, for instance, more than 1,000 people have been prosecuted under the offense of “illegal arrival” that was introduced in 2022 under the Nationality and Borders Act. In Greece, organizations such as 50 Out of Many are attempting to raise both funds and awareness as prosecutions target displaced people who reach the country by boat as smugglers, especially young Sudanese men.

Yet, while refugees, migrants, and the activists who support them increasingly find themselves in courtrooms, the people in power rarely do. In 2024, the EU’s Fundamental Rights Agency issued a bleak assessment of the situation. Despite the broad documentation of border violence, it suggested, accountability remained an exception to the rule. “[A] a sense of impunity prevails,” it stated. “Very few national court proceedings lead to convictions. This is particularly true when compared with the number of credible reports about serious fundamental rights violations.”

Meanwhile, survivors of the deadly pushback in Samos five years ago are left to merely hope for the semblance of accountability. Didier Martial Kouamou was repatriated to Cameroon, but Sidy Keita’s family could not afford to pay for his body to be sent home. In Izmir, Turkey, he is buried in what is known as the Cemetery of the Nameless, a final resting place for people whose families cannot afford a gravestone.

In response to the allegations put to it for this article the Hellenic Coast Guard said its operations comply with Greek, EU, and international law and emphasized its commitment to human rights and search-and-rescue obligations. It pointed to the large numbers of people rescued at sea since 2015, insisting it reviews serious incident reports from Frontex’s Fundamental Rights Officer and investigates allegations of misconduct through its internal oversight mechanisms. It rejected allegations of unlawful actions, including pushbacks and violence.

“Today, as I watch time pass without any reaction from the institutions handling this case, I am tempted to believe — and not just me, but the other victims too — that the Greek authorities’ blatant silence regarding this dispute makes them complicit in these heinous acts,” said Olinga, who now works at a clothing store in Paris.

He is struggling to find a permanent home but remains committed to building a stable life and a future, despite the trauma of the past. He was recently named employee of the month and his smiling photo was put on a noticeboard at his job. Still, he hopes for justice. “In the memory of all those who have left us — for example, Sidy and [Kouamou] — we cannot continue to stand idly by and let people go unpunished, to cover up or become complicit in criminal acts of this kind.”

title: Immigration – Nexus – El Salvador - Massachusetts Lawyers Weekly
description:
“… [The petitioner] argues, inter alia, that the BIA wrongly concluded that there was no nexus between her claims of persecution and a statutorily protected ground.
Because substantial evidence supports the BIA’s no-nexus conclusion, we deny the petition.
… “While living in El Salvador, [the petitioner] was robbed three times.
… “[The petitioner]’s failure to demonstrate nexus means that her asylum claim fails.
Accordingly, [the petitioner]’s withholding of removal claim also fails because it likewise requires a showing of nexus.
text:
Where the Board of Immigration Appeals dismissed a Salvadoran petitioner’s appeal from an immigration judge’s denial of her application for asylum and withholding of removal pursuant to the Immigration and Nationality Act, her petition for review should be denied because substantial evidence supports the BIA’s conclusion that there was no nexus between her claims of persecution and a statutorily protected ground.

“… [The petitioner] argues, inter alia, that the BIA wrongly concluded that there was no nexus between her claims of persecution and a statutorily protected ground. Because substantial evidence supports the BIA’s no-nexus conclusion, we deny the petition. …

“While living in El Salvador, [the petitioner] was robbed three times. …

“[The petitioner] did not report any of the robberies she experienced to the police because she knew people who had been retaliated against by the gangs after making such reports and because she believes the police in El Salvador never arrest gang members. …

“[The petitioner] contends that the agency wrongly disregarded evidence that she was persecuted because of her gender, familial ties, and political opinions. …

“According to [the petitioner], the robber’s use of the slur ‘bitch’ during the January 2015 robbery demonstrates a gender-based motive. However, the record supports the agency’s conclusion that the only reason, central or otherwise, that [the petitioner] was targeted by gang members during those robberies was for financial gain. Each time [the petitioner] was robbed, the gang members wanted items of pecuniary value — such as her money and phone — which does not support the notion that [the petitioner] was targeted based on a protected ground. … Furthermore, during the third robbery, the robbers targeted the store and robbed every customer, not just [the petitioner]. … On this evidence, the fact that the robber used a gendered pejorative during the commission of one robbery is not enough to compel the conclusion that gender was a central reason for [the petitioner] being harmed. …

“Finally, [the petitioner] asserts that her political beliefs are another central reason for her persecution. She claims to hold an anti-gang, pro-rule-of-law political opinion and believes that men should be held accountable for sexual crimes. However, [the petitioner] has alleged only that she was subjected to economic crime and is being threatened by [her niece’s father]. For the reasons already explained, the record supports the conclusion that neither [the petitioner]’s victimization by economic crime nor [the] threats are connected to her ideological opposition to gangs. …

“[The petitioner]’s failure to demonstrate nexus means that her asylum claim fails. Accordingly, [the petitioner]’s withholding of removal claim also fails because it likewise requires a showing of nexus. …”

Monzon Guzman v. Blanche, et al. (Lawyers Weekly No. 01-173-26) (13 pages) (Aframe, J.) Jonathan Ng, Omar Rahman, Abdul Wahab Niaz, Bhuvanyaa Vijay and Law Offices of Johanna M. Herrero on brief for the petitioner; Christina R. Zeidan, Brett A. Shumate and Lisa M. Arnold on brief for the respondent (Docket No. 25-1351) (Aug. 7, 2026).

text:
An undercover Homeland Security Investigations agent parked outside a community center while Rep. Ilhan Omar held a town hall on Aug. 6, the Democratic Congresswoman wrote in a letter to Department of Homeland Security leadership in St. Paul.

According to the letter, a Richfield police officer noticed a woman sitting in a Ford Explorer outside the building and became suspicious of the way she was monitoring the building. He ran the Explorer’s plates, but they didn’t correspond to the vehicle. The officer approached the woman, who initially identified herself as event security.

Richfield Police confirmed with Omar’s security detail that the woman was not part of their team. The woman called her supervisor, then told the police officer that she was an undercover HSI officer stationed outside the community center as part of a nearby undercover drug operation. She then left the property.

HSI is the criminal investigative division of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The presence of the agent was a waste of police resources, and at best, a poor choice of location for an undercover drug raid, Omar wrote in the letter.

“At worst, it emphasizes many Americans’ growing concern that the Trump administration uses ICE to surveil political opponents and may interfere with our democracy,” the letter reads.

Omar has been a frequent target of President Donald Trump since his first term. Trump has said she should be jailed or “sent back to Somalia.”

During a January town hall, a man rushed at Omar as she spoke and squirted her with a liquid — later identified as apple cider vinegar. He pleaded guilty to assaulting a federal officer in federal court in May.

The Richfield Police Department and ICE did not immediately respond to emailed questions.

text:
A group rallied to protest U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Monday, but they’re also a network of information, tracking and documenting reported ICE sightings in neighborhoods.

“All of these raids are causing so much fear and trauma in our communities,” Luba Cortes of Make the Road New York said.

Cortes said there’s an uptick in ICE sightings across the city. That fear is increasingly visible in Corona, Queens, where they’ve tallied the most enforcement.

She said Corona Plaza, once filled with vendors, has thinned out as some immigrants stay away.

“Because of the fear that police will collaborate with ICE, and that they get stopped for a ticket or something that the police would call ICE,” Cortes said.

City law already limits when the NYPD can cooperate with ICE.

Dozens of people joined Monday’s rally, including elected officials and people who came out simply to show support.

“I believe families are being torn apart, and it breaks my heart,” Forest Hills resident Dawn Berry said.

The rally comes as the city let go dozens of Haitian employees with Temporary Protected Status, also known as TPS, after the program ended for them at the end of July.

“We wanted to make sure that we only took this action at the point at which it was legally required to do so because it is not an action we would want to take in any which way or form,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said.

“There’s a lot of fear, a lot of panic, but there’s also a lot of empowerment because a lot of them already know their rights. So they’re protecting each other,” Tony Alaracon with Las Donas said.

While the empty spaces back in Corona are easy to see, advocates said some effects of immigration enforcement are not.

“Right now, there’s a lot of trauma going on. A lot of the families are being separated,” Veronica Torrico, a psychologist, said.

She said that uncertainty can show up differently in children.

“A lot of these children have a regression, and they stop talking, and there are a lot of delays with them,” Torrico said.

It’s one reason advocates said their work goes beyond tracking where immigration agents are to making sure families know what to do if they encounter them.

title: 'They Were Determined to Break Me': Kurdish Filmmaker Recounts ICE Force-Feeding Horror
description:
Iran-born Gabar Choli told Olivares that he went voluntarily with guards to the infirmary at ICE's Port Isabel Service Processing Center in Los Fresnos, Texas, the first time he was force-fed.
“Two guards would hold my feet; two hold my hands; one hold my head—and they would shove tubes in my nose,” Choli told Olivares.
Court records viewed by Olivares showed Choli suffered injuries and medical issues including swollen sinuses, esophageal damage, and stomach problems following his force-feeding.
In early January, ICE deported Choli to Canada, where he was reunited with his siblings.
He told Olivares that he had to learn to eat again.
text:
In the latest articles in his series on former hunger-striking asylum-seekers who were force-fed while detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Guardian immigration reporter José Olivares on Monday featured a Kurdish filmmaker who said he is still suffering from physical and psychological pain from the torture he endured last year.

Iran-born Gabar Choli told Olivares that he went voluntarily with guards to the infirmary at ICE's Port Isabel Service Processing Center in Los Fresnos, Texas, the first time he was force-fed.

“First I did not resist," he said. "But after I saw they were torturing me, I started protesting: ‘I’m not coming with you people.'"

From there, things only got worse. Choli said that guards would pin him down while staff shoved a plastic tube through his nose, down his throat and esophagus, and into his stomach to pump him full of nutritional liquid without his consent.

“Two guards would hold my feet; two hold my hands; one hold my head—and they would shove tubes in my nose,” Choli told Olivares. “It’s not easy to be wrestled to the ground twice a day by men that are stronger than you. And you just take it. You have 60cm (2 feet) of tube going through you, and you just feel every centimeter of it.”

“I was respectful. I just told them I am protesting for humane treatment, nothing else,” he said. “But they were determined to break me.”

Choli recounted how one nurse working for ICE “shoved the tube so hard” that “he tore my nose from the inside.”

“They would take me to solitary cell and I would just choke on my blood and drink the blood from inside [my throat],” he said.

The force-feeding continued for the next eight months. One time, a guard's rough treatment injured his ribs and made breathing painful for weeks. Another time, guards “pressed so hard on my shoulder, I thought my chest was going to break in half."

During another session, medical staff ignored Choli's warnings and accidentally shoved the nasogastric feeding tube into his lung.

On some Fridays, Choli agreed to drink the nutritional shakes if guards let him pray and socialize with other detainees.

Court records viewed by Olivares showed Choli suffered injuries and medical issues including swollen sinuses, esophageal damage, and stomach problems following his force-feeding.

Dr. Chanelle Diaz, an assistant professor at Columbia University’s medical center, told The Guardian, "T hat is just not medical care, that is torture."

Choli admitted: "It just broke me, mentally broke me. It came to a point that I decided to write my body an apology letter.”

The writer and director of short dramas including Waves Goodbye, Love if Loud, and We Don't Understand Him, He Speaks in Broken English, Choli advocates for Kurdish independence and legally sought asylum in the United States upon entering the country from Canada in 2022. He lived legally in Los Angeles, attended his required ICE check-ins, and obtained a US work permit while his asylum case was processed.

An immigration judge denied Choli's asylum claim in 2024, but granted him protection against being deported to Iran, barring the government from sending him back there. He was arrested in February 2025 during a routine ICE check-in following President Donald Trump's return to the White House.

Choli was first sent to the Desert View Annex in Adelanto, California—run by private prison profiteer GEO Group—where detainees have reported medical and mental health neglect, excessive use of force and pepper spray, mold, punsafe drinking water, inadequate food, poor sanitation, and use of solitary confinement, among other alleged abuses.

The following month, as ICE officials pressured him to agree to be deported to Iran—where his advocacy for Kurdish independence could cost him his life—Choli began his hunger strike, demanding better conditions and a fair resolution to his case.

“I am not suicidal,” Choli declared to a judge. “I am using hunger strike as the only available option to protest the abuse and mistreatment.”

Around two weeks after beginning his hunger strike, Choli was transferred to Port Isabel, where he was held in solitary confinement—which survivors and experts call a form of psychological torture—as he continued his hunger strike.

US District Judge Rolando Olvera—an appointee of former President Barack Obama—ordered Choli's force-feeding following a request from ICE, which called the detainee's hunger strike an attempt "to manipulate the immigration system" and “a serious threat to the security and good order” at Port Isabel. Olvera did not meet with Choli, who had no legal representation throughout his ordeal.

The US Department of Homeland Security told The Guardian that ICE “provides involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death."

However, under the World Medical Association’s Declaration of Malta, doctors are advised not to force-feed prisoners who choose to hunger strike and understand the consequences of their actions.

During The Troubles in Northern Ireland, British authorities allowed 10 imprisoned Irish Republican Army members, including former Member of Parliament Bobby Sands, to starve themselves to death.

In contrast, force-feeding is institutional policy in US prisons, including the Guantánamo Bay concentration camp in Cuba, where detainees—most of whom were charged with no crime—were force-fed during the George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations.

During Trump's two terms, hundreds of people have gone on hunger strike at ICE detention centers across the country to protest overcrowded and unsanitary conditions, spoiled and worm-infested food and water, inadequate medical care, delays in immigration procedures, alleged physical and psychological torture, and other mistreatment.

In May, US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin dismissed the hunger strikers as a “handful” of detainees whom he falsely claimed were striking because they “want their ethnic right food.”

"This isn't Holiday Inn," Mullin said, referring to the hotel chain.

In early January, ICE deported Choli to Canada, where he was reunited with his siblings. He told Olivares that he had to learn to eat again.

"The price of it was my kidneys, my gallbladder," he said. "My intestines. My being. My bladder, you know, is damaged. Every time I twist and turn, I feel pain. But this is the price you pay for making a stand for what is right.”

title: Appellate Court Pauses $100,000 H-1B Fee Policy as Appeal Continues | Littler
description:
This came after the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts vacated the controversial $100,000 H-1B proclamation fee, ruling it an unlawful tax and an improper use of executive power.
As a result, the district court’s ruling remains in effect, and the $100,000 H-1B fee cannot currently be enforced while the case continues through the courts.
As it stands, USCIS and the Department of State cannot now assess or require the $100,000 payment for H-1B filings.
The government could seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court by requesting an emergency stay of the decision, reviving the $100,000 fee.
This suit is now pending appeal at U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C.
text:
On July 24, 2026, in State of California v. Noem, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied the U.S. government’s request for a stay on a temporary pause of the $100,000 H-1B fee policy. This came after the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts vacated the controversial $100,000 H-1B proclamation fee, ruling it an unlawful tax and an improper use of executive power. The government appealed, asking the First Circuit to grant an emergency stay (pause) of the decision. The district court briefly stayed its own decision to provide time for the First Circuit to render its decision. The First Circuit ultimately denied the motion to stay, however. As a result, the district court’s ruling remains in effect, and the $100,000 H-1B fee cannot currently be enforced while the case continues through the courts.

The policy at issue was originally outlined in Presidential Proclamation 10973 on September 19, 2025. The proclamation required U.S. employers filing H-1B petitions for certain foreign workers on or after September 21, 2025, to submit an additional $100,000 payment as a condition of eligibility. The agency said it is not planning a 30-foot-high barrier in Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park or the Black Gap Wildlife Management Area.
The agency’s online Smart Wall map outlines projects across the southern border, including projects in the Big Bend region.
Concerns over roads and tourism Residents also worry the infrastructure could affect an economy heavily dependent on visitors to Big Bend National Park and the Rio Grande.

text:
AUSTIN (Nexstar) — U.S. Customs and Border Protection says it does not plan to build a 30-foot-high border wall through Big Bend National Park, but preparations are underway for a broader border infrastructure project that includes new and improved patrol roads, detection technology and vehicle barriers.

The latest details come as residents, environmental advocates and some local law enforcement officials push back against construction plans across the Big Bend region, raising concerns about the potential effects on the landscape, wildlife and tourism.

CBP told Nexstar construction on its Big Bend 4 project, which includes areas inside Big Bend National Park, has not officially started.

According to a CBP spokesperson, crews are currently re-grading roads damaged by recent storms to provide access for surveys. Contractors are also clearing areas to support the project’s design and survey phase ahead of construction.

The agency said it is not planning a 30-foot-high barrier in Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park or the Black Gap Wildlife Management Area. Instead, CBP said current plans call for approximately 200 miles of patrol roads and detection technology, along with roughly 17 miles of vehicle barriers in non-contiguous, strategic locations.

The agency’s online Smart Wall map outlines projects across the southern border, including projects in the Big Bend region. CBP describes its broader Smart Wall system as a combination of steel bollard barriers, roads, cameras, lighting and detection technology, with secondary walls or waterborne barriers in some locations.

CBP said the projects are part of its effort to implement President Donald Trump’s border security directives and are supported by $46.5 billion provided through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

“The Smart Wall based on identified operational requirements provides Border Patrol with both the impedance and denial, domain awareness and the access and mobility required to secure the border,” a CBP spokesperson said.

Republican sheriff questions parts of plan

Opposition has also come from some Republican officials who support stronger border enforcement but question whether physical barriers are the best approach for the region.

Terrell County Sheriff Thaddeus Cleveland, a Republican and retired Border Patrol agent with 26 years of experience, told KXAN he believes some barriers can be useful but does not support the vehicle barriers planned for his county.

“What we do need is more badges, meaning more men and women with a badge on their chest to affect an arrest and more technology,” Cleveland said.

Cleveland said the Big Bend region’s rugged terrain already acts as a natural obstacle in many areas. He said vehicle barriers could make sense in locations where vehicles can cross the Rio Grande, but argued they would serve little purpose in other stretches of the region.

He instead pointed to autonomous surveillance towers and aerial surveillance technology as tools he believes are more effective in the remote region.

“I believe in barriers where barriers work,” Cleveland said. “But I think America has this false sense of security that having a 30-foot wall is going to stop people from coming.”

Opponents say preparations are already affecting the park

While CBP distinguishes the current work from construction, people opposed to the project say they are already seeing significant changes on the ground.

Laiken Jordahl, a national public lands advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity and former National Park Service employee, said bulldozers and excavators are clearing vegetation while construction workers and equipment have moved into the region.

“At the moment, there’s a ton of land being cleared,” Jordahl said.

Jordahl said he plans to document the work around Santa Elena Canyon and its potential impact on native plants and wildlife habitat.

Three Terlingua residents expressed similar concerns.

Rebecca Evans, a longtime Big Bend area resident and former river guide, said she has seen bulldozers working in habitat used by protected species, including the yellow-billed cuckoo. Michael Ryan, a retired National Park Service law enforcement river ranger, said the physical work has made the project more tangible to residents who have been raising concerns for months.

CBP, however, said the work underway is preparation for surveys and design, not the beginning of construction on the Big Bend 4 project.

Concerns over roads and tourism

Residents also worry the infrastructure could affect an economy heavily dependent on visitors to Big Bend National Park and the Rio Grande.

Ryan says tourism drives much of the regional economy, with businesses tied to Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, the Rio Grande and the surrounding landscape.

Evans and other residents argue expanded surveillance technology could provide border security with less disruption to the landscape. He also said drones and other technology already used in the region could reduce the need for new roads and barriers.

CBP maintains the combination of infrastructure and technology is necessary to give Border Patrol agents the ability to detect, slow and respond to illegal crossings.

For now, the agency says the Big Bend 4 project remains in its design and survey phase. But with crews and equipment already on the ground, opponents say they will continue watching closely as CBP moves toward construction.

OXFORD, Miss. — ICE Homeland Security Investigations and its federal, state and local law enforcement partners announced the conclusion of Operation Muddy Waters, a coordinated, two-week, statewide enforcement effort targeting child exploitation offenders and previously convicted sex offenders across Mississippi.

The operation resulted in the arrests of 70 individuals for offenses connected to child exploitation, solicitation of children, possession or distribution of child sexual abuse material, and violations involving previously convicted sex offenders.

“Those who choose to hide behind a computer screen to exploit children will not remain hidden,” said HSI Gulfport Assistant Special Agent in Charge Matthew Reidell. “Operation Muddy Waters demonstrates HSI’s unwavering commitment to protecting children, supporting victims and holding offenders accountable. We will continue working with our federal, state and local partners to bring these crimes to light, pursue those responsible and help prevent further harm.”

Operation Muddy Waters generated multiple new child exploitation investigations, including those involving individuals who allegedly traveled across state lines to engage in sexual activity with kids, suspects allegedly involved in the livestreaming of child sexual exploitation, and individuals accused of downloading, sharing or soliciting child sexual abuse material.

The operation also resulted in criminal illegal aliens unlawfully present in the United States who allegedly traveled across state lines to engage in sex with children, as well as individuals holding positions of public trust suspected of possessing child sexual abuse material.

Operation Muddy Waters was conducted in partnership with the U.S. Attorney’s Offices for the Northern and Southern Districts of Mississippi, the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office, the Mississippi Department of Public Safety, the U.S. Marshals Service, sheriff’s offices in Marshall, DeSoto, Harrison, Pearl River, and Forrest counties, the Oxford Police Department and other federal, state and local partners.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is introducing an interim final rule (IFR) that allows U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to mandate electronic filing, or e-filing, for certain immigration forms.

Under this IFR, USCIS may require future filings of any immigration form that has been available for e-filing for at least 180 days to be submitted online. USCIS will notify the public on its website at least 60 days before requiring e-filing of a form. Filers must use an online account to submit an immigration form to USCIS, either by completing the form online or by uploading a PDF of the completed form and related evidence.

This initiative will eliminate reliance on the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s physical lockbox services and accelerate the shift to electronic fee payments. The transition should deliver substantial cost savings and greater efficiency for the federal government.

By making data easier to receive, store, and access than with paper forms, e-filing enhances fraud detection, streamlines identity management, and improves national security screening through faster data access and expanded analytical capabilities. E-filing also reduces errors, incomplete submissions, and application decision times. The adjudication process becomes more secure, more transparent, and more efficient.

Electronic filing is already common for many USCIS forms. This is not a new process for aliens to file electronic benefit requests. Requestors who cannot file electronically may request a waiver. Waivers are granted at USCIS’ discretion for undue hardship.

text:
Six weeks after local officials issued a public health order concerning a confirmed active case of tuberculosis at an immigration detention center in Aurora, the private company that runs the facility still has not allowed access for health officials to complete a legally-required investigation.

The result is a standoff between state and local government and a company unwilling to cooperate.

On Monday, community advocates once again called for more pressure from the state government, issuing their own “people’s public health order” at the Colorado Capitol, steps from Gov. Jared Polis’ office.

“We are here to demand that the state health department and the governor’s office do everything in their power, including issuing a state public health order, to hold the GEO Group accountable for their wrongdoing,” Maureen Daly, a retired pediatrician, said.

The GEO Group runs the detention facility for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement as a federal contractor.

Advocates, including Daly, worry that state agencies have not pushed harder against GEO’s obstruction out of fear of litigation. GEO is already suing the state over a new law that gives the state increased health and safety inspection authority.

“I don’t think what The GEO Group will do or will not do should have anything to do with this public health decision,” Daly said. “This should be about protecting the health of the people of Colorado.”

The symbolic people’s order, referring to the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, states that the “inaction and lack of urgency from the Governor’s office and CDPHE have lost our trust.”

It demands access to the facility so health officials can complete a proper investigation into the confirmed tuberculosis case and potential spread of the disease. Community members signed an oversized printout of the order in front of the Capitol. An online version also allows people to endorse it. It states that people recently released from the facility have reported people testing positive for tuberculosis through a skin test.

In various statements to reporters, ICE contends that the infected person was “treated, cleared, and removed from the country” and that there are no other cases in the detention center. GEO determined that 61 people were exposed to the original case and placed in a “precautionary cohort,” according to an oversight report last month from Rep. Jason Crow’s office.

State ‘shut out’

Jill Hunsaker Ryan, the executive director of the CDPHE, listened to speakers and spoke with rally attendees on Monday for about 15 minutes.

“I appreciate the advocates,” she said. “I appreciate what they’re doing today and I understand why they’re concerned.”

Ryan said CDPHE used to have a “collegial” relationship with GEO and could enter the facility to inspect and help with disease control. That changed about six months ago, when she said the company began to “shut out” the state.

“We’ve started with the communication route. We used to work together, so we asked our federal partners … to implore them to work with us again. If that doesn’t work, nothing’s off the table,” she said. “It’s an unprecedented situation to have a federal contractor not respond to a public health order.”

CDPHE set a deadline for GEO to comply with Adam County’s public health order by July 17, but that date passed without consequence. Ryan said that a CDPHE-issued public health order would carry the same authority, and she’s unsure it would force compliance. It would, however, have the enforcement weight of the attorney general’s office behind it.

While speaking with Ryan, community members told her the state should start levying fines on GEO, questioned “where the dam breaks” on the issue, and said they will continue putting pressure on the state until there is a CDPHE public health order.

“If we don’t hold the line on this, what is going to make our government act?” said Andrea Loya, the executive director of Casa de Paz, which supports people recently released from the GEO detention center. “If (tuberculosis) isn’t enough, what will be?”

In a statement, Polis spokesperson Ally Sullivan said the governor’s office is “actively monitoring the situation” and has repeatedly requested information from GEO. She did not answer a question about whether the state worries about possible litigation over a second public health order.

“The state is considering next steps including the option of a public health order should it be necessary,” she wrote. “GEO asserts there is not an active case or an outbreak at the facility, and we hope that is true, but we lack critical information to ensure that is the case. The state will continue to evaluate the public health risk and is asking GEO to work with Adams County Health or CDPHE to promptly resolve this matter.”

text:
Latest win comes after winning first lawsuit just six weeks ago against HUD’s continued illegal efforts to undermine program that support permanent housing for people facing housing security or experiencing homelessness

Trump Administration put more than 2,000 Minnesotans at risk of losing their housing

August 10, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison and a multistate coalition have won their latest lawsuit challenging the illegal attempt of the Trump Administration’s Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to cap funding for permanent housing projects that help families facing housing insecurity or experiencing homelessness. If Attorney General Ellison had not successfully challenged HUD’s policy, more than 2,000 Minnesotans would have been at risk of losing their homes.

This win comes just six weeks after the June 30 win that Attorney General Ellison and the coalition secured in their first lawsuit challenging HUD’s attempt to impose illegal conditions on this funding.

“Twice the Trump Administration tried to impose illegal conditions on funding that helps families experiencing housing insecurity or homelessness secure permanent housing, and twice I have sued them over it and won,” said Attorney General Ellison. “For more than 20 years, administrations of both parties have prioritized evidence-based Housing First strategies, and Trump’s repeated efforts to cut or divert funding from it is both illegal and cruel. My job is to help Minnesotans afford their lives and live with dignity, safety, and respect, and if that means suing Trump to help keep vulnerable folks in permanent housing and restore the rule of law, I’ll do it.”

For more than two decades, HUD has embraced a commitment to permanent housing programs and the Housing First model, which prioritizes rapid placement in permanent housing without requiring people to first meet conditions such as sobriety or a minimum income threshold. The Trump Administration, however, has rejected that commitment and undermined the Continuum of Care (CoC) program.

In November 2025, Attorney General Ellison and a coalition of states sued HUD over the agency’s decision last year to impose illegal conditions on billions of dollars in funding for the CoC program, including an attempt to impose a cap on the amount of CoC funds that can support permanent supportive housing. On June 30, 2026, Attorney General Ellison and the coalition won that lawsuit when a federal court in Rhode Island granted critical parts of the coalition’s motion for summary judgment, ruling that HUD’s conditions restricting CoC funding are unlawful and cannot be implemented.

After that cap was struck down as unlawful, HUD changed its tactics. They issued a new notice of funding opportunity that would have created a $1.3 billion set-aside for new projects prioritizing such things as transitional housing, which would have resulted in a de facto cap on permanent housing. That shift threatened housing for at least 97,000 residents of CoC-funded permanent housing across the country, including more than 2,000 in Minnesota, according to the National Alliance to End Homelessness.

On July 7, 2026, just one week after winning the prior lawsuit against HUD, Attorney General Ellison again joined a coalition of states in suing to block HUD’s latest version of these harmful changes. Today, the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island granted critical parts of the coalition’s motion for summary judgment, ruling that HUD’s set-aside was unlawful and cannot be implemented.

Joining Attorney General Ellison in the lawsuit are New York Attorney General Letitia James, Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha, and Washington Attorney General Nick Brown, who led the coalition, and the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia, and Wisconsin, and the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania.

text:
An Argentine soccer player who plays for a local Miami team remains detained in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody.

Matías Alejandro Pourrain, 34, has been in the United States since 2019, when he entered on a tourist visa.

Pourrain reportedly filed an immigration application that is still pending, but he was granted a work permit that is currently valid, attorney Regina de Moraes told Telemundo 51 in an interview.

The attorney says it all began last Thursday, when the player and his team, Miami United FC, were trying to travel to Los Angeles to play in the UPSL final.

According to her, the players had cleared Transportation Security Administration (TSA) screening and were waiting to board their flight when three men in plainclothes approached Pourrain.

“They asked for his name, he confirmed his name, and they said they needed to ask him a couple of questions,” De Moraes explained. “There was no commotion or a fight, nothing,” she added.

Pourrain was separated from his teammates. That was when someone on the team—who knows the attorney—contacted her, and she in turn reached out to ICE officers who told her, she says, that the young man would be detained and that he “could seek bond with an immigration judge or sign for voluntary self-deportation.”

That day, the player was taken to the ICE detention center in Miramar, where he stayed until this Saturday, when, according to the attorney, he began being transferred to the Krome North Service Processing Center in Miami.

The ICE detainee locator confirms he is in custody, although it still does not specify at which facility. Telemundo 51 contacted ICE, and so far, they have not been able to confirm the details of the detention or which agency carried it out.

Detentions at airports are increasing

De Moraes stresses that her client has no criminal record: “Matías doesn’t have any criminal offenses. He’s never been arrested for a DUI, domestic violence, theft—nothing,” she said. Telemundo 51 was able to confirm there are no police records that include his name, at least in Miami-Dade and Broward counties.

De Moraes also said that while he was in Miramar, agents tried to persuade him to sign his voluntary self-deportation, and she even mentioned offers of money to those who agreed to sign. The soccer player did not sign anything.

When asked about a reason for the detention, she indicated that Matías has a pending immigration petition—neither approved nor denied—and that this can be grounds for detention.

“It’s a gray area in immigration… there’s nothing that says they can’t do that,” she said. She added that “under other administrations, someone like Matías wouldn’t be arrested; he would simply be detained, processed, and released,” attributing the case to stricter immigration policies.

The arrest comes as reports point to an increase in detentions of migrants at airport terminals, even when they are not crossing an international border.

On this point, Telemundo immigration analyst Kathia Quirós says it is a real risk even to approach or stop in an airport parking lot: “TSA is sharing these individuals’ information with ICE and Border Patrol.”

In Matías’ case, his family hopes a bond request can be filed. Meanwhile, his team—where he not only plays, but also coaches children—has rallied around him and said in a statement on social media:

“Matías is not only an exceptional soccer player but, above all, an even better person and an important part of the Miami United family. His teammates, coaches, staff, and the entire Club stand firmly by his side and with his family.”

The Department of Homeland Security released the following statement:

"“On August 6, 2026, ICE arrested Matias Alejandro Pourrain, an illegal alien from Argentina, at the Fort Lauderdale International Airport. On November 12, 2019, Pourrain was legally admitted into the country at the Atlanta Intercontinental Airport, with permission to stay for six months. He chose to stay beyond May 11, 2020, in violation of our nation’s laws.

“Pourrain will remain in ICE custody pending his removal proceedings and will receive full due process.

“Being in detention is a choice. Emails and other communication from state or local agencies for ICE guidance on how to respond to requests for information or public records and ICE’s responses to these requests; and

text:
Portland Mayor Keith Wilson and Councilor Steve Novick today announced a combined $20,000 contribution to support the City of Newport's ongoing legal fight to prevent a federal contractor from establishing an ICE detention and processing facility at the Newport Municipal Airport.

"Our support reflects Portland's responsibility to stand alongside communities and mayors across Oregon to keep communities safe, keep families together, and ensure every person is treated with dignity and respect," Mayor Wilson said. "Portland is proud to support Mayor Kaplan of Newport and cities across Oregon when federal overreach threatens community safety. I want to thank Councilor Steve Novick for his important contribution, and Brenda Alvarado for her leadership in ensuring our sanctuary commitments help those they are meant to serve."

The contribution, $10,000 from the Mayor's Office budget and $10,000 from Councilor Novick's Office budget, comes in response to a formal request from Newport Mayor Jan Kaplan.

"Just as we share resources with other communities when they're fighting fires, we should help to make sure Newport has the legal resources it needs to fight ICE," Novick said. "Their fight is our fight. And it makes me proud of our state that not just Portland, but Ashland, and Yachats, and Benton County have rallied to Newport's side."

This work was coordinated and led by Brenda Alvarado, the City of Portland's Immigrant Affairs Lead, appointed earlier this year to oversee sanctuary compliance, immigrant safety initiatives, and community coordination on immigration‑related issues. Alvarado worked closely with legal partners, advocates like Portland Immigrant Rights Coalition, ensuring Portland's response aligned with legal precedent and community‑driven priorities.

"As the statewide hotline for reporting ICE activity, PIRC sees every day how interconnected our communities around Oregon are," the Portland Immigrant Rights Coalition said. "It is critical that we see cross-state coordination and advocacy to defend our hard-won protections. We applaud elected leaders around the state collaborating to protect our communities from ICE encroachment.

A regional challenge with statewide consequences

According to information provided by the City of Newport, in late 2025, Newport learned that federal contractors were attempting to convert airport property into an ICE detention center, a plan that also involved removing the Coast Guard's Search and Rescue helicopter. The news prompted immediate community response: more than 800 residents attended a special meeting on November 12, the city received over 300 emails opposing the proposal, and Members of Oregon's Congressional Delegation led efforts to prevent the plan from moving forward.

Days later, the Newport City Council passed a resolution objecting to any ICE facility and hired Stoll Berne to pursue legal action. Newport has since sued the federal government, arguing required processes were not followed. DHS and ICE have acknowledged they were exploring the facility and have stated they are "no longer planning" to move forward, but Newport continues to seek permanent restrictions.

Legal costs have reached nearly $500,000, with support from Yachats, Ashland, Benton County, and now Portland.

Portland's sanctuary commitments

Portland's support for Newport aligns with the city's long‑standing commitment to protecting immigrant communities. In 2025, the City Council unanimously approved the Sanctuary Ordinance 192115 and Protect Portland Initiative, formally codifying Portland as a sanctuary city and establishing clear prohibitions on assisting federal immigration enforcement.

Under the initiative, Portland:

Prohibits City employees from assisting federal immigration enforcement without a judicial warrant

Bars the use of City resources for immigration enforcement

Requires policies, training and signage to guide interactions with federal agents

Directs the City to file FOIA requests with DHS and ICE

Directs the Office of Government Relations to advocate for federal immigration reforms and civil‑rights protections

Five months after establishing the Immigrant Affairs Lead position, Portland has built a coordinated, citywide strategy to uphold its sanctuary commitments and strengthen support for immigrant communities. The City is implementing a comprehensive framework that unites City bureaus, legal partners, community organizations, government partners, and immigrant leaders around a shared goal: using every lawful tool available to protect City employees and immigrant families.

This work includes strengthening sanctuary protocols, advancing emergency preparedness planning, developing sanctuary training for more than 7,000 City employees, expanding Know Your Rights and family preparedness initiatives, convening immigrant community forums, and deepening regional partnerships to ensure Portland is prepared to respond with coordination, compassion, and resolve.
