title: Urge Your Members of Congress to Pass the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act - CWS
description:
The Protecting Sensitive Locations Act (H.R.
Why Sensitive Locations Protections Matter: In the three decades leading up to the second Trump administration, Democratic and Republican presidents alike maintained policies limiting immigration enforcement in sensitive locations.
“My name is [insert name], and as your constituent from [City/Town], I urge you to support the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act.
Pass the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act so that all of our neighbors can attend worship services without fearing arrest, detention, and deportation.
Pass the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act.
text:
Right now, there are no policies in place to prevent federal immigration enforcement agents from deliberately targeting spaces that represent key pillars of civic, religious, and community life. The threat of immigration enforcement at “sensitive locations” – such as houses of worship, schools, hospitals, courthouses, food pantries, and places where people receive essential services – is preventing refugees and immigrants across the country from accessing the resources they need.

The Protecting Sensitive Locations Act (H.R. 1061/S.455) would limit immigration enforcement at sensitive locations or within 1,000 feet of such places. See CWS’s explainer for more on the bill and the history of sensitive locations protections.

Use the tool below to urge your elected officials to codify limits on immigration enforcement so refugees and immigrants can seek spiritual support, education, medical care, and other key resources without the fear of arrest, detention, or separation from their families.

Why Sensitive Locations Protections Matter:

In the three decades leading up to the second Trump administration, Democratic and Republican presidents alike maintained policies limiting immigration enforcement in sensitive locations.

Then, on the first day of President Trump’s second term, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) rescinded the most recent version of the guidance, which had advised federal immigration enforcement agents to avoid making arrests at places where people receive essential services. Decisions about enforcement in or near sensitive locations are now largely up to individual officers’ discretion. Today, many members of our communities live in fear that they may face arrest while participating in worship services, pursuing an education, receiving health care, or attending immigration court hearings.

With a one-page memo, the Trump administration erased over 30 years of precedent that upheld religious freedom and safeguarded families’ access to essential services because Congress still hasn’t codified limitations on immigration enforcement activity in sensitive locations.

Both Democratic and Republican Members of Congress have publicly recognized that sensitive locations protections are necessary to uphold religious freedom and ensure community members can safely access crucial services.

The Protecting Sensitive Locations Act – led in the 119th Congress by Representative Adriano Espaillat and Senator Richard Blumenthal – would restore the sense of security that community members need so that they can fully engage with the resources and opportunities that strengthen congregations, neighborhoods, and local economies.

EMAIL YOUR MEMBERS OF CONGRESS

Using the tool above, you can send an email to your Member of Congress.

Sample Email: “My name is [insert name], and as your constituent from [City/Town] and a [person of faith/refugee/member of community], I urge you to cosponsor and pass the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act (H.R. 1061/S.455) to limit immigration enforcement at houses of worship, schools, hospitals, courthouses, and other places where people receive essential services.

For over 30 years, Democratic and Republican presidential administrations maintained policies limiting immigration enforcement at or near “sensitive locations,” recognizing that all communities stand to benefit when everyone can attend religious services, take their children to school, go to the doctor, or appear in court without fear.

On the first day of President Trump’s second term, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) upended decades of precedent by rescinding guidance limiting immigration enforcement actions at sensitive locations.

Congress must pass the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act so that everyone can attend religious services, pursue an education, and receive health care without fearing arrest, detention, deportation, and separation from their family.

The legislation would limit immigration enforcement at or within 1,000 feet of locations such as:

Places of worship and sites of religious ceremonies

Health care facilities

Schools and educational settings

Child-focused locations, including childcare centers, foster care facilities, playgrounds, and school bus stops

Disaster relief and social service locations, including shelters, food banks, and community service providers

Civic and government locations, such as courthouses, congressional offices, Social Security offices, DMVs, and polling places

Public institutions, including libraries and labor union halls

The bill includes exceptions for “exigent” circumstances involving threats to public safety, and establishes guardrails requiring officers to track and report in writing all instances in which they invoke exceptions to perform immigration enforcement at or near sensitive locations.

I urge you to support the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act so that everyone in our community can freely exercise their religion, access the services they need, and fully participate in civic life.”

CALL YOUR MEMBERS OF CONGRESS

Call your federal elected officials using the tool above.

“My name is [insert name], and as your constituent from [City/Town], I urge you to support the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act. The bill limits immigration enforcement at houses of worship, schools, hospitals, courthouses, and other places where people receive essential services.

For over 30 years leading up to the second Trump administration, Democratic and Republican presidential administrations maintained policies limiting immigration enforcement at or near sensitive locations. President Trump rescinded the policy on the first day of his second term.

Now, immigrants, refugees, and their family members across the country are increasingly afraid to participate in religious services, attend school, or seek medical care, fearing that they could be arrested, detained and deported.

I urge you to support the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act so that everyone in our community can freely exercise their religion, access the services they need, and fully participate in civic life.”

POST ON SOCIAL MEDIA

Share this message with your elected officials on social media. See below for sample posts:

text:
Donald Trump’s administration is facing questions over whether it is using Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to “surveil political opponents” after after an investigative agent was apparently stationed outside Democratic representative Ilhan Omar’s monthly town hall meeting in Richfield, Minnesota.

After the incident, Omar demanded the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) clarify whether Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents have been used to monitor “any other activity” involving “local, state, or federal officials” in the state.

In a letter to Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), an arm of ICE, the congresswoman said an agent claiming to be conducting an undercover drug operation was parked outside the community center where she was holding an event last Thursday, without prior coordination with local law enforcement.

According to Omar, who represents Minnesota’s fifth congressional district, a Richfield police officer noticed the agent sitting in a Ford Explorer and “became suspicious of the way she was monitoring the building”.

“He proceeded to run the plates attached to the vehicle and discovered they were registered to a different vehicle,” said Omar. “He approached the woman in the vehicle to ask about the purpose for her presence there and why the plates on her vehicle did not match the government’s records. Like any reasonable officer, he was concerned that she harbored ill intentions and may be in a stolen vehicle.”

The woman initially identified herself as security, but later called her supervisor and said she was an HSI agent conducting an undercover drug operation in the area, Omar said. Richfield police had not been informed of the operation beforehand, according the congresswoman.

Omar said that despite a visible sign indicating that a town hall was taking place at the community center, the agent remained parked there until speaking with her supervisor, after which she left the property.

“HSI’s actions yesterday evening put an entire community at risk,” she said. “Instead of monitoring the area for those who might wish harm to me and my constituents, Richfield Police were required to devote time to investigating why an HSI agent was outside of a Congressional event in a vehicle with mismatched plates.”

Omar added: “It also raises serious and uncomfortable questions about the purpose of HSI’s presence outside of my event. At best, your agent was unable to assess that the parking lot of a community center hosting a congressional event wasn’t the best place to conduct a drug operation.

“At worst, it emphasizes many Americans’ growing concern that the Trump administration uses ICE to surveil political opponents and may interfere with our democracy.”

In her letter, Omar is demanding answers about why the agent was at the community center, how the agent and her supervisor knew she was holding a town hall there and what action they took in response to that knowledge.

The Guardian has contacted DHS for comment.

Inside the department, HSI is a federal law enforcement agency and the main investigative branch of ICE. ICE operations in Minnesota have sparked widespread protests across the state this year and have also resulted in the deaths of two Americans, Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, who were killed by federal agents.

In January, a man sprayed Omar with an unidentified substance from a syringe during a town hall where she called for ICE to be abolished “for good”.

The incident drew widespread condemnation from local and state leaders, with Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey calling it “unacceptable” and saying: “We can disagree without putting people at risk.”

title: “All Hands on Deck”: How Trump Is Overwhelming Immigration Courts | The New Republic
description:
President Donald Trump’s sweeping mass deportation scheme is completely crushing the U.S. court system—and that’s by design, Politico reported Sunday.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has bet big on video gamers to fix the country’s dangerous shortage of air traffic controllers—but it probably won’t pay off.
Air traffic controllers experience extreme stress and burnout, and it doesn’t seem that the FAA is going to be able to fix that problem any time soon.
In May, the FAA announced that it would reduce its air traffic controller staffing target from 14,633 to 12,563, citing modernized staffing models.
In reality, the agency planned to increase the amount of time employees spent managing air traffic after discovering that air traffic controllers had logged 2.2 million hours of overtime in 2024, costing the government roughly $200 million.
text:
President Donald Trump’s sweeping mass deportation scheme is completely crushing the U.S. court system—and that’s by design, Politico reported Sunday.

On July 8, 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement published a two-page memo expanding its policy on mandatory detention without bond to apply not only to immigrants who were caught illegally crossing the U.S. border, but to any undocumented immigrant.

Under the new policy, every undocumented immigrant is treated as someone “seeking” to enter the U.S., even if they have lived here for years, have families, hold jobs, and are in the process of seeking citizenship. Previous administrations have never applied this rule to immigrants already in the United States.

The result was an unprecedented surge on the legal system, as judges scrambled to hear thousands of detainees’ cases before ICE could whisk them away to other states.

Judge Fred Biery in the Western District of Texas told Politico that his courthouse typically sees 1,500 lawsuits every year—but as of May, they’d already hit 4,000 cases. “We’ve never seen anything like this in my career,” he told Politico.

Since ICE’s new policy on mandatory detention without bond was implemented, 469 judges have ruled that it is unlawful, while just 54 have sided with the Trump administration. Judges have ruled against detentions without bond more than 16,000 times in the last year.

“The third branch of government is saying no. We’re not going to do it this way,” Biery said.

Judge Troy Nunley, the chief judge in the Eastern District of California, told Politico that the strain has been felt by judges and court staff alike. “All of our judges, we were up in the wee hours of the morning doing these cases because we had never seen these before. It was all hands on deck,” he said.

In 2021, Nunley’s court saw just four immigration habeas cases. In May alone, his court saw 675. The judge has had to pull in other jurists from Hawaii and California to help shoulder the burden.

All over the country, the courts are pushing back, U.S. District Judge Patrick Schiltz told Politico. Until July 1, Schiltz was the chief of Minnesota’s federal district court. “The judiciary is the glue that’s holding the country together,” he said. “I do believe that’s true right now.”

Meanwhile, the Trump administration has moved to fast-track hundreds of thousands of asylum applicants directly into deportation proceedings without interviewing them. The government has also rapidly expedited the removal of immigrant children.

President Donald Trump’s repeated attempts to punish former Olympian David Hearn on the made-up vandalism of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool may backfire.

The U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, was forced to drop the felony charges against Hearn on July 31 due to a lack of evidence, faulting Trump’s handpicked contractor for a shoddy renovation instead. But on Sunday, Trump was still pushing his false claim that Hearn actively vandalized the pool’s lining, claiming on Truth Social that a National Park Service career employee, “a highly credible witness,” watched Hearn “‘violently’ ripping and tugging at the Pool’s somewhat delicate coating.”

Hearn’s lawyers—Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Fund, Mary Dohrmann of Washington Litigation Group, and Steve Levin of Steptoe LLP—said in a statement Monday that they aren’t going to take “continued harassment” from the president.

“The government is continuing to attack an innocent man. Our first filing in the case on July 10 included photographic evidence from before Mr. Hearn touched the Reflecting Pool proving that he caused no damage,” the lawyers told Mediaite. “Our other filings provided even more proof. Finally, the U.S. Attorney’s own motion on July 31 admitted the damage was caused by a ‘botched installation and not vandalism.’ We are reviewing all legal remedies, including for this continued harassment. It is outrageous.”

This means that Hearn could sue Trump and the Department of Justice over the false claims, which the DOJ have already disavowed in court. There are a lot of unanswered questions over how Pirro’s office secured an indictment against Hearn in the first place with such faulty evidence. She later blamed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum for deliberately misleading her office about Hearn’s actions.

The New Republic’s Greg Sargent reports that Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee are looking to open an investigation into how Hearn was charged and demand documents from the Justice and Interior Departments relating to that decision. Hearn’s lawyers are also seeking access to transcripts of the federal grand jury proceedings. Trump’s tantrum over the failed Reflecting Pool renovations may soon turn into a big legal headache for him and his administration.

Taylor Farms, the source of this summer’s cyclospora outbreak that’s causing an explosive diarrhea epidemic, now has to recall multiple products over a salmonella risk.

On Sunday, the Trump-linked company announced it was recalling a dozen different prepared food products, including jalapeño peppers, salsas, and guacamole due to salmonella contamination. Taylor Farms said the products came from Coast Citrus Distributors, and that the company was no longer sourcing peppers from one Sinaloa, Mexico, farmer.

The recall comes a week after another salmonella outbreak linked to jalapeño peppers from Mexico, which has made at least 345 people sick in 27 different states and resulted in 36 hospitalizations. Restaurant chains including Chipotle and Qdoba have since stopped using the peppers.

This summer has seen numerous food-borne illnesses spread across the U.S. following layoffs and staff cuts in regulatory agencies. The cyclospora outbreak has resulted in at least 18,517 cases across nine states listed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, according to a New Republic analysis, and two deaths were reported in Michigan last week. (State officials noted that cyclosporiasis is usually not a life-threatening illness, and that both people who died had underlying health conditions.)

Last month, close to 1.6 million white shell eggs and brown cage-free shell eggs produced in Texas had to be recalled due to salmonella fears. The New World screwworm, a flesh-eating parasite, has infested cattle in Texas and spread to other states, causing an estimated $1 billion in damages.

Last year, Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency cut a monitoring program for the screwworm and gutted the CDC team that would have handled the cyclospora outbreak. The people left behind, led by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., are now dealing with one crisis after another with little public confidence that more aren’t on the way.

It seems President Donald Trump’s fascination with AI-generated images must be genetic.

In two separate posts on Instagram Sunday evening, Eric Trump shared a series of photographs from the LIV New York Golf tournament at the Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, New Jersey.

Both posts included the same picture of the president, who was photographed grinning beside two of his grandchildren—and the image appeared to have been altered using AI.

The background of the photograph was warped into an improbable-looking armchair, and a hint of loose flesh could be spotted floating behind one of the grandkid’s ears.

Looks like it was a very normal weekend with grandpa!

Donald Trump himself also posted an AI-altered image from his weekend at Bedminster—thinning his body, straightening his posture, and transforming his slack-jawed appearance into his once-signature steely look.

In reality, photographs of the 80-year-old president revealed bruises on his arm.

Trump’s affinity for self-aggrandizing AI slop wouldn’t matter so much if he were just someone’s elderly relative posting on Facebook. But the president of the United States is clearly more interested in leading his own fan club than he is in, well, governing.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has bet big on video gamers to fix the country’s dangerous shortage of air traffic controllers—but it probably won’t pay off.

Duffy announced the results of DOT’s unorthodox hiring campaign to use a “supercharged” hiring process to recruit gamers Sunday night. Since launching in April, the DOT has reached 94 percent of its hiring goal, bringing in more than 2,000 new air traffic controllers—“the most in a single year.”

The secretary claimed candidates belonging to the “best and brightest” campaign were now “reaching the Academy quicker than any class before them, thanks to the most streamlined hiring process.”

But Duffy may be counting his chickens before they’ve hatched. Turning a trainee into a certified professional controller takes up to two years, and roughly one third of trainees never complete the process. Every unsuccessful trainee costs the government roughly $130,000.

While gamers may have the multi-tasking skills, high cognitive function, and spatial awareness the Federal Aviation Administration is seeking, will they be given the support they need not to rage quit?

Air traffic controllers experience extreme stress and burnout, and it doesn’t seem that the FAA is going to be able to fix that problem any time soon.

In May, the FAA announced that it would reduce its air traffic controller staffing target from 14,633 to 12,563, citing modernized staffing models. In reality, the agency planned to increase the amount of time employees spent managing air traffic after discovering that air traffic controllers had logged 2.2 million hours of overtime in 2024, costing the government roughly $200 million. Even with the reduced targets, the FAA remains short roughly 1,800 controllers. Nationally, about two-thirds of the FAA’s largest facilities remain below 85 percent of their staffing targets.

It’s also surprising that simply a “streamlined” hiring process would result in so many applicants being approved for training. Typically, less than 10 percent of applicants gain admission to the training academy in Oklahoma City.

The FAA announced in March 2025 that it had streamlined the process of hiring air traffic controllers by implementing a “fully automated” qualification process, allowing applicants to proceed individually, not in a group, and making the comprehensive medical and security checks concurrent. It’s not immediately clear why those changes would dramatically boost the number of successful applicants if the application process still includes pre-employment tests, including an aptitude test designed to weed out applicants lacking mental acuity.

text:
CLAYTON COUNTY, Ga. — A Cartersville man said ICE agents wrongly detained him at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport.

The American citizen told Channel 2’s Ashlyn Webb that he’s still shaken by what happened.

John Phillips had made it through TSA, had his ID checked and went through facial recognition before agents stopped him as he was boarding, he said.

“I’ll never approach a door of an aircraft without wondering if there’s guys standing back there,” he said.

It was supposed to be a routine work trip to Las Vegas, but a Delta agent told him the airline was working to upgrade his seat.

He just needed to board last.

Phillips says three ICE agents in tactical gear stopped him in the jet bridge, pinned him to the wall and put him in handcuffs.

He says he didn’t resist but told them he was an American citizen.

“They cuff me and start asking me, ‘What’s your name? What’s your birthday?’” he said.

He says after about five minutes in handcuffs, agents found his Georgia ID and showed him a picture of the man they were actually looking for.

“He looks nothing like me, other than that he’s a white guy and I’m a white guy,” Phillips said.

Agents told him the other man was from England but shared his name and birthday.

Immigration attorney Charles Kuck said ICE still must have probable cause to make an arrest.

“There is no probable cause here. A matching name and birth date is not probable cause,” Kuck said.

Phillips now wants to know how this happened.

“I just am flabbergasted that all of the security that we have at the airport, that they don’t know that I am the John Phillips that lives in Georgia and is not an English guy,” he said.

ICE confirmed the incident but said it is still working on a full statement.

Delta released a statement which read in part:

“Delta employees do not have insight into or control over law enforcement decisions, and our role is to ensure flights operate safely and customers are treated with respect. We are reviewing this event internally and are reaching out to the customer directly.”

CHICAGO (WLS) -- A group of Chicago residents and their attorneys filed nine police reports Monday, alleging violent encounters with federal immigration agents during "Operation Midway Blitz" and calling for criminal charges against those involved.

The attorneys representing the individuals said nearly a year after "Operation Midway Blitz," no charges have been filed against Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. They said they hope the filings will lead to criminal prosecutions, including felony charges.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

Among those filing reports was Marimar Martinez, who was shot five times by a Border Patrol agent.

"This man shot five bullets directly at me and tried to kill me. My car and body were pierced with bullets," Martinez said.

Martinez said she believes the federal government has failed to act against the agent involved.

"It has been 10 months since Charles Exum tried to kill me, and the federal government has failed to act or even discipline Charles Exum," she said.

Martinez was initially charged, but those charges were dropped.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement Monday, "On October 4, Border Patrol law enforcement officers were ambushed by rioters that hit federal agents with their vehicles."

DHS went on to say the Border Patrol agent who shot Martinez was placed on administrative leave. DHS said the Department of Justice would answer any further questions on the case.

Other individuals involved in the filings said that action does not go far enough.

"Those who violated me operate in the shadows, masked, nameless and shameless," Dayanne Figueroa said.

The nine police reports were filed in connection with "Operation Midway Blitz." Attorneys for the group said they want law enforcement and prosecutors to pursue criminal cases.

"Our hope today is either one, a police officer takes the step to charge these officers with a misdemeanor, or the Cook County State's Attorney's Office approves these charges for criminal prosecutions," said Brian Orozco of Kulis Law Ltd. and the Chicago Project.

Supporters of the filings pointed to findings released earlier this year by the Illinois Accountability Commission. In April, the commission released a special report that they said highlighted unconstitutional uses of force.

"We saw ICE officers ramming their cars into other people. We saw them chase folks through grocery stores, through other people's yards, for no apparent reason," said Jimmy Arce of the Illinois Accountability Commission.

Cook County Commissioner Jessica Vásquez said advocates will continue pressing for accountability.

"We are committed to do the work and to continue pushing for justice for all of our people," Vásquez said.

The Cook County State's Attorney's Office said in a statement that federal agents are not exempt from prosecution when evidence supports criminal charges.

"No one is above the law - including federal agents - and the CCSAO will not hesitate to prosecute any case when it is supported by the evidence and the law," the office said. "Under state law, law enforcement must investigate alleged criminal conduct before prosecutors can file charges."

The office added that it previously released a protocol to assist law enforcement agencies investigating incidents stemming from "Operation Midway Blitz," and said it remains committed to supporting those investigations, including an ongoing Illinois State Police investigation into the death of Silverio Villegas González.

ICE says every officer working in the field will have a body camera by the end of the month.

text:
Jewish Family and Community Services has filed a lawsuit against the United States Department of Homeland Security and Secretary Markwayne Mullin on behalf of six children.

The 159-page complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, argues that procedural changes adopted by immigration courts have eliminated due process protections Congress enacted in 1990 for abused, neglected and trafficked immigrant children.

Dana Gold, JFCS’ chief operating officer, said that this is the first time in the organization’s history that it has been a plaintiff in a lawsuit of this kind but that they felt it was necessary to protect their clients.

Get The Jewish Chronicle Weekly Edition by email and never miss our top stories Free Sign Up

“What we’ve seen locally was a pattern of taking away their legislative protections,” Gold said. “When you have minor children who have no one to stand up for them, they do have the rule of law to protect them. We have to stand up for that rule of law to be applied as it was meant to be done.”

Sarah Hough, JFCS’ director of immigration legal services, said that there have been attempts to limit the children’s access to counsel, curtail their opportunity to pursue legal cases and to “do an end around the legislative protections they are entitled to under a number of categories.”

“The only option left for some our clients was to take federal action to protest the policies themselves,” she said.

JFCS’ participation as a plaintiff in the lawsuit, Hough explained, isn’t litigating any individual cases, rather, it’s litigating against the policies themselves, which she said, has dramatically impacted the work of JFCS and the organization’s ability to perform work “ethically and do the things we are required to do for these kids under the law.”

If JFCS wants to continue to represent the children in a meaningful way, she said, it was left with no option but to pursue a legal course of action.

There have been issues, Hough explained, since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term in office. Beginning in February 2025 when, she said, JFCS received a stop work order from the administration cutting off aid and service to immigrants. In March, the government terminated JFCS’ and other organization’s contracts. That order has been a subject of ongoing litigation in which the courts have consistently said the federal government must pay for the services under the contracts and reaffirmed that children are entitled to representation, Hough said.

The pace of immigration hearings is central to the case, Hough said. Children are now required to appear in courts every two or three weeks, in proceedings JFCS’ lawsuit describes as “decoupled from the steps necessary to establish their eligibility for relief.”

The children at the heart of the lawsuit have special immigration juvenile status, Hough explained — a protection Congress created for children determined by a state court to have been a victim of abuse, neglect or abandonment — that established a legal pathway to citizenship when their visa time is eligible.

The accelerated pace, she said, affects attorneys’ ability to do the investigative work on the filings needed to protect their clients.

It also affects the children, Hough said.

“The kids are missing school,” she said. “The way the court is structured, everybody sits in an online waiting room until their case is called. In some cases, that can be an entire day. So, every two weeks the kids are being pulled away from their activities, doctor’s appointments, school,” she said.

On top of that, the Board of Immigration Appeals ruled in June that the time between earning special immigration juvenile status and the granting of a green card is so long “it is no longer in the interest of the government to wait and that they should be ordered to be removed,” Hough said.

That order has been extended to children who have undergone “a severe form of human trafficking,” she said, “whether it’s for labor or sex.”

JFCS decided to file suit in July when one of the children it represented was ordered removed.

“The kids are entitled to this relief under law, but we were no longer able to effectively advocate for them in the immigration court while the policy remains in place,” Hough offered.

When the children are returned to their countries of origin, Gold said, they are trafficked again by the same people who abused them the first time.

“That’s why this protection was put in place and now the government is violating its own policy to protect these children,” Gold said.

As to the time the children are waiting between gaining special immigration juvenile status and the time they can apply for a green card, Gold is clear, “It’s not their fault.”

“It’s because the courts are backed up,” she said. “Through no fault of their own, these children who have had horrible things happen to them are being ordered removed.”

Because of that, Gold said, JFCS and its leadership determined that they needed to “protect the children,” and “hold the government accountable to the legislations and protections that they had put in place.”

At the time of the Chronicle’s interview with Gold and Hough, though the government had not responded in court to JFCS’ lawsuit, a DHS spokesman quoted in JFCS’ statement said that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is working to stop human trafficking of children.

“President Trump and DHS are laser-focused on protecting children and will continue to work with federal, state and local law enforcement officers to reunite children with their families,” the spokesperson said. “All illegal aliens receive due process.”

JFCS lost $4 million last year due to decisions by the administration, Gold said, noting that every aspect of the organization’s work has been impacted by the Trump administration.

“We’re looking at losing another $800,000 this year and who knows what happens if this contract remains terminated,” she said. “Our ability to continue to be present in the community and strategize around and find ways to respond, so we can continue to be here to provide immigration legal services, providing food, providing trauma counseling, providing career services, all those things are much harder now.”

As to the children affected, Hough is clear.

“Through their short lives, these kids have faced situations that no one should ever have to face and yet, they come here with hope. They give us their trust. They’re brave enough to share their stories. It’s incumbent upon us to honor that trust from them, to advocate as best we can and try to keep them safe and protect them from being returned to unimaginable circumstances,” Hough said.

JFCS’ lawsuit asks the court to vacate the administrative changes at issue and to prevent the removal of the six children while they pursue their claims. PJC

text:
The Trump administration is suing the state of Connecticut, alleging discrimination against U.S. citizens by providing in-state tuition benefits and financial assistance to state residents without regard for immigration status.

Specifically, the lawsuit demands Connecticut end tuition benefits to noncitizens, including veterans, whether they are here legally or not.

The Department of Justice said it had filed lawsuits against Connecticut as well as New York and Vermont, charging that the states “seek to undermine our Nation by placing aliens over citizens in clear defiance of Congress’s commands.”

The lawsuit refers to U.S.C. § 1623(a), a 1996 law that states “Notwithstanding any other provision of law, an alien who is not lawfully present in the United States shall not be eligible on the basis of residence within a State (or a political subdivision) for any postsecondary education benefit unless a citizen or national of the United States is eligible for such a benefit (in no less an amount, duration, and scope) without regard to whether the citizen or national is such a resident.”

The Department of Justice in its suit against Connecticut charges that “Connecticut has ignored this federal law for over a decade,” naming a handful of state statutes, including Connecticut Gen. Stat. § 10a29(9), a 2011 that extends in-state tuition eligibility to those students who are legally in the U.S., live in Connecticut and graduated from a Connecticut high school after attending at least two years.

The Connecticut statute notes “Students without legal immigration status who meet the above criteria must file an affidavit with the institution stating that they have applied to legalize their immigration status or will do so as soon as they are eligible.”

A 2015 law, updated in 2018 and in 2020 in apparent anticipation of passage of the Dream Act, further extends institutional aid to undocumented people brought to the United States as children and veterans without legal immigration status. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 10a-161d states that those shall be eligible to apply for and receive, to the extent permitted by federal law, institutional financial aid to attend a public institution of higher education in the state.” It mandates that eligible students must certify they have or will apply for legal status.

Other challenged laws include specific aid from Connecticut community colleges, the need-based Roberta B. Willis Scholarship and student loans.

“Accordingly, under the Supremacy Clause of our Nation’s Constitution, Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 10a-29(9), 10a-161d, 10a-77(f), § 10a-173(d), and 10a-19m are unconstitutional, and must yield to federal law,” the lawsuit claims.

Charging that such benefits discriminate against out-of-state citizens, “create incentives for illegal immigration, and reward illegal aliens with benefits that U.S. citizens are not eligible for,” the DOJ says its goal is to block the named Connecticut laws and prevent the state from offering academic benefits to any resident “aliens,” regardless of whether they are legally present.

In response, Attorney General William Tong said, “Note to Trump — stay out of Connecticut. How we run our schools and teach our kids is none of your business and you have no authority to force the sovereign state of Connecticut to deny our kids a future. I fought for this bill as a legislator when it passed in 2011, and I’ll fight to defend Connecticut families now from this cruel attack.

“Connecticut offers in-state tuition and financial aid to all eligible Connecticut students because all kids deserve the opportunity to learn, to advance, and to achieve their dreams. Donald Trump doesn’t run UConn or any of our state colleges, and we’re not about to let him start,” Tong said in a statement.

Gov. Ned Lamont’s office, the Connecticut State College and University System and the UConn Board of Trustees did immediately reply to a request for comment.

Connecticut sues over Trump policy barring international students from U.S. if classes are entirely online

The University of Connecticut is the subject of another lawsuit brought by Trump’s Department of Justice in an effort to dispel DEI practices. That suit charges that UConn offers discriminatory housing based on race and ethnicity, specifically naming the ScHOLA²RS House, BSOUL House and La Comunidad Intelectual. UConn noted that it offers nearly 20 living and learning communities “organized around students who may have similar interests, backgrounds, or academic pursuits, including the three that were specifically named. However, these communities are open to all students and no student is denied access to these communities based on their identity.”

text:
CLEARFIELD — In mid-July, ICE published a request for information on “turn-key detention services” for four regions across the country, including central Pennsylvania, where it already has the largest immigration detention facility in the Northeast.

Local activists worry ICE is either trying to contract directly with GEO Group — which owns and operates Moshannon Valley Processing Center — or even potentially buy the facility.

When asked about what the RFI means for Moshannon, an ICE spokesperson told Spotlight PA in an Aug. 10 email that “ICE has access to over 80,000 beds across its entire detention network in a mixture of dedicated and non-dedicated facilities. As existing detention contracts in certain locations approach expiration, ICE is working to ensure continued access to detention capacity in those areas. As part of this effort, ICE is evaluating options, including the potential purchase of turnkey detention facilities where appropriate, or other contracting solutions to support continuity of operations.”

Currently, Clearfield County acts as a middleman between ICE and GEO Group, an arrangement that provides the county government with a “minor” level of oversight over the facility, which has long been accused of physical and psychological abuse, poor healthcare, and inhumane conditions.

Clearfield County’s five-year contracts with ICE and GEO Group are set to expire in late September. The setup offered a workaround to former President Joe Biden’s 2021 executive order banning private federal prisons, which President Donald Trump reversed in 2025.

Stay informed

Sign up for Talk of the Town, an update of the news that matters to your community — from the PA Wilds to Happy Valley.

Email address

Activist Tim Smith, who says he has been fighting against immigration detention facilities for 23 years, first alerted commissioners about the RFI in an email on July 13.

Smith was a plaintiff in an October 2021 lawsuit filed by the ACLU of Pennsylvania against the Clearfield County commissioners for failing to comply with the state’s open meetings law in regard to approving contracts with ICE and GEO Group.

“What’s happening now is even more stark than what was happening five years ago,” Smith said during public comment at the July 14 commissioners meeting. “I would hope that today on Bastille Day that we take at least an emergency measure to show your disapproval of what is coming.”

“The [Moshannon] warden talked to us and swears GEO isn’t selling the facility to ICE,” Clearfield County Commissioner Dave Glass told the newsroom in a July 22 email. As for a potential contract between ICE and GEO Group, the warden had no information, Glass said. “And we’ve heard nothing else.”

The warden did not return a request for comment, nor did GEO Group.

However, the company’s founder and CEO George Zoley told shareholders in a second-quarter earnings call last week that GEO Group is “engaged in an active process for the sale of several of our turnkey facilities, subject to mutual agreement on price and our continued management of those facilities under long-term support services contracts.”

He also said that “several other GEO facilities have support services

contracts that expire later this year. ICE has initiated a procurement process

involving four facilities that we hope will result in new long-term support services

contracts being awarded.”

Zoley did not specify during the call which facilities he was referring to for potential sales or renewed contracts.

According to the RFI posting, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security “requires one or more Contractor Owned/Contractor-Operated detention facilities” in the Denver, Miami, Seattle, and Philadelphia “areas of responsibility.”

The Philadelphia AOR — which includes Pennsylvania, Delaware, and West Virginia — facility should have a minimum of 1,800 detention beds and be located within 30 driving miles of State College Regional Airport.

Moshannon Valley has a bed capacity of 1,876 and is a roughly 27-mile drive from the airport.

The airport has become a major hub for ICE flights, with a massive jump from two flights in all of 2025 to 28 in April, 25 in May, and 23 in June, according to data from Human Rights First, a nonprofit that advocates for refugees and immigrants.

The RFI expands potential sites to include turnkey existing facilities, those requiring upgrades, and new constructions, with the caveat that properties must be able to begin housing detainees within 30 days of contract award and only house ICE detainees.

ICE is using the RFI to see what markets have available and how quickly it can ramp up its detention numbers, said César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández, a law professor at Ohio State who specializes in the intersection of criminal and immigration law.

With the lack of transparency, it’s difficult to say whether this RFI is an effort to get ahead of Clearfield’s upcoming contract renewals with ICE and GEO Group, García Hernández told Spotlight PA.

“So often, it’s hard to understand just what they’re doing, nonetheless, why they’re doing it, and the reason for that is that oftentimes they don’t tell us,” he said.

In September 2021, Clearfield County commissioners voted to enter into a five-year intergovernmental service agreement with ICE “to provide detention services for detainees,” according to the agreement.

Commissioners also approved a services contract with GEO Group, an international company based in Florida that owns and operates correctional and detention facilities around the globe. It “requires GEO to perform all duties and accept all responsibilities incumbent upon” the county under its agreement with ICE, according to the contract.

With the contracts ending in September, some community members worry that ICE will cut the county out of the equation rather than renew the arrangement.

For Jasmine Rivera, executive director of the Pennsylvania Immigration Coalition, it doesn’t matter who holds the contract, because the facility is still running, separating families, and incarcerating loved ones.

“It’s always unjust, always abusive, and it’s always unnecessary, regardless of who or how detention centers are being operated,” Rivera told Spotlight PA.

Pennsylvania U.S. Reps. Chris Deluzio, Madeleine Dean, and Summer Lee, all Democrats, wrote letters to ICE and GEO Group last week “to demand answers on GEO’s failure to comply with federal standards of adequate staffing and medical care to detainees, as well as obstruction of congressional oversight,” according to a news release.

Dean conducted a visit to Moshannon Valley Processing Center on June 17. Lee and Deluzio also went to the facility unannounced on May 28, and spoke to pregnant women who said they were receiving poor medical care.

“These failures are not accidental; they are the predictable result of a privatized, for-profit detention business model,” Dean, Deluzio, and Lee wrote in their letter to GEO Group.

Local activists have implored commissioners to take on more oversight at the facility. The intergovernmental agreement allows commissioners to enter the facility with 24-hour notice, but the officials have been denied access in the past, raising concerns about how much oversight they actually have.

“I think we all need to just be very honest that this ‘so-called’ oversight doesn’t prevent abuse,” Rivera said.

“We are the lowest common denominator,” Commissioner Tim Winters said during the July 14 meeting. “We cannot open or close this facility. We have a minor say and a minor oversight.”

At the July 28 commissioners meeting, Winters said there have been no updates to ICE’s and GEO Group’s contract with the county, but that it’s “in process.” Commissioners noted that this is in line with the time frame of the 2021 contract.

“If they offer a contract, we’ll certainly look at it. I’ve already said I’m going to vote no on it,” Glass said during the July 14 meeting.

title: Kozak Says Lawsuit Against Him Looks Like CheckGate Backlash | Cowboy State Daily
description:
The plaintiffs through their attorney Drake Hill filed a Thursday motion asking Laramie County District Court Judge Robin Cooley to hold Kozak in contempt of court.
Cowboy State Daily asked Kozak to extend the outlet’s interview invitation to the anonymous members.
“Cindy Hill and Kevin Lewis will discuss the recently filed lawsuit against Sheriff Brian Kozak,” the email says.
Connections Kozak noted correctly that Drake Hill and Lewis are both linked with Honor Wyoming.
Lewis was a lead staffer under Superintendent Hill, and Lewis and Drake Hill together operate Fidelity Registered Agents LLC.
text:
Laramie County’s sheriff says the public records lawsuit two Freedom Caucus-aligned Cheyenne residents have filed against him is at least partly a political maneuver – and that his investigation of the February “CheckGate” controversy has “stirred the hornets’ nest.”

Colorado-based firm Lichter Immigration and its investigator Kevin Lewis filed a civil complaint against Laramie County Sheriff Brian Kozak and his office June 30.

The lawsuit accuses Kozak’s office of wrongly withholding body camera video and information that a Mexican national, Mario Fabian Valenzuela Robles, needed for his ongoing immigration case.

The plaintiffs through their attorney Drake Hill filed a Thursday motion asking Laramie County District Court Judge Robin Cooley to hold Kozak in contempt of court. They allege Kozak’s office hasn’t obeyed Cooley’s order to turn over documents pertaining to Robles.

“The situation presented here creates the potential for the sheriff to face serious legal consequences, including contempt of court charges, as in this motion, fines, or removal from office,” the filing says.

Kozak bristled at the filing and cast the case’s motivation as dubious.

He told Cowboy State Daily on Friday his office has turned over the body camera video, which he indicated was initially withheld to ensure it could be released according to the narrow provisions allowed in public records law.

As for other documents, Kozak said his counsel, Laramie County Attorney Mark Voss, had already conferred with the plaintiffs and worked out a time extension, since the search terms the plaintiffs requested returned around 7,700 generally irrelevant emails.

The documents were originally due Aug. 5, court documents say.

“It’s confusing to us why this contempt motion was filed when there was an agreement we could go beyond the deadline date, when the search criteria was so large,” Kozak said Friday.

Kozak took a stronger stance in a Saturday email.

“It is clear to me that the motive behind the motion and original court filing was, at least in part, to discredit the Sheriff’s Office for political reasons,” he wrote, adding that he hopes Cooley will “take appropriate action” if the plaintiffs’ filings were “misleading or unethical.”

“If the Court does not impose sanctions against the plaintiffs, I will consider filing a complaint with the Wyoming State Bar,” he added.

Cooley has set a hearing for Oct. 16.

In response to Kozak's statements, Lewis said the sheriff is shifting blame.

"Rather than trying to blame others, he should focus on doing his work and complying with the Court’s order," said Lewis in a Monday email.

The Presentation

Kozak said several members of the Laramie County Conservative Coalition warned him that would happen, and they gave him a copy of an email notice of a meeting Wyoming Freedom Caucus member Rep. Ann Lucas, R-Cheyenne, dispatched.

Cowboy State Daily asked Kozak to extend the outlet’s interview invitation to the anonymous members. They declined, he said.

The email in question, which Kozak sent to Cowboy State Daily, shows a July 9 letter from Lucas previewing “a very interesting program for this coming Sunday” for the Laramie County Conservative Coalition.

“Cindy Hill and Kevin Lewis will discuss the recently filed lawsuit against Sheriff Brian Kozak,” the email says. The email also recounts details of the case from Cowboy State Daily’s reporting.

Cindy Hill is Drake Hill’s wife. She’s also the former state superintendent of public instruction, whom the Legislature tried, unconstitutionally, to remove from office, and who waged an unsuccessful defamation case against former legislator Tim Stubson.

“These allegations point to issues regarding civil rights,” says the email. “This subject is guaranteed to stimulate conversation. Don’t miss it.”

Cindy Hill did not respond by publication to a Monday-morning request for comment.

Kozak pointed to his decision to launch an investigation into “CheckGate.”

That was the Feb. 9 incident in which Teton County activist Rebecca Bextel, who’s now the Constitution Party nominee in the governor’s race, handed out campaign checks to Freedom Caucus members on the floor of the state House of Representatives – two days before they were set to vote on a bill she’d championed.

Multiple legislators and the entire Wyoming Senate condemned the act, but the House of Representatives cleared its involved members of bribery and misconduct after an in-house investigation.

Kozak said his criminal investigation into the matter is still ongoing.

“The Sheriff’s Office’s recent search warrants in the CheckGate investigation have clearly stirred the hornets’ nest,” he said in his email. “There also appears to be a connection between Lewis and Hill through their involvement with Honor Wyoming and the Freedom Caucus, some members of which are reportedly subjects of the Checkgate investigation.”

Kozak added, “It is unfortunate to see this type of political activity in Wyoming, especially when I am upholding conservative principals (sic).”

“However,” the sheriff continued, “it will not discourage me from doing my job. I will gladly take the criticism and political pressure if it allows my deputies to perform their duties without political influence.”

Lucas in a Monday text message to Cowboy State Daily countered.

She wasn’t involved in CheckGate in any capacity and doesn’t see a connection between that investigation and “an education community meeting about immigration law and the Constitution.”

“Calling this political isn’t accurate,” added Lucas.

She said at the July 12 meeting in question Lewis walked meeting attendees through the case and the surrounding legal issues. Lucas also said she’s not involved in the legal case and attended the talk only for the education.

Here Kozak volleyed back.

“Have you ever heard of a (litigant) doing that before – a public meeting on a case they’re representing an immigrant on?” asked the sheriff. “Seems a little weird.”

Lucas had said in her text that the group has invited Kozak to speak and he’s done so twice. He said he’s never gone to one of their events and never been invited.

‘That’s A Lie’

Lewis said in a Friday phone interview that the sheriff’s office did not secure an extension for handing over documents.

“That’s a lie, right,” said Lewis. “And Kozak’s counsel set the due date for compliance … So there’s no extension. No request for extension. No communication about extension.”

Lewis emphasized that a judge’s order should be taken seriously and said that Kozak has “simply ignored the deadline of the court order.”

As of Friday, Lewis said, plaintiffs were still waiting on documents from the sheriff’s office.

Cowboy State Daily asked if this case has political implications.

“I’m not commenting about politics. I’m working for an attorney in Colorado,” said Lewis, before promptly saying he had to leave the call.

Lewis expounded in a Monday email.

"We had to sue (Kozak) for evidence and he waited until the day of an emergency hearing to provide only partial evidence," said Lewis. "Then we had to bring a motion for his contempt of the Court Order, and then he did not provide a complete response to what the Court has ordered." Lewis asserted that as of Monday, Kozak has not complied with the order.

"The Sheriff’s excuses are ridiculous. He was sued for not doing what he was clearly required to do under the law. Now he has violated the Court’s Order, purely and simply," he said, adding that Kozak "invents motives."

Drake Hill, whom Cowboy State Daily emailed Friday and Monday, had referred the outlet to Lewis for comment.

Connections

Kozak noted correctly that Drake Hill and Lewis are both linked with Honor Wyoming.

Bextel is too.

The 2026 business filing for Honor Wyoming lists three directors: Carol Armstrong, Thomas James Anderson, and Blair Maus. They all list their addresses as the same location on Columbia Drive in Cheyenne – which Laramie County mapping records in turn list as Lewis’s property.

Drake Hill represented the group at a November meeting of the Wyoming Legislature’s Management Council.

Lewis was a lead staffer under Superintendent Hill, and Lewis and Drake Hill together operate Fidelity Registered Agents LLC.

Bextel has worked as an organizer for Honor Wyoming, and in a 2024 Facebook post called herself an “active volunteer” for the group.

Bextel did not respond to a Monday-morning text message request for comment by publication.

‘In That Direction’

Lewis was an unpaid lobbyist for Honor Wyoming during the 2024 legislative session and registered with the Secretary of State’s Office for it. Lewis told Cowboy State Daily in 2024 that, given his past political activities, it shouldn’t come as a surprise to anyone that he’s involved with the group.

“Everybody knows I lean in that direction,” he said with a laugh.

Honor Wyoming appears to equate Freedom Caucus-style policymaking with integrity. Its website contains a “Wyoming political integrity index” that it says is based on constitutional rights and major party platforms.

Borrowing cowboy-style verbiage, the site ranks all known Freedom Caucus members as “top hand” on the integrity index, including the three known Freedom Caucus members who received checks on the House floor Feb. 9.

Those were Republican Reps. Darin McCann (Rock Springs), Joe Webb (Lyman), and Christopher Knapp (Gillette).

The fourth check recipient, Rep. Marlene Brady, R-Green River, is at least aligned with the Freedom Caucus. Honor Wyoming also calls her a “top hand.”

House Speaker and Freedom Caucus member Chip Neiman has in past interviews rebutted implications of bribery – by noting that the delegates who received checks had already voted in favor in 2025 of a measure similar to the one embroiled in this case.

“You don’t have to pay me to do the right thing,” said Neiman, who did not receive a campaign donation on the floor, but was handed one in his office.

According to state and federal campaign finance filings, Drake Hill has given campaign donations to Freedom Caucus member and former Rep. Ben Hornok, and to Secretary of State Chuck Gray, who is an early founder of the Freedom Caucus.

Lewis has given campaign donations to Lucas and to Gray, Wyoming campaign finance filings show.

The County Attorney Says...

Voss on Friday filed a verified report explaining to the court the steps the county has reportedly taken to answer Lewis’ and Lichter’s requests for documents, and saying that all relevant documents have been handed over.

“As counsel for the Defendants writes this verified report,” wrote Voss on behalf of the sheriff’s department, “the County has received yet another pleading from the Plaintiffs indicating a desire, again, that the Sheriff be held in contempt, presumably for not supplying some form of instant gratification in regard to their records requests.”

“As Plaintiffs have clearly set the tone for this interaction,” Voss continued, “counsel for the Defendants is more than willing to participate at their level.”

A first search of the agreed-upon search terms yielded the 7,700 largely irrelevant results in the countywide email system, says the report.

Some of the hits, for example, involved an unrelated divorce case involving a different attorney surnamed “Hill,” wrote Voss.

In the second and third attempts, the IT team used a different configuration of search terms that produced 1,107 hits, says the report. The IT department ground down further and produced around 200 emails, which the County Attorney’s Office must review for privileged material, the report adds.

Voss wrote that the sheriff’s office’s interaction with Robles, the immigrant Lewis is reportedly helping, was minimal and “entirely anodyne.” It was a traffic stop resulting in a handoff to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, he wrote.

A deputy involved filed his report days after the encounter and at first conflated two similar traffic stops, wrote Voss.

Lewis and Lichter had initially related alleged statements by the Cheyenne Police Department that the initial report was a “complete fabrication.”

Voss’s filing says the plaintiffs’ characterization of the report as false is in itself, “knowingly false and goes beyond hyperbole or invective.”

The report says Voss’s office is giving Hill all the shareable emails in the narrowed search, but had significant concerns about plaintiffs’ request for “all of the detentions associated with (ICE)” from April, due to the potential those might fall under privileged criminal history information.

Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senators Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), along with Representatives Chrissy Houlahan (D-Pa.), Maggie Goodlander (D-N.H.), Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), and Lizzie Fletcher (D-Texas) led a bicameral letter pressing the Department of Defense (DoD), the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Veterans Affairs (VA), U.S. Customs and Border Protection, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on their efforts to coordinate to arrest, and detain, and deport hundreds of veterans and military families.In April 2025, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) rescinded its long-standing policy that treated military service a “significant mitigating factor” when deciding whether to pursue immigration enforcement, and replaced it with a new policy stating that military service alone “does not automatically exempt” non-citizens from enforcement actions.

In September 2025, Senator Warren opened an investigation into the impacts of these policy changes on military families. The investigation revealed that ICE has attempted to deport 282 veterans and their relatives. But DHS refused to disclose the number of active-duty troops and their families who have been threatened by the administration’s policy.

But new reports indicate that DoDand DHS appear to be coordinating to convert military bases into “traps” for individuals this administration deems deportable and has detained non-citizens during routine check-ins, visits, and drop-offs at or near military installations. At the same time, DoD has continued to recruit new service members with the promise of immigration protections.

Recent reporting by the Associated Press reveals that, since January 2025, more than 50 parents and spouses of active-duty service members have been detained, and at least six have been deported. ICE’s statistics show that the agency has arrested 16 non-citizen armed forces members since the beginning of Fiscal Year 2026. Some service members have reportedly needed to take leave or delay deployment because ICE detained their families.

“These efforts imperil military readiness, weaken service members’ morale, and betray America’s promises to the people who put their lives on the line for our nation,” wrote the lawmakers. Alarmingly, DoD has been reportedly targeting individuals at military installations, detaining them on military property, and turning them over to ICE — effectively converting military bases into “traps” for noncitizens. For example, a 22-year-old military wife was recently detained while attempting to obtain a military spouse I.D. Military officials allegedly called DHS and held her in a room until ICE agents arrived to take her to a detention center.

“DoD’s participation in civil immigration enforcement activities raises both ethical and legal concerns, including potential violations of the Posse Comitatus Act, which prohibits using the armed forces of the military for civilian law enforcement,” wrote the lawmakers.

The coalition warned that if service members were to be swept up in any of these enforcement actions, it could separately constitute a violation of the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which provides protections to all members of the United States military on active duty, including non-citizens, from civil actions—such as immigration proceedings—that interfere with their military duties.

“Service members must have confidence that their sacrifices will be honored, not used against them or to target their loved ones,” wrote the lawmakers. “DoD’s new anti-immigrant practices risk deterring future recruits and damaging the credibility of military recruitment efforts—which promised to care for service members even after their time in uniform.”

The lawmakers requested that the agencies explain the enhanced coordination between DoD and DHS, restore long-standing immigration protections for family members of service members, and explain what steps they are taking to protect troops, veterans, and their families from unjust immigration enforcement by August 23, 2026.

The letter was signed by Senators Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Ed Markey (D-Mass.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Brian Schatz (D-HI), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.), Peter Welch (D-Vt.), and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.).

Representatives Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.), Nanette Barragán (D-Calif.), André Carson (D-Ind.), Greg Casar (D-Texas), Sean Casten (D-Ill.), Joaquin Castro (D-Texas), Gil Cisneros (D-Calif.), Bonnie Watson Coleman (D-N.J.), Daniel Davis (D-Ill.), Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.), Diana DeGette (D-Colo.), Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.), Maxine Dexter (D-Ore.), Veronica Escobar (D-Texas), Bill Foster (D-Ill.), Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.), Chuy García (D-Ill.), Sylvia Garcia (D-Texas), Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.), Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.), Hank Johnson (D-Ga.), Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), John Larson (D-Conn.), Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.), Seth Magaziner (D-R.I.), Seth Moulton (D-Mass.), Kevin Mullin (D-Calif.), Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), Mike Quigley (D-Ill.), Jan Schakowsky (D-Ill.), Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.), Marilyn Strickland (D-Wash.), Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Mark Takano (D-Calif.), Dina Titus (D-Nev.), Marc Veasey (D-Texas), Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), joined in signing the letter.

The letter was endorsed by the Immigration Defenders Law Center, the Seattle Clemency Project, Common Defense, Repatriate Our Patriots, and League of United Latin American Citizens.

“It is hard to imagine a more profound betrayal than targeting service members, veterans, and military families for deportation,” said Jennie Pasquarella, interim executive director of the Seattle Clemency Project. “This administration is abandoning decades of bipartisan policies that recognized a simple truth: protecting those who serve makes our military stronger and our nation safer. Targeting the very communities that have sacrificed for this country is not just morally indefensible, it is a direct attack on military readiness, recruitment, and trust.”

“This administration has made a conscious decision to abandon its promises to military families and fail those who put their lives on the line for our nation,” said Amanda Schuft, director of legal services at Immigrant Defenders Law Center. “We have seen the devastating human cost firsthand. Our client, the father of an active-duty Army service member, was detained by ICE despite suffering from terminal renal failure, forcing his son to take leave from military service to plead for his release and provide evidence of his grave medical condition. The government ignored those pleas. After his health deteriorated in detention, our client was eventually released, only to die within weeks.”

“Family readiness directly impacts mission readiness. Behind every military spouse or parent in detention is a servicemember who could deploy at any moment. Without a strong homefront, we cannot have a ready force. Our government must honor its commitments to those who serve,” said Danitza G. James, MSW, President, Repatriate Our Patriots.

text:
The US State Department has revoked more than 175,000 visas from foreign nationals under President Donald Trump, as it continues a sweeping immigration crackdown that has stripped travel and immigration privileges from tens of thousands more people.

Most of the visa revocations stemmed from law-enforcement encounters involving criminal activity, alongside visa violations, fraud, calls for violence and other threats to national security, according to a fact sheet released by the department on Monday.

The extent of the revocations reflects the broad immigration crackdown initiated when Trump returned to the White House last year, deporting an unprecedented number of migrants including some who held valid visas.

“The revocations come as a result of the State Department’s continuous vetting operations, which ensure that visa recipients abide by the terms of their visa and do not endanger Americans,” the department said.

Assault, driving under the influence, theft and drug offences were among the leading reasons for the cancellations.

Specific cases cited by the department included a person charged with felony rape and sexual battery, another charged with kidnapping and human trafficking, and a person facing more than a dozen counts of possessing child sexual abuse material.

A US embassy in North Africa revoked more than 100 visas from “birth tourist” parents who allegedly came to the United States primarily to give birth so their children would receive US citizenship, it said.

Some of the revocations involved “foreign nationals who celebrated the assassination of Charlie Kirk, including one who stated ‘when fascists die, democrats don’t complain’ and another who said he ‘died too late’,” the statement said. Kirk was a popular conservative activist who was assassinated last year.

The department said the Trump administration would continue identifying and investigating foreign nationals who it believes threaten US safety or national security.

“A US visa is a privilege, not a right,” the State Department said, adding that it would continue using available authorities to revoke visas from people who abuse that privilege.

In January, the department said it had revoked more than 100,000 visas, a record at the time.

The administration has also adopted a stricter policy on granting visas, with tightened social media vetting and expanded screening.

Rights advocates and human rights experts have condemned the Trump administration’s social media screening efforts, which they say threaten free speech and are akin to surveillance and singling out of immigrants.

The ATRC is a specialized federal court created in 1996 to hear deportation proceedings against noncitizens suspected of terrorism in which the government wants to use undisclosed classified evidence. Court rules do not allow challenges to the evidence even if unlawfully obtained. Government lawyers allege that Zada pledged loyalty to the Islamic State (also known as ISIS) but have not charged her with any crime. She ultimately could be deported on the basis of a preponderance of evidence that she was an “alien terrorist.” Her lawyers have stated that only a summary of the evidence against her has been made available to them. US courts have repeatedly found that using secret evidence in deportation proceedings violates due process.

Zada is at risk of being returned to Afghanistan even though it is not a safe country for any forced returns. The United Nations high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has cautioned against involuntary returns to Afghanistan absent individualized risk assessments because of arbitrary arrests, detention, torture, and other ill-treatment. While all women in Afghanistan face gender persecution, a woman labeled as an ISIS sympathizer and returned to the Taliban, which consider ISIS an enemy, faces additional danger.

text:
Survey findings released on Monday show over 3,000 educators in Minnesota said they were directly or indirectly impacted by Operation Metro Surge, according to the union Education Minnesota.

The assessment, conducted by Voss Research and Strategy, asked 4,460 members of the union about their experiences during the operation, which involved an influx of agents from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security Investigations and Border Patrol in the state between December 2025 and early 2026.

The union said 72% of the educators (3,211) who took the survey reported being affected by the surge, 68% reported students absent from class, 67% saw increased fear or anxiety among students and 37% said staff members were fearful or unable to come to work.

"You cannot teach children who are terrified," Monica Byron, president of Education Minnesota, said in response to the survey. "You cannot reach students who are absent."

Byron added that it's too soon to predict the impacts of the raid on test scores, but that research "consistently shows that chronic absenteeism, elevated anxiety, and disrupted learning time are strong predictors of lower academic performance."
